noticias.titulo: Australia sanctions suspects in Iran-linked anti-Semitic attacks
noticias.resumen: Sanctions aim to restrict funds for two men alleged to have planned attacks for IRGC.
noticias.texto:
Australia sanctions suspects in Iran-linked anti-Semitic attacks
Sanctions aim to restrict funds for two men alleged to have planned attacks for IRGC.
Australia has imposed sanctions on two men accused of orchestrating anti-Semitic arson attacks on behalf of Iran.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said in a statement on Friday that the “counterterrorism financing sanctions” targeted Zohair Hassib and Kazem Hamad.
The pair is alleged to have used a “complex chain of proxies” to attack a kosher restaurant in Sydney and the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne in 2024 at the behest of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Wong said the sanctions would restrict the pair’s access to funds that could be used to carry out attacks, by making it a criminal offence to make assets available to them.
“These sanctions are an important step in disrupting the IRGC’s ability to conduct attacks against Australians and Australian interests,” she said.
In the aftermath of the 2024 attacks, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the launch of a police task force on anti-Semitism.
In August 2025, Australia accused Iran of orchestrating the fires, a charge that Tehran denied. The Iranian ambassador was ordered to leave the country, while Canberra suspended operations at its Tehran embassy and ‌listed the IRGC as a “terrorist” organisation.
The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation said in its annual threat assessment in June it was investigating alleged Iran-linked agents, sharing details of their activities but withholding their names.
Spy chief Mike Burgess described them as an Australian who was “a senior agent of the IRGC Quds Force running its networks around the world,” and an Australian crime figure recruited by Iran through a web of Iraqi-based militia groups who had been arrested in Iraq in January.
“Knowing full well they were being directed ‌by ‌the Iranian regime, these individuals orchestrated two attacks on buildings associated with Jewish Australians,” Burgess said.
Friday’s statement named the men for the first time.
The sanctions listing shows Hassib was born in Australia and is a citizen of Australia and Afghanistan, and is now living in Iran.
Hamad, alleged to be behind an illicit tobacco ring in Australia, was arrested in Iraq after a joint investigation by police from both countries.

noticias.titulo: Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
noticias.resumen: The US FCC authorised the plan on Wednesday, calling it a first in the history of the country.
noticias.texto:
Why does Elon Musk want to put a million satellite data centres in space?
The US FCC authorised the plan on Wednesday, calling it a first in the history of the country.
SpaceX founder and billionaire Elon Musk’s plan to launch a million satellites was approved this week by the United States, as controversy over data centres needed to drive the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution leads to a scramble for alternative locations.
On Wednesday, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) authorised the plan, named “Starmind”, and said it marks a first in the history of the country.
“At this pivotal time in America’s development of super intelligence [artificial intelligence], the FCC is granting SpaceX authorisation to deploy 1,000,000 orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the FCC said in a statement posted on X by Chairman Brendan Carr.
Carr said under President Donald Trump’s leadership, the US was “moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers benefits for the American people”.
“This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership and expand prosperity here at home,” he said.
Here’s everything we know about the plan to send a million satellites to space:
What is Musk’s plan?
With data centres being the crucial backbone behind AI computing, and with demand for the software rapidly growing, Musk’s plan provides an alternative: Using the sun as a power source for them.
According to SpaceX, which manufactures rockets and spacecraft, the new project works by using “satellites with localised AI compute, where the results are beamed back from [a] low-latency, sun-synchronous orbit”.
This, SpaceX claims, is “the fastest way to scale given the growing difficulty of finding electrical power sources on Earth”.
On its website, SpaceX calls the plan “low-cost [and] high performance”.
But Musk’s company already has satellites in space, with Starmind only expected to add to the constellation.
According to SatFleet Live, which tracks satellites in real time, there are 16,928 active satellites in orbit now. Of that, 11,190 (66 percent) are SpaceX Starlink satellites, the company’s internet outfit.
Under the FCC’s licence, SpaceX must begin its deployment of the satellite data centres no later than November 2033; send 10 percent of the maximum number, 100,000, no later than November 2035 in the same month; deploy 50 percent to space by November 2038 and the whole constellation by 2040.
Why does Musk want to send them up, and what’s the advantage?
As AI scales up rapidly, the need for data centres grows.
But data centres need vast tracts of land, and guzzle water and power, while churning out tonnes of fossil fuel emissions. They generate intense heat, and cooling systems need large amounts of water to keep the technology running, putting pressure on water supplies and communities facing drought, especially as climate change raises global temperatures.
According to an article published by the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a US nonprofit, in 2025, “large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day, equivalent to the water use of a town populated by 10,000 to 50,000 people.”
These concerns have set off mass protests against data centres, from the US to Kenya to India. Widespread opposition to data centres was a key issue for many voters in the US midterm elections earlier this month, per polling data.
In July, demonstrators against the rapid expansion of data centres held 142 protests across 42 states in a nationwide effort against AI infrastructure expansion.
Satellite-based data centres face no similar land constraints, and they can, in theory, use solar power – as SpaceX says is the plan – to fuel their processing. But cooling in space remains a challenge: Unlike on Earth, there is no air or water, so heat released can’t escape via conduction or convection.
Has there been pushback to the plan?
Yes.
Astronomers and environmentalists have criticised the plan, saying it will amplify sky pollution that makes it harder to see the night sky.
On Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said in a statement that it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s approval of the plan.
“As the AAS stated in its earlier filings to the FCC, the proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the statement read.
“The AAS is gravely concerned about the future of federally funded astronomical research under such a fundamentally altered night sky, and the resulting waste of taxpayer dollars invested in astronomical facilities throughout the country and the world,” it said. “While we hope that SpaceX will continue to coordinate with the National Science Foundation, we remain concerned by the lack of formal coordination requirements in the license granted to SpaceX in this case.”

noticias.titulo: ‘I cannot go to work’: Iranians contend with pollution as well as US war
noticias.resumen: Hospital admissions for respiratory ailments have soared as the winter smog sets in.
noticias.texto:
‘I cannot go to work’: Iranians contend with pollution as well as US war
Hospital admissions for respiratory ailments have soared as the winter smog sets in.
Tehran, Iran – The headaches, shortness of breath and blurred vision which Ghoral, 40, a Tehran resident, once only experienced during the heavily polluted, cold seasons of the year have become year-round symptoms.
“The nausea hit me even before the Meteorological Organization announces that the air is polluted,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“On heavily polluted days, I try to leave the house as little as possible, which means I sometimes cannot go to work, affecting my income. At the same time, air pollution increases the cost of seeing a doctor and buying the medication I need to manage my breathing problems. All of this is happening simply because I have no choice but to live in a polluted city.”
The threat of American bombs is not the only danger the residents of Iran’s capital city must contend with these days: checking the air quality has become part of everyone’s daily routine.
Weather apps are no longer used primarily to check the forecast for rain or thunderstorms, but rather to view the latest readings on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) – the tiny, airborne particles which can be deadly when breathed in over a prolonged period.
Hossein, 36, a resident of the capital, tells Al Jazeera: “For someone like me, who both lives and works in the city centre, air pollution is no longer just a part of life; it has become life itself.”
There is little anyone can do about it except escape the city as often as possible, particularly during the winter months when pollution is at its worst.
“At the very least, I try to spend my weekends in nearby cities where the air quality is better,” Hossein says.
Remote work and traffic restrictions
The second half of the year in Iran has traditionally been a time of what is known as “temperature inversion”. This occurs when a layer of warm air traps cooler air and pollutants close to the ground, preventing them from dispersing.
While pollution has become a year-round problem, it is particularly bad in the winter, when this phenomenon is common, bringing prolonged periods of polluted air to cities and industrial areas.
Other major Iranian cities, including Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Ahvaz, are also grappling with air pollution.
For more than half of the autumn and winter months, air pollution warnings are regular, advising people with heart and respiratory conditions to take precautions. Children, older people and pregnant women are also advised to stay indoors and avoid outdoor activities.
In Iran, the Meteorological Organization uses a “yellow weather warning” to signal days on which air pollution levels are particularly high. On those days, schools typically cancel outdoor physical education classes.
When pollution levels approach the threshold for an “orange weather warning” – generally associated with an air quality index (on a scale of 0-500) above 140 – additional restrictions may follow. Some employees switch to remote work, traffic restrictions under the odd-even licence plate scheme are imposed to reduce the number of cars on the streets, schools are closed and some university classes move online.
Hospital admissions surge
Dr Hadi Yazdani, who works at a medical centre in Isfahan, tells Al Jazeera: “One of the first signs of rising air pollution is an increase in hospital visits by patients with chronic asthma and other respiratory conditions.”
According to figures from the Ministry of Health, hospital visits for these conditions, as well as for heart conditions, rise by as much as 50 percent in the winter. Eye and skin problems also tend to become more common as a result of air pollution.
“Children and older people are particularly vulnerable,” says Yazdani. “They may develop new illnesses or experience a worsening of existing conditions. In addition, because air pollution reduces the circulation of fresh air, respiratory infections such as influenza and COVID also become more prevalent.”
Evidence that hospitals across Iran experience a surge in emergency department visits as a result of air pollution has prompted the country’s Emergency Medical Services Organization to adopt different plans for managing patient demand during the colder months.
As pollution levels worsen, specially equipped buses are deployed in public squares in some of Iran’s major cities. They provide basic treatment for less severe pollution-related conditions, such as shortness of breath and chest pain. The buses are intended both to reduce the need for ambulances to travel across congested cities and to serve as the first point of contact for people seeking medical assistance.
This year, amid concerns that a renewed war with the United States could force schools to close again anyway, the Ministry of Education has also decided to delegate decisions about school closures due to air pollution to local education authorities.
Few remedies
Although air pollution in Iran is caused by both natural events, such as dust storms, as well as industrial and human-made sources, Iran’s Department of Environment has focused its efforts on tackling pollution caused by human activity.
Ahmad Taheri, head of the National Center for Air and Climate Change at the Department of Environment, tells Al Jazeera: “Alongside efforts to improve the standards of petrol and diesel used by vehicles, we are putting pressure on car manufacturers to produce vehicles that meet higher standards. We are also working to reduce gas flaring at refineries, which contributes both to air pollution and global warming.”
However, the efforts of Iran’s environmental authorities have done little to reassure the public about the country’s air pollution problem.
Every year, as concentrations of air pollutants rise and public health concerns mount, advertisements for vitamins and fresh food products marketed as protective against the effects of air pollution have become increasingly common.
But Yazdani says there is little substantial research demonstrating that vitamins can reduce the health effects of air pollution. He notes that people tend to experience more mood-related problems on polluted days and believes that advertisers are capitalising on public anxiety about the impact of air pollution on health.
The World Health Organization estimates that 99 percent of the world’s population lives in places where air quality falls below the levels it recommends. Knowing this, however, does little to ease people’s concerns about the toll that air pollution is taking on their physical and mental health and Iranians are turning to anything they can find that might help.

noticias.titulo: Democrats want to end Trump’s Iran war. But how different are they?
noticias.resumen: Decades of bipartisan pressure on Tehran raises questions about how far Democrats are willing to change US policy.
noticias.texto:
Democrats want to end Trump’s Iran war. But how different are they?
Decades of bipartisan pressure on Tehran raise questions about how far they are willing to change US policy.
The Democrats’ thumping victory in the United States midterm elections this month came amid widespread public opposition to the US-Israel war on Iran, which has sent energy prices soaring across the country and globally.
Democratic Party leaders, including those regarded as traditionally more hawkish on Iran, have called for an immediate end to the nine-month war.
“We have to work and move aggressively to end the reckless and costly war of choice in Iran right out of the gate,” presumptive incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries said last week, when asked about his priorities come January.
A day after the Democrats’ decisive victory, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who opposed the landmark 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran, said Americans did not know “what the heck we’re fighting for in Iran”.
But the Democrats’ electoral triumph has been met with scepticism in Tehran. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has warned that anyone expecting the election outcome to change Washington’s policy towards Iran is “seriously mistaken”.
While Democratic opposition to the war has drawn a distinction between the party and Trump, analysts are sceptical about whether it reflects a fundamentally different approach towards Iran – a country that successive US administrations, Democrat and Republican, have sought to isolate diplomatically and economically.
Decades of bipartisan hostility
For much of the period since the 1979 Islamic revolution, hostility towards Iran has superseded partisanship in Washington.
It was under Democratic President Jimmy Carter that the US began imposing sanctions on Iran following the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, eight months after US-backed monarch Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi was overthrown in a popular uprising led by former Supreme Leader Ruhollah Khomeini.
Successive Republican administrations maintained pressure on Iran. But it was Democratic President Bill Clinton who substantially expanded its economic isolation through a policy of “dual containment”, targeting both Tehran and Iraq under its former president, the late Saddam Hussein.
In 1996, Clinton signed legislation imposing sanctions on foreign companies investing in Iran’s energy sector, a move that enjoyed overwhelming bipartisan support, with the bill passing 415–0 in the US House of Representatives.
Even when Washington and Tehran found common strategic interests, opportunities for rapprochement were short-lived.
Following the September 11, 2001, attacks, Iran cooperated with the US against its common foe – the Taliban in Afghanistan — helping end their first stint in power. Yet, just months later, Republican President George W Bush branded Iran part of an “axis of evil”, alongside Iraq and North Korea.
“Bush’s proclamation shocked both reformists in Tehran and those US military leaders who were collaborating with the Islamic Republic at the time,” Golnar Nikpour, a historian at Dartmouth College, told Al Jazeera.
For Maryam Jamshidi, associate professor of law at the University of Colorado Boulder, such hostility is rooted partly in Washington’s unwillingness to accept Iran’s independent regional influence — a legacy of the 1979 embassy takeover and Israel’s influence on US foreign policy.
“When it comes to Iran policy, there hasn’t been much variation between Republicans and Democrats,” Jamshidi told Al Jazeera. “Both parties have broadly viewed post-revolutionary Iran as an enemy to be constrained, marginalised, and suffocated.”
“Indeed, until Trump, the worst rounds of Iran sanctions came under Democratic presidencies, specifically Clinton and Obama,” she said.
In 2010, Obama intensified economic pressure on Tehran by signing into law the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability and Divestment Act, targeting foreign companies supplying Iran with refined petroleum products or helping expand its oil refining capabilities. The bill passed by an overwhelming majority of 408-8 in the House and 99-0 in the Senate.
But according to political analyst Negar Mortazavi, the continuity of economic pressure does not necessarily mean the two parties have pursued identical policies.
“It would be historically inaccurate to suggest that their approaches towards Iran have been essentially the same,” Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera.
The distinction, Mortazavi argued, is particularly evident in the contrast between Obama’s “diplomatic breakthrough” and Trump’s decision to wage war.
Obama’s pivot and Biden’s retreat
While the Obama administration helped impose sweeping international sanctions on Iran, it also challenged decades of US foreign policy by engaging directly with Tehran, culminating in the 2015 nuclear agreement.
Under the agreement signed in Vienna with six world powers and the European Union, Iran agreed to curb its uranium enrichment activities and pledged not to develop nuclear weapons. In return, the US loosened many of the sanctions against Iran and released some of Iran’s previously frozen funds.
“The JCPOA was much more than a nuclear agreement,” Mortazavi said, referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. “It represented the possibility of a fundamentally different relationship between Washington and Tehran, based on diplomacy rather than confrontation.”
During Obama’s second term, the US and Iran also tacitly cooperated in fighting a shared enemy in ISIL (ISIS), especially in Iraq.
However, that did not mean Obama’s diplomatic outreach to Iran was without pushback within his own party.
Among the Democrats who opposed the nuclear agreement was the staunchly pro-Israel Schumer, now one of the most prominent voices calling for an end to Trump’s war.
The subsequent presidency of Joe Biden, Obama’s vice president for eight years, further reduced any substantive difference between Democrats and Republicans in how they dealt with Iran.
Despite campaigning on a promise to restore the nuclear agreement after Trump’s withdrawal in 2018 during his first presidency, Biden failed to revive it, while retaining much of Trump’s “maximum pressure” tactics against Iran.
For Mortazavi, however, Biden’s failure to build on Obama’s diplomatic legacy demonstrates that ideological divisions exist within the Democratic Party rather than the absence of meaningful differences between Democrats and Republicans.
“Biden, by contrast, represented the more hawkish, traditional establishment wing of the Democratic Party,” she said.
“His broader Middle East policy was equally consequential. The Biden administration provided extensive military, financial and diplomatic support to Israel throughout its genocide in Gaza, continuing to supply weapons and shield Israel diplomatically despite the enormous civilian death toll and destruction.”
Nevertheless — unlike Trump — even Biden stopped short of launching an all-out war against Iran, Mortazavi noted.
The erosion of trust in Tehran
Iranian distrust of Washington predates the Islamic Republic, dating back to 1953, when the CIA supported the United Kingdom in engineering a coup and backing the once-deposed monarch, Pahlavi, back into power as shah.
Pahlavi remained a staunch ally of the US until his overthrow 26 years later, a rule defined by censorship, torture and wealth inequality.
More recently, for Iranian leaders, recognising any distinction between Democratic and Republican administrations has been complicated by the lack of any meaningful and long-lasting settlement, despite multiple attempts at negotiations.
“The Obama administration committed to meaningful sanctions relief but largely failed to deliver,” law professor Jamshidi said.
While Obama lifted nuclear-related sanctions on foreign companies dealing with Iran under the 2015 agreement, unlocking billions in frozen assets, he retained a broad trade embargo on the country.
Similar grievances emerged under Biden. In September 2023, Washington and Tehran reached a Qatar-mediated prisoner exchange agreement that allowed for the transfer of $6bn in frozen Iranian funds from South Korea to Qatar for humanitarian purchases.
However, access to the funds was subsequently blocked following the October 7 attacks on Israel. “Both Biden and Obama failed to follow through on their promises,” Jamshidi noted.
The consequences of these diplomatic failures between Tehran and Washington have also reshaped political debates within Iran itself, analysts say.
The 2015 agreement represented a political victory for Iranian officials who advocated engagement with Washington over those who maintained that the US could not be trusted.
But Trump’s withdrawal, Biden’s failure to revive the deal and the subsequent outbreak of war have strengthened the arguments of those who believe Washington ultimately seeks regime change, history professor Nikpour said.
Differences also persist amid the war within Iran’s political establishment over how to capitalise on the mounting domestic pressure on Trump to end the war.
“There remain pragmatists among Islamic Republic leaders who believe that ultimately, Iran’s military and political wins must lead to diplomatic and economic wins while Iran maintains any negotiating leverage, even if that includes some concessions,” Nikpour said.
“There are also more hawkish voices who believe that Iran should accept nothing less than total victory at the negotiating table.”
What comes next?
The Democrats’ election victory comes amid a broader debate within the party over Washington’s role in the Middle East, particularly its longstanding support for Israel and its reliance on military intervention to advance US interests in the region.
Mortazavi pointed to a growing progressive and antiwar wing challenging the party’s traditional foreign policy establishment. Some Democrats such as Darializa Chevalier and Adam Hamawy, recently elected to Congress, have explicitly called for a shift in the broader approach towards Iran.
However, unlike Obama in 2009, the Democrats will not have control of the White House, limiting their ability to pursue a fundamentally different foreign policy towards Iran.
Their immediate test, according to analysts like Mortazavi, will be whether they are willing to use their congressional power to challenge Trump’s continuation of the nine-month-old war.
“They have significant legislative tools, particularly the power to restrict war funding, investigate military operations and prevent further escalation,” Mortazavi said.
While Congress has the constitutional authority to control federal spending, legislative efforts to restrict the administration’s military operations could face a presidential veto, requiring support from Republican lawmakers to pass such measures that need a two-thirds majority.
However, questions remain over the political willingness of the Democratic establishment to confront Trump over Iran.
“Recent developments, like the selection of pro-Israel Congressman Jeffries as the Democratic nominee for House Speaker, strongly suggest Democrats won’t fulfil their campaign promise to end the war any time soon, if at all,” CU Boulder’s Jamshidi asserted.
Neither Jeffries nor Schumer, who is in the running to become majority leader in the Senate, has committed to how they will end the war.
Even if Democrats succeed in bringing the war to an end, their willingness to pivot away from the broader framework of economic sanctions, military pressure and economic isolation that often defines Washington’s relationship with Tehran remains to be seen.
For Iranian leaders, the experience of successive Democratic administrations suggests that an opening for diplomacy does not necessarily guarantee a lasting change in US policy.
“None of Iran’s various leadership factions believe that they should sit back and expect Democrats to change the course of US policy towards Iran,” Nikpour said, “though they likely internally understand that Democrats are at least in theory more likely than Republicans to be open to diplomatic solutions.”

noticias.titulo: South Korea sends rescued fishermen back to North
noticias.resumen: Pyongyang has not commented on a seventh fisherman who chose to remain in the South.
noticias.texto:
South Korea sends rescued fishermen back to North
Pyongyang has not commented on a seventh fisherman who chose to remain in the South.
South Korea has repatriated six of the seven North Korean fishermen it rescued from their drifting boat earlier this month.
The six fishermen crossed the maritime border between the rival states off the Korean Peninsula’s east coast on board their vessel early on Friday. They were met by a waiting North Korean ship.
On November 3, the South Korean military and coastguard authorities had rescued and towed the fishing boat after it drifted into international waters near the country’s Ulleung island.
South Korea has confirmed that the six men sent to the North had expressed a wish to return. A seventh fisherman chose to defect, according to the Unification Ministry.
Seoul added that it had notified Pyongyang of the plan through the multilateral United Nations Command, and also sent updates on Friday over an international maritime communications network.
North Korea has not commented on the fisherman who chose to remain, but the waiting vessel suggested that Pyongyang had received all communications.
North Korea severed direct communications with the South in 2024. Border tensions have escalated between the two this year.
South Korea considers North Koreans as its citizens and offers protection to defectors or repatriates those who wish to return.
Pyongyang usually takes defections seriously and has accused the South of enticing its citizens to the other side, a charge that Seoul denies.
Some 31,500 North Koreans were registered as living in the South by June, according to Unification Ministry data.

noticias.titulo: India upbeat about first Olympic Games after ‘very good’ 2036 presentation
noticias.resumen: India makes Ahmedabad pitch for 2036 Games as it bids to host first Olympics, but Qatar and South Africa strong rivals.
noticias.texto:
India upbeat about first Olympic Games after ‘very good’ 2036 presentation
India makes Ahmedabad pitch for 2036 Games as it bids to host first Olympics, but Qatar and South Africa strong rivals.
Indian officials said they were confident of advancing to the next phase of the race to stage the 2036 Olympic Games after presenting plans for Ahmedabad as the host city.
The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) delivered an online presentation to the International Olympic Committee’s Future Host Commission on Thursday, outlining its vision for staging the mega sporting event in the western city of Ahmedabad.
Ahmedabad, in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state of Gujarat, is already set to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games in a key test of its organisational credentials.
“It was a very, very good presentation that was made,” IOA chief executive Raghuram Iyer told reporters, saying discussions had been held at a “very macro level”.
India is one of seven countries pursuing the 2036 games, alongside Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea and Turkiye.
The Indian bid comes after internal disputes within the IOA.
Earlier this month, the IOC warned the association to resolve governance issues, while President P T Usha announced she would not seek re-election in December after alleging a “big fraud” in the nomination process.
Iyer said the bid was in a “continuous dialogue” phase with the IOC, with successful candidates expected to move into a strategic dialogue stage next year.
“We are in this continuous dialogue phase and if you are successful you move onto the stage of strategic dialogue, which will happen in March or April.”
He stressed that hosting an Olympic Games required backing from all levels of government.
“When a country is pitching for the Olympics, doing something so large, it requires the complete support and backing of the city, of the state, of the union.”
A final decision on the 2036 host is not expected until after the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, or in early 2029, he added.

noticias.titulo: Costa Rica denies entry to UN’s Albanese over ‘links to terrorist acts’
noticias.resumen: Authorities said the UN special rapporteur was blocked from entering the country due to 'national security' risks.
noticias.texto:
Costa Rica denies entry to UN’s Albanese over ‘links to terrorist acts’
Authorities said the UN special rapporteur was blocked from entering the country due to ‘national security’ risks.
Costa Rica has barred United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese from entering the country, citing “national security” concerns.
Albanese slammed her detention on Friday, branding it a “disgrace”. She was halted and held at Juan Santamaria International Airport the previous day, according to local authorities.
The director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, Omer Badilla, said in a video posted on social media that Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”. He did not specify which country put out the alert.
“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here, our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system,” Badilla said.
Albanese was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 and, like other independent experts, does not speak on behalf of the UN. She was travelling to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica in recognition of academic and human rights work.
She has faced harsh pushback from Israel and its allies, including the United States, over her advocacy for Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank and accusations that Israel has committed genocide and other war crimes.
Speaking while held at the airport, Albanese told local media that her detention was “a disgrace” and “appalling”.
“You see the face of the empire the day you touch a nerve or cross its boundaries,” she wrote on social media.
The US imposed sanctions on Albanese after she criticised Washington’s policy on Gaza.
Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez is a close ally of US President Donald Trump and has pursued closer trade ties with Israel since she took office in May.
Albanese told the student outlet Semanario Universidad that while she understood her name was on the US sanctions list, that did not explain why Costa Rica had detained her.
“We are not in the United States. We are in Costa Rica,” she stated. “Is Costa Rica a sovereign country?”
She noted that the only country she knew she could not enter was Israel, which had declared her “persona non grata” in 2024.
Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, praised Costa Rica on social media.
“Those who exploit their UN mandate to spread vile propaganda, legitimize terrorist organizations, desecrate the memory of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, and relentlessly vilify the US and Israel should face consequences,” he wrote.

noticias.titulo: ‘Will I get taller?’: Gaza’s children suffer stunting amid war, blockade
noticias.resumen: One in eight children is stunted. Many have bones that have not matured the way they should. Treatment is elusive.
noticias.texto:
‘Will I get taller?’: Gaza’s children suffer stunting amid war, blockade
One in eight children is stunted. Many have bones that have not matured the way they should. And treatment is hard to find – and harder to afford.
Khan Younis, Gaza – Every time seven-year-old Nabigha al-Zaqzouq stands beside children her age, she notices the difference in their heights and asks her mother, Alia: “Will I ever get taller?”
Nabigha is 99cm (3.2ft) tall and weighs just 10kg (22lb), making her appear several years younger than she actually is.
At home, the family’s dining table reflects part of her struggle. Bread and canned food are among the few options available, while meat, fruit and vegetables are beyond the family’s means. Alia tries to provide her daughter with a varied diet but struggles to afford food, as well as the medicines and medical tests needed to monitor her growth.
“We lived through extremely harsh days during the war, and after the ceasefire, we are living under a suffocating blockade. Let them allow medicines and treatments in,” she says. During medical visits, Alia has also started noticing other children with similar growth problems.
Five-year-old Tala Zidan faces a similar struggle. She is 94cm (3ft) tall, about 15-16cm shorter than the average for children her age.
Her father, Tahrir Zidan, says her height has remained almost unchanged over the past two years, while she has lost some weight. Since the family was displaced from Khuza’a to al-Mawasi amid Israel’s genocide, he has lost his job, making food a daily challenge. The family now relies on meals provided by charitable community kitchens.
“I have not been able to buy even one kilogramme (2.2lb) of meat, a chicken or a kilogramme of fruit,” he says. “The meal I get from the community kitchen is usually finished while most of us are still hungry.”
Tala and her brother Mohammed suffer from malnutrition and growth difficulties, as their family cannot afford a healthy diet. Their father fears the deprivation will have lasting consequences for their health.
A crisis beyond food shortages
The experiences of Nabigha and Tala reflect a wider challenge eating away at the future of Gaza’s children. The war has deprived families of adequate food and essential nutrients at a time when healthcare services have been severely disrupted, making access to diagnosis and treatment increasingly difficult.
A nutritional survey by UNICEF and its partners in accessible areas of the Gaza Strip between May 31 and June 15, 2026 found that 12.2 percent of children below five were stunted. Only 22.4 percent of children aged six to 23 months received a minimum acceptable diet.
Nutritionist Nada Abu al-Nada says the crisis concerns not only the quantity of food available, but also its quality and diversity. As purchasing power has declined and prices have risen, many families have reduced their consumption of meat, chicken, fish, eggs, milk, vegetables and fruit, relying increasingly on bread, rice and pasta.
Children need balanced diets containing proteins and essential nutrients, including iron, zinc and calcium, to support bone and muscle development. When they do not receive enough energy and nutrients, the body prioritises vital functions over growth. Prolonged deficiencies can slow height gain and affect muscles, tissues and bone formation.
“Before the war, average food availability was about 2,580 calories per person per day, while estimated average consumption has fallen to approximately 1,000 calories. This is not enough,” Abu al-Nada says.
She explains that the first 1,000 days from conception until a child turns two are particularly critical for development. However, older children are also vulnerable to prolonged deprivation. Diarrhoea, gastrointestinal illnesses and contaminated water can further reduce the body’s ability to absorb nutrients, worsening malnutrition.
Delayed growth and unavailable treatment
At Nasser Hospital, endocrinologist and diabetes specialist Hani Sayed Zuhair has noticed an increase in children seeking medical attention for growth problems. The number of cases during a single clinic session has risen from about 15 to 20 before the war to between 30 and 40 now, sometimes more.
He says the cases indicate an increase in growth disorders and stunting, particularly following periods of hunger and shortages of food, vitamins and medicines.
The consequences extend beyond nutritional deprivation to disrupted diagnosis and treatment, including hormonal therapies required by some children. The effects of malnutrition may not appear immediately but can emerge months or years later.
Zuhair cites cases of eight-year-old children whose bones are at the stage of development normally seen in those half their age, indicating a significant delay in skeletal maturation.
However, he stresses that short stature is not necessarily caused by malnutrition alone. It may also result from hormonal disorders or chronic illnesses, which can be exacerbated by nutritional deprivation, or from a combination of factors.
“We have noticed that many children suffering from malnutrition and short stature also have hormonal deficiencies, but in a number of these cases, the primary problem was nutritional deprivation,” he says.
Diagnosing delayed growth requires monitoring children’s height and weight against growth charts, alongside the necessary medical tests.
But access to diagnosis and treatment is increasingly difficult. Growth hormone stimulation tests are unavailable in Ministry of Health laboratories, while some private laboratories offer them only on a limited basis because of shortages of supplies. According to Zuhair, the tests cost between 350 ($106) and 400 shekels ($120).
Growth hormone injections cost between 80 ($24) and 120 shekels ($36) per dose, depending on availability. Children may require repeated injections according to their weight and prescribed treatment plans, placing an additional financial burden on families that have lost their sources of income.
The injections must also be stored at appropriate temperatures, with regular medical follow-up and adherence to prescribed doses – conditions that are difficult to maintain amid a war and blockade.
Consequences that may extend into the future
Abu al-Nada says a number of children may be able to catch up in their growth if their nutrition improves and intervention comes early enough. However, recovery depends on age, the duration and severity of deprivation, and other health factors. Regaining lost growth becomes more difficult once the bone growth plates close.
The risks extend beyond height. Protein and micronutrient deficiencies can reduce muscle mass, cause anaemia and weaken immunity, while also affecting concentration, learning and cognitive development. These consequences are compounded by psychological stress, sleep deprivation, recurrent illnesses and displacement.
Meanwhile, Alia al-Zaqzouq remains unable to answer her daughter’s question about when she might grow taller, while access to treatment is far from guaranteed. And Tahrir Zidan is still struggling to secure enough food for his children, let alone the balanced diet they need to grow.
“We are exhausted,” says Alia.

noticias.titulo: New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
noticias.resumen: Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
noticias.texto:
New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political wrangling is likely in the weeks ahead.
The results, released on Friday, showed that the ruling centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s conservative National Party has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority.
Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023, but National and its junior partners – the populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT – won just 65 seats between them. National secured 40 seats while ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.
The result reflects a loss of support for Luxon driven by a stagnant economy, and leaves the former businessman and his coalition partners to seek additional help to secure a majority.
“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term,” Luxon told a news conference on Friday.
Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats, leaving it far below the 66-seat threshold in the 130-member parliament.
The results appear to position Qiulae Wong’s centrist Opportunity Party, which clinched 7 seats, as kingmaker. However, talks with the conservative and populist incumbents are likely to prove tricky.
The former consultant has promised a universal basic income of up to NZ$370 (US$208) a week, greater action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, and healthcare reforms.
She has also campaigned for a kinder approach to politics. Wong has pledged to do “everything we can” to ensure a stable government.
Her style contrasts with that of potential suitors such as Winston Peters of New Zealand First. The controversial foreign minister has called opponents “morons” and drew shock earlier this year when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country”. His party promises to tighten immigration flows and withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord.
Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and has promised massive cuts to state spending.
Failure to meet an agreement could see Kiwis return to the polls next year.
Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters news agency a deal was likely, although it could be challenging.
“I don’t know exactly what kind of shape that will be yet, but it’ll be highly likely that there will be a right bloc formed and not a second election,” he said.

noticias.titulo: ‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
noticias.resumen: Prices are climbing again across Europe as energy costs surge.
noticias.texto:
‘Borrowing to make ends meet’: The rising cost of living in Europe
Prices are climbing again across Europe as energy costs surge.
As winter closes in, millions of people across Europe are bracing for another season of rising bills, tighter budgets and hard choices at home.
Inflation in the eurozone has climbed to its highest level in three years, as conflict in the Middle East disrupts oil and gas supplies and drives up energy prices, pushing up the cost of everything from heating to the weekly food shop.
Where are prices rising fastest?
In Athens, Giorgos*, a 40-year-old journalist and father of an 11-year-old, says his salary has risen from 800 euros ($878) to 1,100 euros ($1,208) a month over the past two years, but he has not felt the raise.
“Just as before, I’m still borrowing money just to make ends meet,” he said. Even a gyros souvlaki sandwich, long considered Greece’s “people’s food”, now costs more than 4 euros, he added.
His experience is shared across much of Europe, where prices are rising again after two years of relative calm. Inflation in the eurozone has doubled from 2 percent in December 2025 to 4 percent in October 2026, its highest level in three years.
Energy has been the biggest driver, with energy inflation rising to 21 percent in October, its highest level since December 2022, when it was 25.5 percent in the first winter after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Eurostat.
Energy prices have risen far faster than any other category and are pushing up the cost of transport, heating and food.
According to the European Central Bank (ECB) Lithuania (6.1 percent), Bulgaria (5.9 percent) and Greece (5.7 percent) now have the highest inflation rates in the eurozone, adding pressure on households already among the most stretched in the region.
Inflation in Cyprus jumped from 0.1 percent at the end of last year to 5.4 percent, and in Italy from 1.2 percent to 5.6 percent.
Prices have also accelerated quickly in Belgium, where inflation rose from 2.2 percent to 5.2 percent, and in France, where it rose from 0.7 percent to 3.7 percent.
A handful of countries have bucked the trend. Between December 2025 and October 2026, inflation has eased in Slovakia (from 4.1 percent to 2.9 percent), Estonia (3.6 percent), Latvia (3.1), Austria (3.5) and Malta (2.3), setting Lithuania apart from its Baltic neighbours.
The current rise is still well below the peak that followed the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, but for many families it is a second shock before they have fully recovered from the first.
How much more expensive has life become?
In North London, Emma*, 33, who works in corporate governance and lives alone, says the cost of food and bills keeps rising, with rent “the biggest killer”.
She has cancelled streaming subscriptions and switched to a cheaper brand of cat food for her pet cat after the one she always purchased started putting less in each can at a higher price.
She now sees her friends less, because nearly 10 pounds ($13) for a return Tube journey is “ridiculous”.
“I think this is detrimental to our mental health and has exacerbated the loneliness epidemic,” she said.
She’s not alone in feeling she has to make choices to survive. This squeeze is being felt across Europe.
According to Eurostat, a typical basket of goods and services such as food, housing, energy and transport now costs 69 percent more than it did in 2000, and around two-fifths of that increase has come in just the past four years.
The sharpest rise came in 2022, when prices jumped by more than 8 percent in a single year as energy costs soared after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The steepest increases have been in Central and Eastern Europe.
Prices in Hungary have more than tripled since 2000, meaning the goods and services that cost 100 euros ($115) in 2000 now cost about 335 Euros ($385), with a surge of 17 percent in 2023 alone. Estonia and Latvia are not far behind.
How difficult is it to find a job?
Finding work in Europe is far easier than it was a decade ago, but in many countries it has been getting harder again since 2022.
According to Eurostat, southern Europe has seen the biggest turnaround.
At the height of the eurozone debt crisis in 2013, unemployment reached 27.8 percent in Greece and 26.1 percent in Spain, meaning more than a quarter of people looking for work could not find a job.
Unemployment in both countries has fallen steadily since then as their economies recovered, to 8.9 percent in Greece and 10.5 percent in Spain in 2025, although Spain still has the highest rate in the EU.
The picture has shifted in northern Europe, where unemployment has risen since 2022 as economies slowed.
Unemployment in Finland has climbed to 9.7 percent in 2025, giving it the second-highest jobless rate in the bloc, ahead of Greece (8.9 percent) and Sweden (8.8 percent).
How much room do governments have to help?
When prices rise, people often look to their governments for financial support. But how much help a government can provide depends partly on how much debt it already carries.
The debt-to-GDP ratio compares a country’s total government debt with the value of everything its economy produces in a year. A ratio of 100 percent means the government owes as much as the economy produces in a year. The higher the ratio, the more money the government may have to spend on interest payments, leaving less available to help households.
Emma believes governments are spending in the wrong places. “Stop using taxpayer money to subsidise high energy bills while fossil fuel and grid companies continue making record profits,” she said, calling for windfall tax loopholes to be closed so those profits fund household relief directly.
According to data from International Monetary Fund (IMF), Italy and Greece carry the heaviest debts in Europe, each owing well over a year’s worth of economic output.
France, Ukraine, Belgium and the UK also owe more than their economies produce in a year.
At the other end of the scale, Estonia, Denmark and Luxembourg owe relatively little, giving them far more room to respond.
Several of the countries with the highest inflation, including Greece, Italy and Belgium, are also among the most indebted, leaving them with the least room to cushion the blow.
Education and healthcare: What governments are choosing to spend on.
In Belgium, Maya*, a university lecturer in her 50s, is searching for student housing for her daughter, who starts university next year.
“It used to be you could get a place, no problem, for 300 euros,” she said. “One of my neighbours just told me she paid 900 a month for her kid.”
She says more of her students now commute an hour or more to get to class, which she finds “undemocratic” because it shapes who can afford to live near campus.
In France, where student protests over overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages have grown into a nationwide movement, high school student Marius Mesnil told Al Jazeera that conditions in schools have deteriorated year after year.
“With every budget, there are fewer teachers,” he said.
Across Europe, how much governments spend on schools and hospitals shows what they are prioritising, and how much support they can give people as costs rise.
Sweden and Iceland spend the most on education in Europe, while spending has stayed largely unchanged in most Western European countries since 2016.
Denmark is a notable exception, with spending falling sharply over the period.
Many countries in Eastern Europe have increased their spending, including Slovakia, Bulgaria and Lithuania. Some of the countries carrying the heaviest debts, including Greece and Italy, are among those spending the least on education.
Healthcare spending rose across Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since fallen back in most countries, though it remains higher than before the pandemic in most of them.
Austria now spends the most, at 9.5 percent of its GDP in 2024, followed by Czechia and Croatia (9 percent each) and France (8.9 percent).
As temperatures drop, people are finding ways to stay warm without turning up the heating. Emma in London has bought a heated blanket so she does not need to heat her whole flat, and says she has had to put food and water before heating.
In Belgium, Maya’s family move around the house in wearable blankets; her daughters sleep with hot water bottles.
In Athens, Giorgos plans to keep his heater to a minimum and stock up on rugs, blankets and fleeces, admitting there have been winters when he had to choose between heating and food.
The worry never lifts. “Anxiety is something of a constant,” he said. “It doesn’t go away – if anything, it’s only intensifying now.”
*Names have been changed at the interviewees’ request to protect their identities.

noticias.titulo: Sandpapergate forum to investigate Australia-England Ashes Tests
noticias.resumen: Sandpapergate forum scope to cover entire 2017-18 season, including Ashes series, in South Africa allegations follow-up.
noticias.texto:
Sandpapergate forum to investigate Australia-England Ashes Tests
Sandpapergate forum scope to cover entire 2017-18 season, including Ashes series, in South Africa allegations follow-up.
Cricket Australia (CA)’s forum into Sandpapergate will consider “ball-management practices” during the entire 2017-18 season, including the Ashes series, in the lead-up to the tour of South Africa, according to its terms of reference published on Friday.
The ball-tampering scandal was reignited this month after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja said the whole team had known about the cheating in South Africa, not just the three players found culpable by CA’s integrity unit.
CA announced on November 18 it would open an independent forum for players and staff to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 without fear of sanction.
The six-week forum, to be overseen by Australian barrister Fiona McLeod, will include all four tests of the 2018 South Africa tour but also extend to ball-management practices during the 2017-18 season.
That season included the five-test Ashes series, which Australia won 4-0. There ‌were no reports of Australia manipulating the ball illegally during the series.
The forum will also cover the conduct and scope of the 2018 integrity investigation, which found only three players culpable: Former captain Steve Smith and opening batters David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.
Smith and Warner were banned for 12 months, with Bancroft suspended for nine.
Khawaja’s former teammates Warner, Bancroft and Chadd Sayers have supported his comments that the wider playing group and staff were aware of the ball-tampering.
However, captain Pat Cummins and bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have strongly denied any prior knowledge.
CA backed Cummins to remain captain of the Test and one-day international sides last week and rejected any suggestion his integrity had been compromised amid the renewed furore.
McLeod will provide a report of findings from the forum to CA’s board but will not share the underlying accounts given by participants, the terms of reference said.
The report will be made public.
“This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn,” CA Chair David Boon said in a statement.
Participation in the forum will be voluntary, and it will not make any adverse findings or determine the responsibility of any individual involved.
“Its purpose is to support the welfare of those impacted and to provide Participants with an opportunity to be heard and to have their experience acknowledged and understood without fear of retribution or disadvantage,” the terms said.
The Australian players’ union said it had not been consulted on developing the terms of reference.
“As such we don’t yet have a position on whether we support it and have advised ‌all relevant players of this as well as the fact that we are currently reviewing these terms and will update them once we have formed views,” Australian Cricketers’ Association boss Paul Marsh said in a statement.
Bancroft has said he will participate in the ‌forum, and former head coach Darren Lehmann told local media he would be open to it, saying he had nothing to hide.
Sayers said last week he was not sure whether he would participate, while Warner declined to confirm whether he would.

noticias.titulo: Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
noticias.resumen: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye meet in Islamabad as Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue and Iran talks stay open.
noticias.texto:
Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye meet in Islamabad as Houthi attacks on the kingdom continue and Iran talks stay open.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are meeting in Islamabad on Friday to discuss their Mecca defence pact, as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and sporadic Iranian strikes on other Gulf countries continue.
The officials are meeting for the third time since the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three.
The agreement was signed amid a wider war that began with United States-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told the AFP news agency earlier this week that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia” – a reference to Yemen, where the Houthis are based – would be on the agenda. He confirmed that the defence and foreign ministers of all three countries would attend the Islamabad meeting.
“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.
He described the pact as still being at an early stage.
“Initially we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he said.
Pakistan has pledged to defend Saudi territory but has ruled out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.
A pledge with limits
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs set out that boundary on October 9. Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistani troops stationed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance would not cross into Yemen to attack the Houthis.
“It is an alliance intended to defend the three countries against aggression,” he said at the weekly news briefing.
On April 11, as Islamabad hosted talks between US and Iranian officials aimed at ending the war, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defence said a Pakistani force, including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz airbase in the country’s Eastern Province under a bilateral mutual defence agreement that Islamabad and Riyadh had signed in 2025.
Muhammad Faisal, a Sydney-based security and foreign policy analyst, said much of the Pakistani military presence in Saudi Arabia rested on that older bilateral arrangement.
“Importantly, Pakistan’s existing military presence and defence coordination with Saudi Arabia largely predate the Mecca Pact,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to the bilateral mutual defence pact inked in September 2025, at a time when Gulf countries were reevaluating their dependence on US security guarantees after Israel struck Qatar.
Faisal added that Riyadh had not publicly pressed Islamabad to take part in offensive operations inside Yemen.
But Umer Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies in Riyadh, said that limit fell short of what Saudi Arabia wanted.
Therein lies a dilemma, both for Pakistan and for Saudi Arabia: The deeper Pakistan becomes involved against the Houthis, Karim said, the weaker its diplomatic role would become in US-Iran mediation and in its more recent efforts to mediate between Iran and Saudi Arabia. That’s because Iran is the principal external backer of the Houthis.
“Saudi Arabia wants Pakistan to contribute to its defence against the Houthis, and perhaps to act more against the Houthis in an offensive manner, but it also wants to retain Pakistan as a conduit of diplomatic engagement with Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pressure on the ground
On November 24, the Saudi Civil Defence said 11 people were injured when a tower in Riyadh’s financial centre was hit in a Houthi attack.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.
At an emergency meeting of the pact’s member countries in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.
The joint statement did not name Yemen or the Houthis.
On November 21, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told Turkish media: “Our current policy is aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia; no decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia.”
Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based analyst and nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, expected the alliance to remain defensive for the moment.
“As of now, as the Saudis only requested defensive support, I do not expect the Mecca Pact to get involved in offensive military operations against the Houthi militias in Yemen,” he told Al Jazeera.
Nawaf Obaid, a senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, outlined the scope of Pakistan’s commitment.
“Pakistan’s military commitment to the defence of Saudi Arabia encompasses capabilities across the land and air domains, including combat aviation, ground formations, integrated air and missile defence, and geospatial intelligence support. Defensive military operations can involve direct combat,” he told Al Jazeera.
Building the alliance
The Riyadh meeting was also attended by retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood, a former three-star Pakistani general, who was appointed earlier in September as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.
The secretariat is based in Riyadh, where Mahmood met Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud on November 19 to review efforts to build the alliance’s institutional framework, according to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said on October 23 that Islamabad and Riyadh had completed their ratification processes. Turkiye’s parliament approved the agreement on November 5 by 279 votes to 119. On Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan signed off on the ratification.
Eyup Ersoy, a visiting research fellow at Pembroke College, University of Oxford, said the alliance had moved quickly.
“The speed and scale of the formation of legal and institutional foundations of the agreement so far attest to the noteworthy performance of the agreement as well,” he told Al Jazeera.
Ozkizilcik, however, pointed to its limits.
“The Mecca Pact does not include a superpower. So, its capabilities and power projections will always be limited, in that it’s an alliance of regional or middle powers,” he said.
The alliance has not publicly detailed how it would decide on a joint military response, which forces it would call on or who would command them.
The Tehran channel
On October 26, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, and Turkiye’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in Tehran.
That meeting is widely believed to have been facilitated by Islamabad. “This showcased Pakistan’s dual role as an active member of the Mecca alliance and a diplomatic bridge between Riyadh and Tehran,” Faisal, the Sydney-based analyst, said.
Obaid said Tehran understood Pakistan’s position.
“Pakistan is not strategically neutral when it comes to Saudi Arabia and Iran, and the Iranians understand this perfectly well. Islamabad has an immediate national security interest in preventing a renewed military confrontation between the United States and Iran, which explains its mediation efforts,” he said.
On October 31, Rezaei told Iranian state television that Prince Khalid had warned that Israel would go after Turkiye once it was done with Iran, and then Saudi Arabia. Riyadh, Ankara and Islamabad have not publicly commented on his account.
Javad Heiran-Nia, director of the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Iran viewed the pact through that lens.
“Iran welcomes any mechanism that creates a balance against Israel and weakens the American order in the region,” he told Al Jazeera, even as Tehran “knows that one dimension of the Mecca Pact, and of possible participation in it, is to control Iran and its proxy forces”.
At a weekly briefing on November 20, Pakistani spokesperson Khan said the agreement “is defensive in nature and is not directed against any country”.
The text of the agreement, as submitted to the Turkish parliament, names no country or region as a threat.
Pakistan’s dilemma
Asif declined to tell AFP how the pact would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia. He named Israel as a possible threat to the region.
“The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said.
Karim, from the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, said pressure on Pakistan could grow if Riyadh’s outreach to Tehran stalled.
“Once Saudi Arabia recognises diplomatic engagement with Iran is not bringing any meaningful outcomes, only then perhaps will it further pressure Pakistan to be more openly involved against the Houthis, which would indeed imperil its goodwill with Iran,” he said.
“The balancing act for Pakistan becomes difficult every day because Iran is unwilling to oblige its concerns and those of Saudi Arabia on Yemen. But for now, it has not crossed a breakdown threshold.”

noticias.titulo: How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry
noticias.resumen: When East Germany could no longer afford to import coffee, it introduced a substitute blend containing rye and chicory in 1977. A public outcry ensued. The solution to the problem lay 9,000 kilometers away — in Vietnam.
noticias.texto:
How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry
November 27, 2026
Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?
Foreign currency deficit versus soaring prices
A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.
Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.
However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin. "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices."
The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes."
In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.
Even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.
'Pure rat poison'
Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product and with biting sarcasm. "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.." A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison."
More than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).
To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's important to recognize coffee's special place in East German society. "Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," says Wolle. During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak."
Care packages from relatives in the West
According to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky. "Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.
It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher. "Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle says. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care." Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.
Trading weapons for coffee
East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia. "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war."
But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam. "Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good."
Coffee from Vietnam: Too late for East Germany
Starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested."
By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past. "But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," says Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that."
There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print. "The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," says Wolle.
Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: AI can combine mathematical ideas on a scale beyond individual human minds. But could it produce ideas likes Einstein?
noticias.resumen: It once struggled to get simple sums right. But AI is now tackling tough mathematical problems like the Riemann hypothesis. How AI made this extraordinary leap. And why mathematicians should be "deeply worried."
noticias.texto:
AI: From math dunce to genius
November 27, 2026
Last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.
A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he said, often get simple calculations wrong.
Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.
That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.
How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?
Why was AI so bad at math?
The answer lies in how AI processes information, said Andrea Asperti, a professor in computer science at Italy's University of Bologna.
Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.
Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.
"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.
Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.
"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.
How AI got so much better at math
Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.
AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.
"What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti said.
Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.
"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti said.
Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.
"I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were. AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.
What makes AI so good at math
Ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.
"When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono said.
Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.
"Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono said.
The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.
And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.
Ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii."
He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.
"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono said.
A 'superhuman' achievement
Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.
"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he said.
Ono called the achievement "superhuman."
Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.
Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.
AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti said.
'Deep worry' for mathematicians' future
Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.
Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.
"Shoot for the moon! The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time."
"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that."
Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.
"Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he said.
Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra."
How mathematicians can rethink their role
In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.
"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," said Buzzard, "so we need new methods."
