Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.
"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he said.
But, he said, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button."
So, that is the issue of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?
Ono said: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet."

noticias.titulo: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
noticias.resumen: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
noticias.texto:
Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
November 27, 2026
Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.
The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.
Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.
"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.
He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.
Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.
Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire
Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.
A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.
Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.
"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.
The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.
This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.
Language a key hurdle
Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.
"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.
David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.
"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.
Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.
Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.
"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."
Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.
Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?
German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.
But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.
The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.
These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.
"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.
The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.
"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.
While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.
"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.
"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."
Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.
"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."
What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?
Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.
In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.
Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.
"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

noticias.titulo: German Catholic Church: Abuse victims may receive higher compensation
noticias.resumen: In a landmark ruling, judges in Cologne found the Catholic Church responsible for abuse committed by clergy members. Victims could now be entitled to more compensation.
noticias.texto:
German Catholic Church: Abuse victims may receive higher compensation
November 27, 2026
The Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.
The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priest for several years.
Melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.
Abortion carried out without consent
In determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges said that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.
Born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.
Beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.
In its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.
The Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.
The 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.
The Church's position served as a 'cover'
But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed.
In their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection.
His role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.
After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it."
The Archdiocese of Cologne said it "respectfully" took note of the decision.
The perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.
"The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.
From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.
'A day of hope for survivors of sexual abuse'
Schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards.
However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he said, describing the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches."
Matthias Katsch, spokesperson for the survivor advocacy group Eckiger Tisch, also called the ruling "good news."
"Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he said. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences.
"The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he said, allowing the crimes to happen. Melanie F. had sought compensation of between €800,000 and €900,000.
In March 2026, the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments (UKA), which was established by the German Bishops' Conference in 2021, announced that it had approved payments totaling approximately €93 million for survivors in all dioceses. Since then, several dioceses have published additional studies containing new reports of abuse cases.
Sixteen years after survivors and Jesuit priest Klaus Mertes helped bring the abuse scandal to light, the German Bishops' Conference will now have to prepare for significantly higher compensation payments.
Churches should reach out to survivors
In the United States, where civil lawsuits seeking compensation often involve far higher sums than in Germany, a number of Catholic dioceses have filed for bankruptcy. But that is unlikely to happen in Germany. The Bonn-based law firm of Eberhard Luetjohann, Melanie F.'s attorney, has reported receiving inquiries from hundreds of abuse survivors seeking higher compensation.
Spokesperson for Eckiger Tisch, Matthias Katsch, called on church leaders to engage in dialogue with survivors and their advocacy groups. Katsch said the question of the Church's liability for crimes committed by priests lies at the heart of most cases in which survivors are dissatisfied with the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments' decisions and believe they are entitled to higher compensation.
It is unacceptable, he said, that these survivors must go to court to obtain the compensation they deserve.
This article was originally written in German.
*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Parliament to vote on €556 billion 2027 budget
noticias.resumen: German lawmakers are set to vote on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Parliament to vote on €556 billion 2027 budget
Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack
German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has confirmed that two of its employees had been killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.
"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, providing technical support for air-defense systems," the Düsseldorf-based company said in a statement.
"Protecting the people of that country was a matter of deep personal importance to them. Both the company's leadership and the entire workforce are devastated by the loss of our colleagues. We share in the grief of those they have left behind."
The two victims were Italian citizens who worked as technicians for subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirmed in Rome.
Tajani said the pair had been at an air surveillance station in Kuwait when it was attacked by two Iranian drones. Two other people, a Pakistani national and Kuwaiti army captain, were also injured.
The Iranian foreign ministry has denied any involvement in the deadly attack.
Rheinmetall secured a contract to supply the Kuwaiti navy with defense systems in July.
BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference
Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.
The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.
After initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
BSW split over stance on AfD
Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which with it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.
Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain issues which an AfD minority government would want to implement.
The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.
The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy."
"We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but said: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media."
Wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority."
But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.
"Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term."
They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier."
Left Party hosts international femicide summit
Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is on Friday hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.
Under the title "Voices Against Femicide," the summit in Berlin brings together activists, politicians and researchers from around the world, including Kenya, Nigeria, Kurdistan, India, Afghanistan, Syria, Mexico, Argentina, Spain and Germany.
Across three panel discussions, the speakers will highlight women's rights, feminist struggles and legal perspectives and debate political measures which are urgently needed in Germany to effectively combat femicides and patriarchal violence.
The summit comes just two days after Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, marked Orange Day, the United Nations' officially named day for the elimination of violence against women, with a minute's silence and a series of speeches.
Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office reported a total of 1,176 female victims of attempted and completed homicide in 2025, up from 859 in 2024.
The number of female victims of domestic violence in Germany in 2025 rose by 2.8% to 197,667.
German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027
German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.
The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.
The plans call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germanyis talking about on Friday, 27 November.
The German parliament, the Bundestag, is set to vote on a 2027 federal budget that foresees around €556 billion ($610 billion) in spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.
Also in Berlin, Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.
Meanwhile, the left-wing populist BSW party is holding its party convention in Dresden as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats.

noticias.titulo: India's Modi government calls special sitting of parliament
noticias.resumen: The sitting of the Indian parliament comes after its monsoon session was adjourned indefinitely in August. Follow DW.
noticias.texto:
India's Modi government calls special sitting of parliament
Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
What you need to know
These are our rolling updates from India on Friday, November 27:
- A brief sitting of the Indian parliament will take place after the monsoon session was adjourned indefinitely back in August
- India's Lok Sabha is set to meet on Monday
- The Rajya Sabha will resume proceedings on Wednesday
Cricket: Black Caps 246-5 on day 1 of 2nd India vs New Zealand test
New Zealand stuck to their guns, or rather bats, as they went to stumps at 246 for five on the first day of the second test cricket match against India at Christchurch’s Hagley Oval.
The Black Caps started by losing their 10th straight toss in international matches on this tour.
India captain Shubman Gill opted to bowl first.
New Zealand's Tom Blundell lodged an unbeaten 117-ball 53 in his 50th Test while Glenn Phillips was 36 off 64 balls at the end of the first day.
India fast bowler Akash Deep struck twice in successive overs post-lunch and conceded 52 runs in his 21-over-spell. Deep dismissed Tom Latham for 59 and Rachin Ravindra for a duck, both caught behind.
This is the final test match between the two teams. Both sides are fighting for a series win after the first test in Wellington culminated in a draw.
India had one change in its lineup from the Wellington match, with speedster Gurnoor Brar making his debut in place of Prasidh Krishna. The 26-year-old soon clinched the wicket of Devon Conway.
The test is also crucial for India and New Zealand's hopes of reaching the final of the World Test Championship.
New Zealand is placed third in the championship while India is fourth.
WATCH: Would you send or accept an AI-written personal message?
Is it OK to generate a personal message with AI? People from India, Egypt and Argentina told DW about what kinds of texts they let chatbots write for them and if they would mind receiving an AI-generated message.
Find out more in this report:
India presents its case to IOC for hosting 2036 Olympics
India, which has tossed its hat in the ring in the bid to stage the 2036 Olympics, presented its plans to the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Future Host Commission on Thursday and appeared confident of advancing to the next phase.
India is pitching for Ahmedabad, located in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat and a major business hub, to be the host city.
"I think we presented a good case and we are very, very hopeful that we will move to the next ‌stage (of the bidding process)," Indian Olympic Association (IOA) chief executive Raghuram Iyer told the media, after the virtual presentation.
India is competing with six other nations to host one of the world’s biggest sporting events — Germany, Hungary, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea and Turkey.
Iyer said that a final pick for the 2036 games is not expected until after the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, or in early 2029.
Meanwhile, Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games and is also bidding for the 2038 Asian Games.
India minister says US trade deal nearing completion
India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday said that a trade deal with the United States was "close to culmination."
"The process and pathway, which was always something which held back finalising the deal, is now taking some shape," Goyal told the India Debt Capital Market Summit in a virtual address on Friday.
Goyal's statement comes after the office of the United States Representative (USTR) on Wednesday proposed a 25% tariff on Indian imports after conducting a probe into 16 major US trading partners over alleged excess capacity.
The US proposal came with a provision to slash the levies on India to 17% if a bilateral trade deal, negotiations for which have experienced road bumps over several months, is reached.
Special parliament sitting: What is on Modi government's agenda?
Union Minister Kiren Rijiju and the communications from the two houses do not elaborate on why Modi's government has called the sitting.
But political and Indian media circles are abuzz with guesswork that a bill to expand assemblies, contentiously linked to the implementation of a 33% quota for women in the national Parliament and state assemblies, could be back on the table after failing to get a two-thirds passing majority when it was proposed by the government in April.
While the women's reservation broadly has bipartisan support, it is tied to a separate Delimitation Bill that seeks to redraw constituency boundaries based on population — which is the bone of contention.
The opposition is concerned that a population-based redistribution of seats would swing the balance in BJP's favor, as the party has a large support base in the densely populated northern states.
Meanwhile, leaders of southern states, where birthrates have declined, fear that when it comes to political representation the population-based delimitation would favor the northern states, where population growth has been higher.
How has india's opposition reacted to the reconvening of parliament?
India's main opposition Congress party has deemed the move by Modi's government to call for the brief sitting of the parliament "an assault on the Constitution of India" which Congress General Secretary in-charge Communications and MP Jairam Ramesh said "must and will be resisted with all might."
In a post on X, Ramesh accused the government of "moving to manufacture a fraudulent two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha"
Ramesh also listed out a three-point Congress stance on delimitation and women's quota, which includes:
- Maintaining the current strength of the Lok Sabha for another 25 years.
- Maintaining the current state-wise distribution of seats in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years
- Implementation of one-third reservation for women and reservation within reservation for women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from the next general elections, slated for 2029.
A meeting of the Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group is also expected to be held on Saturday to discuss the gameplan for the upcoming parliament sitting, news agency ANI reported.
Indian parliament to hold special sitting after a gap of more than 100 days
A political storm could be on the horizon in India as both houses of India's bicameral parliament are set to reconvene next week for a special sitting at the request of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The Lok Sabha (lower house) is slated to sit on November 30 while the Rajya Sabha (upper house) will meet on December 2, official memos said, adding that the session may conclude on December 3.
"The Government has requested Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha and Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026 respectively to transact essential Government Business," Union Minister of Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju wrote on X, announcing the government's request on Thursday evening.
The resumption of parliament comes after the monsoon session, which is the second regular session of India's legislative body, saw both the houses being adjourned sine die (indefinitely) on August 13.
The session never ended formally and has remained unprorogued for a record over 100 days, while a winter session that typically starts early December looks delayed.
The monsoon session was turbulent as it began amid a massive youth-led protest called by India's "Cockroach" movement that sought, and later managed to get, the resignation of Modi's then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.
The parliament, itself, became a protest ground as both Modi's ruling coalition, led by his Bharatiya Janata Party, and the opposition INDIA bloc, ledby Congress, held demonstrations within its premises.
The political deadlock was unrelenting and the parliament struggled to get much business underway, culminating in the adjournment.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with your daily dose of news from India.
Here is what's creating a buzz in the world's largest democracy this morning:
Indian lawmakers are making their way back to the parliament next week, more than three months after a rocky — and not formal — conclusion of the monsoon session of the country's supreme legislative body which struggled to conduct its business amid an outpouring of protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over student issues.
The Modi government's request to reconvene both houses of the parliament for a special sitting has been accepted, with parliamentarians huddling in the Lok Sabha — the lower house — on November 30 and Rajya Sabha — the upper house — on December 2.
The ruling coalition has not explicitly stated what affairs it wants to discuss during the short session and has only said it wants to "transact essential government business."
However, speculation is rife that Modi's government could once again push a package of defeated bills — including a contentious population-based redrawing of voting boundaries and a women's quota intertwined with it.
And in the world of cricket, it is day one of the second test match between India and New Zealand in Christchurch's Hagley Oval . Both teams are vying for a series win in this final match after the first one in Wellington ended in a draw.
Read along for more.

noticias.titulo: New Zealand election ends in hung parliament
noticias.resumen: A final vote count showed that neither the center-right bloc nor the opposition left bloc was able to secure a majority.
noticias.texto:
New Zealand election ends in hung parliament
November 27, 2026
The final vote in New Zealand's election showed on Friday that neither the ruling conservatives nor the opposition bloc has enough seats to form a majority government.
The incumbent three-way coalition government is led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon of the center-right National Party.
He governed with two other smaller right parties. The incumbent coalition government won 65 seats, two down from election night, final results show.
The left-wing opposition bloc, led by the Labour Party's Chris Hipkins, won 58 seats, up by one from election night.
In terms of vote share of each of the main parties, Luxon's center-right National Party secured 40 seats, while Hipkins main center-left Labour Party won 36 seats.
The official vote count was released after election authorities counted 400,000 so-called special votes.
Those include ballots cast by New Zealanders living abroad.
Opportunity Party to play kingmaker role in formation of next government
Preliminary results from the November 7 election showed that the ruling coalition held a slim, two-seat majority — that's now been adjusted to the coalition falling short of a majority by a single seat.
The figures leave a new entrant to parliament, the Opportunity Party, as having a preeminent position because it will decide the shape of the next government.
The leader of the centrist party, Qiulae Wong, a 38-year-old former business consultant and a political newcomer, has said earlier this month that she was willing to speak with either party to form a government.
Luxon says negotiations with Opportunity Party will take time
Luxon will have to negotiate with the Opportunity Party if he wants to form the next government.
He said those negotiations will be "challenging" and will take time.
"I want to be upfront with New Zealanders. These negotiations may be challenging, and they could take some time," he told journalists.
"But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly. New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together, and will last for the full term," he added.
Experts say that if Luxon is not able to form a government with Opportunity, then New Zealanders will have to return to the polls for a new election, according to Australia's public broadcaster.

noticias.titulo: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
noticias.resumen: A powerful storm knocked out power for nearly 1 million customers and flooded streets. And, experts predict inflation will not dampen American spending for the holidays
noticias.texto:
Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
Thanksgiving Storm Aftermath, Black Friday Economy, Eisenkot's Coalition Talks
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.
- 🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.
Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.
- 🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.
The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.
Behind the story
This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent
I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."
After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.
New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.
Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.
Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.
I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).
Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.
Once again, my shopping cart is empty.
My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.
Weekend picks
Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:
🍿 Movies: The holiday season is packed full of can't-miss films. These are 17 movies that you should see before the year ends.
📺 TV: Parks and Recreation star Amy Poehler and creator Michael Schur reunite for Dig, an ensemble comedy about a team of archaeologists caught up in a series of mysterious events after uncovering an ancient artifact in Greece.
📚 Books: Why settle for one book recommendation when you can get more than 300? Now's the time to browse this year's Books We Love.
🎵 Music: NPR Music's Stephen Thompson and Lars Gotrich join host All Songs Considered Robin Hilton to attempt to build a canon of music for giving thanks, spending time with loved ones and, of course, celebrating food. Check out their playlist here.
🍴 Food: A few years ago, Israeli American chef Alon Shaya spearheaded the Rescue Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, exploring food's role in World War II. He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
3 things to know before you go
- Rocker the coonhound has won best in show at this year's National Dog Show. His glossy coat and big, floppy ears bested six other dogs that each won top honors in their groups.
- When Dungeons & Dragons came on the scene 50 years ago, some parents complained it kept their kids holed up inside. These days, the once-nerdy pastime is a screen-free parent's dream.
- Bakers across the country have taken inspiration from Little Free Libraries to offer free sweet treats to their neighbors.
This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

noticias.titulo: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
noticias.resumen: The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
noticias.texto:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.
Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.
Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.
On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.
"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.
Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.
Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

noticias.titulo: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
noticias.resumen: A storm battered much of the country on Thursday, knocking out power to thousands of homes and disrupting travel. Today, Black Friday shopping deals kick off, and on Saturday New York City will hold the postponed Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
noticias.texto:
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.
More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.
Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.
"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.
On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.
New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.
Iconic Macy's parade postponed
Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.
Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.
There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.
Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.
"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.
"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.
This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.
Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.
Black Friday kicks off
Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.
The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.
The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.
The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.

noticias.titulo: Can luxury save Macy's?
noticias.resumen: This week's celebration of Macy's 100th Thanksgiving parade finds the department store at a turning point. After years of losing sales, the retailer is reimagining itself — as a higher-end destination.
noticias.texto:
Can luxury save Macy's?
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.
Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."
Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.
"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."
How far can luxury sales take Macy's?
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.
"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.
Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.
"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.
"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."
One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.
But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.
"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

noticias.titulo: Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
noticias.resumen: Trump's sweeping immigration changes — an asylum ban, mass firings and new legal maneuvers — have all but ended asylum. The high court will soon consider whether some shifts deny people due process.
noticias.texto:
Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.
The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.
The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.
"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.
Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.
But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.
Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.
In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.
The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.
If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.
"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."
Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.
One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.
Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.
"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.
But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.
In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.
It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.
Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.
"He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.
According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.
The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.
"Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.
During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.
Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."
In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.
"There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.
She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

noticias.titulo: Screen free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
noticias.resumen: Some parents, fed up with screens, have found an analog oasis in the role-playing game invented in the 1970s.
noticias.texto:
Screen free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than fifty years.
In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10 minute piece on it in 1979. In recent years, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows like Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream – a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.
"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of nine to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."
Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host things like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.
"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.
In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.
"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."
"And collaboration!" added her nine-year-old brother Leo Watson.
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For fellow nine-year-old, Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.
"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.
And for Benjamin Cho, also nine, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."
To listen to the full piece and follow along on the kids' D&D session, click above to listen.

noticias.titulo: 12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
noticias.resumen: Here's something you can do as you gather with family and friends this holiday season: Take a free, five-minute quiz to assess your brain health. You'll learn simple changes to keep your mind sharp.
noticias.texto:
12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.
In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.
A score for your brain
So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.
It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.
"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."
The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:
- Physical health: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight
- Lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol
- Social and emotional health: stress management, relationships and a sense of purpose
According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."
Why blood pressure matters for your brain
High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.
"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.
That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. If you've been prescribed medication for high blood pressure, he says, taking the medicine is one of the most important things you can do.
Small gains add up
What if you take the quiz and don't love your number? The whole point of knowing your score is to use it as an assessment, a place to begin and a way to strategize about what changes you can make to your daily lifestyle habits. There's no need to overhaul your life.
In an analysis of real-world data from thousands of adults, each one-point improvement in the Brain Care Score was linked to up to a 4% lower risk of dementia, stroke or late-life depression. And even people who change their habits late in life can benefit.
The key is to pick one change that feels doable, such as:
- Adding 30 minutes of sleep to your daily routine if you're not well rested
- Putting an extra serving of greens on your plate
- Adding in a 20-minute walk each day and resistance bands for strength training
- Calling a friend to get together or joining a group activity
- Getting your blood pressure checked
Researchers say one healthy change often leads to others. Better sleep, for example, can make it easier to exercise and eat well, so the benefits can multiply across the score.
Purpose and connection count too
One part of the score that surprises people is the value placed on relationships and purpose. A 2025 study found that people with a higher sense of purpose were about 28% less likely to develop cognitive impairment.
That means joining the class or the volunteer gig you've been putting off can be considered a form of brain care.
You can retake the quiz over time to track your progress, and you can share it with family and friends. Healthy habits can be contagious.
