noticias.titulo: Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
noticias.resumen: Eagles QB Joe Milton threw two long touchdowns against the quarterback's former team, the Dallas Cowboys, for the the start of quite a comeback, after being down 31-10 early in the third quarter.
noticias.texto:
Eagles rally to stun Cowboys coming back from 21 points behind
ARLINGTON, Texas — Joe Milton rolled to his left while motioning DeVonta Smith where to go near the end zone, then threw the kind of deep ball the Dallas Cowboys always knew he was capable of when he was playing for them.
That 50-yarder was the first of two long touchdowns for the Philadelphia duo against the quarterback's former team, and the start of quite a comeback.
Milton, who was Dak Prescott's backup all last season, threw three touchdowns and ran for another one in a 39-38 win Thursday in his third start for the Eagles, who signed him off the Dallas practice squad on Oct. 16.
"The guy's a rock star. ... True example of being cool, calm, collected, and just keep playing the next play, no matter what the outcome," said Eagles tackle Jordan Mailata, who was then asked about the long TD passes. "We've seen it in practice a couple of times. The oohs and aahs were still there, but not as much. It was just like you know he can get that throw done."
After 50- and 45-yard touchdown passes to Smith, Milton ran 15 yards for a score in the fourth quarter and threw a 24-yard TD to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left before Philadelphia lined up for a 2-point conversion. Milton connected with Smith in the end zone, but a holding call against Mailata wiped out the tying score before another try was broken up at the goal line.
But the Eagles (4-7), who were down 31-10 early in the third quarter, got one more chance after sacking Prescott on fourth-and-1 for a nine-yard loss to their 48 in the final minute. After a couple of short completions to Smith and a pass interference call against Dallas, Jake Elliott kicked a 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.
Milton, signed by the Eagles about the same time they were determining that Jalen Hurts' season was over because of diagnosis of blood clots, completed 21 of 31 passes for a career-best 331 yards.
"You never know when your opportunity is going to come. You never know, when, where, how. The only thing you can do is just prepare yourself," Milton said. "That's just the main thing I did. There wasn't a day where I was in a Cowboys facility and I didn't take notes. I didn't let a day go by where I didn't ask a question. So just being prepared for the moment and I mean, it showed up when it needed to. ... Really trying to hold my emotions in up here. Just thankful for the moment."
While he was sacked five times, and the Cowboys defense had him on the run throughout, Milton made several big plays out of the pocket.
On the 50-yard TD late in the first half, Milton rolled to his left and was in front of the Cowboys sideline when he threw back toward the center of the field — the ball was in the air more than 60 yards before Smith caught it at the goal line. Milton then looked toward the Dallas bench and made some seemingly good-natured gestures with a huge smile on his face.
"Can't even remember doing that, but it was just kind of in a moment," he said.
Then late in the third quarter, while rolling to his right toward his sideline, Milton threw deep to an open Smith, who after the catch had to take only a few steps into the end zone to complete the 45-yard score. Smith had 11 catches for 200 yards.
Milton's quick sprint down the sideline on his touchdown run got the Eagles within 38-30 with 9:09 left.
"He played his butt off. He played really good, made some throws that only he can make," coach Nick Sirianni said. "He played an outstanding game, super composed throughout."
After appearing in four games for Dallas last season, Milton lost his backup role to Sam Howell in training camp this year. But Milton stayed with the Cowboys on their practice squad until getting signed by their NFC East rival.
The Eagles lost their seventh game in a row, 19-11 to the New York Giants in Milton's first start Nov. 8. After a bye week, they won 19-16 last Sunday over Pittsburgh, when Milton got them in range for a field goal and a two-score lead with four minutes remaining and then converted a third down in the final minute that allowed them to run out the clock.
Only one of Milton's regular-season appearances for the Cowboys was at AT&T Stadium, in a 34-17 loss to the Los Angeles Chargers last Dec. 21.
His third start Thursday was only his eighth regular-season game in the NFL after appearing in nine preseason games — six for the Cowboys this season and last, along with three for New England in 2024 after the Patriots drafted him in the sixth round that year.

noticias.titulo: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
noticias.resumen: Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
noticias.texto:
Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.
The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.
After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.
Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.
"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

noticias.titulo: A travel guide to Ljubljana – a 2027 European Capital of Tourism
noticias.resumen: Named one of the European Capitals of Tourism for 2027, Ljubljana offers travellers riverside cafés, historic landmarks and traditional cuisine. Here’s why you should visit the Slovenian capital.
noticias.texto:
Named one of the European Capitals of Tourism for 2027, Ljubljana offers travellers riverside cafés, historic landmarks and traditional cuisine. Here’s why you should visit the Slovenian capital.
Ljubljana was named one of the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism by the European Commission, earning the top spot in the category for cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants.
The jury was especially impressed with the city’s “commitment to knowledge sharing, continuous learning and resident-focused initiatives”, with the European Commission adding that it has an “ambitious programme of activities planned for 2027”.
If you’re curious about travelling to the Slovenian capital and finding out what there is to see and do, here’s all you need to know.
The city’s ‘lounge’ along the river
The Visit Ljubljana tourism board describes the embankments of the Ljubljanica River as the heart of the capital’s social scene – “densely scattered with lively cafés offering outdoor seating”.
The scenic riverbanks have a history dating back to Roman times and are an important archaeological site, where excavations have uncovered objects from prehistory to the early modern period.
It is also ideal for adventure tourists, especially during the summer when the city centre can be explored by stand-up paddleboard or by joining a guided kayak tour.
An ideal destination for a stroll or ride
For travellers looking to stretch their legs, Ljubljana’s compact size and car-free old town are ideal for exploring on foot or by bike.
The city’s historic centre sits along the Ljubljanica River, a stone’s throw away from Prešeren Square. Here, visitors will find a monument to Slovenian poet, France Prešeren, as well as the nearby Triple Bridge. Its stairways on each side of the bridges lead to terraces filled with poplar trees along the river.
In the old town itself, visitors can stroll to the Central Market, which combines indoor and open marketplaces within a striking colonnade. Fruits, balcony flowers, local cheeses and dry-cured meats are among the produce on offer, and in the indoor venue there is a fish market with a small restaurant.
Overlooking the old town, Ljubljana Castle sits atop Castle Hill, just a short climb from the city centre. Perched at an elevation of 400 metres above sea level, its history spans around 900 years, with the landmark now being home to exhibitions and cultural events year-round.
Other attractions and landmarks
While strolling in the city, these are some must-visit spots to add to your itinerary.
For an insight into the architect who moulded Ljubljana’s cityscape, make a beeline for Plečnik House. The complex comprises two houses that once belonged to Slovenian architect, Jože Plečnik – the marvel behind the city’s National and University Library as well as the Church of St. Michael.
The complex displays his original sketches, plans, photographs and models of his creations, including projects that never came to fruition.
The National Gallery is a hub for historical art, holding the country’s largest collection of fine art from the High Middle Ages to the 20th-century. Its permanent collection is made up of nearly 600 works by Slovenian and European artists, including a permanent exhibition by Slovenian modernist painter, Zoran Mušič.
The Dragon Bridge, adorned with four statues of the mythical creature, was constructed from 1900 to 1901. The bridge across the Ljubljanica River is a scenic spot for taking holiday snaps.
Where to stay
The city has no shortage of hotels and accommodation options.
At InterContinental Ljubljana, visitors can choose from 165 rooms and larger suites. The one-bedroom suite with castle views features a cosy fireplace, private sauna and a separate area for dining. Located on the 19th floor, it also offers panoramic views of the city. Guests can unwind at the Serenity Spa & Gym and also sample Slovene cuisine at its B-Restaurant.
Aside from hotels and hostels, visitors can opt to stay at a holiday farm. Located just outside of the city, Pri Lazarju tourist farm is more than 300 years old and offers guests the chance to experience farm life. Beyond its scenic surroundings, guests can get involved in barn and pasture work and take guided tours of local landmarks, including the Besnica River, or hike along the Borovničeva trail.
Meanwhile, Ljubljana Resort Hotel & Camp is the only campsite within the capital, situated just five kilometres north of the city centre. The vast site extends across three acres and is situated by the River Sava. Along the river, guests can enjoy outdoor activities, including fly fishing. The wider complex also features hotel accommodation, complete with an outdoor swimming pool, fitness centre, beach volleyball courts and a restaurant.
Slovenian cuisine to try
Slovenia’s culinary traditions have developed over centuries, with much of the traditional fare being served in “gostilnas”, which are family-run restaurants where classic dishes are served.
What has been coined as a “typical Ljubljana lunch” dates back to the 19th century, when locals would visit a gostilna on the city’s outskirts on the weekends. The meal has changed little since then. Popular dishes include boiled beef tongue and traditional “bleki” noodles in a soup. Another lunch class is Vodnik's lamb's lettuce salad from Valentin Vodnik's “Kuharske bukve” (The Cookbook), which was published in 1799 as the first cookbook ever written in Slovenian.
Another popular dish, “Leteči žganci”, or flying “žganci”, harks back to the 17th-century. Made from fried chicken legs and wings, it was popularised by workers at the town port by the Ljubljana River. According to Visit Ljubljana, žganci itself is an “everyday dish of boiled flour commonly associated with poverty and struggle for survival".
Meanwhile, since 2013, the city’s “Odprta kuhna”, or open kitchen, has become a popular culinary staple, taking place in the Pogačarjev Trg Square. The food market opens every Friday from March to October annually, bringing Slovenian cuisine, international eateries, sweet treats and even artisanal crafts.
Ljubljana and its surroundings also have a strong presence in the Michelin Guide, with 20 selected restaurants. The Guide described Gostilna na Gradu, which offers traditional cuisine, as being "worth queuing for", especially for its location in Ljubljana Castle's vast inner courtyard.

noticias.titulo: Portugal's parliament orders public TV to air bullfights again, sparking 86,000-name petition
noticias.resumen: After six years away, bullfights are set to return to RTP programming in 2027, via a Chega proposal, sparking controversy and a petition with over 86,000 signatures.
noticias.texto:
After six years away, bullfights are set to return to RTP programming in 2027, via a Chega proposal, sparking controversy and a petition with over 86,000 signatures.
Bullfights are set to return to Portuguese television in 2027, after a six-year absence from the schedule of public broadcaster RTP. Like bullfighting itself, the decision approved by parliament is far from consensual and is being widely challenged, with a petition already gathering more than 86,000 signatures against forcing bullfights into the channel's television programming.
At the root of the backlash is a proposal from the far-right Chega party requiring public broadcaster RTP to ensure the broadcast of bullfighting events.
The proposal was approved during the line-by-line votes on the State Budget for 2027, with votes in favour from the centre-right Social Democratic Party (PSD), the conservative CDS-PP and Chega, with the Socialist Party (PS) initially abstaining. The PS later switched to voting against when the measure was taken to the plenary at the request of People-Animals-Nature (PAN), but the majority confirmed the proposal, despite the other opposition parties voting against.
The same PSD, CDS-PP and Chega majority had already lowered VAT on bullfight tickets from 23% to 6% in the State Budget for 2025.
The Chega initiative now approved stipulates that, during 2027, RTP "shall ensure, in fulfilment of the public service obligations incumbent on it under the concession contract in force, the broadcast of bullfighting events on its television programme services, as part of the heritage of Portuguese popular culture".
The proposal also stipulates that it is for RTP, in exercising its editorial autonomy and safeguarding the independence laid down in the Constitution, to choose which events to broadcast, as well as which programme services to use and the time slots for their transmission.
The measure must be implemented at no additional cost to the State Budget, and RTP will have to inform parliament, by 31 January 2028, of the events broadcast and their audience figures.
The parliamentary decision has triggered a strong internal reaction at RTP. In comments to Portuguese radio station TSF (source in Portuguese), Nicolau Santos, chair of RTP's board of directors, described the measure as a violation of the Television Law, saying it was an attempt to interfere with the channel's editorial autonomy.
"After consulting our legal department, this guidance violates the provisions of the Television Law," said Santos, referring to article 26 of the legislation in question. "Except in the cases provided for in this law, the activity of television and on-demand audiovisual services is based on freedom of programming, and the public administration or any security body, with the exception of the courts, cannot prevent, condition or impose the broadcasting of any programmes," Santos said, quoting the law.
In light of that provision, he argued that "this decision requires a change to the Television Law, which is currently in force, and in that sense MPs will also have to work to amend the Television Law".
Speaking to TSF, Santos also said that RTP will defend its editorial autonomy, both in news and in programming. He indicated that the channel's concession contract, which defends animal welfare, will also have to be amended before public television can broadcast bullfights again.
"This seems extremely serious to me. It opens a Pandora's box and I think that, surely, there will be very deep reflection on this measure," he said.
The reaction from RTP's Workers' Committee and the Porto Workers' Subcommittee went even further, saying the proposal constitutes an "attack on the company's autonomy" and a "dangerous and outdated intrusion of political power" into the editorial decisions of a media outlet.
"It is yet another episode in the context of the suffocation to which the public media service in Portugal has been subjected (...) Today it is bullfights. Tomorrow it could be any other content that a given party believes should be part of RTP's programming," they warned in a statement quoted by the Portuguese news agency Lusa.
For the workers, the proposal in question clashes with the Television Law, which establishes freedom of programming and safeguards that no sovereign body can prevent or impose the broadcasting of particular programmes.
The statement also notes that RTP's concession contract enshrines independence and autonomy in setting programming. Added to this is the evolution of the legal framework on animal protection.
In addition, RTP's Workers' Committee warns that individual rights are also at stake, given that the Constitution enshrines the inviolability of freedom of conscience and the Labour Code recognises that employers and workers have the right to their physical and moral integrity.
"A parliamentary imposition does not remove the rights of those who work at RTP, nor does it exempt the company from listening to and considering its professionals' concerns," they stressed in a statement, adding that "RTP cannot have its content scheduled according to parliamentary majorities".
The protests also extend to a public petition (source in Portuguese) against the mandatory broadcasting of bullfights on RTP, which has already passed 86,000 signatures and continues to gain signatories at a rapid pace.
In the text of the petition, the organisers emphasise that the debate is not about "removing the individual freedom of those who enjoy or wish to watch" bullfighting shows, but rather "questioning whether the State should compel the public television service to broadcast them, regardless of their relevance to the public service mission and the wishes of a significant part of the population".
"Bullfighting is a controversial practice that involves animal suffering and whose television broadcasting should not be imposed by political decision, much less through an obligation placed on a public operator funded by taxpayers," the petition organisers argue.
They also contend that RTP "should have editorial autonomy to decide the content it broadcasts, in line with its programming criteria and public responsibility, without political impositions of this kind".
"A tradition, however old it may be, is not above democratic debate, evolving social values and concern for the suffering of animals," they stress.
ERC says broadcasting is an editorial decision
Although parliament has approved Chega's proposal to ensure that RTP broadcasts bullfights, the media regulator, the Entidade Reguladora para a Comunicação Social (ERC), believes that the decision to broadcast them falls within RTP's editorial freedom and freedom of programming.
In a reply to Lusa, ERC reiterates that article 26 of the Television Law "enshrines the principle of freedom of programming, establishing that, except in the cases provided for in the law itself, no sovereign body, with the exception of the courts, may prevent, condition or impose the broadcasting of any programmes".
The body recalls that "prior to approval of the proposal from Chega's parliamentary group, in response to requests for information on the issue, the regulatory council expressed the view that neither the LTSAP nor the Public Media Service Concession Contract sets out any specific obligation regarding the broadcasting of bullfighting events". The LTSAP is the Law on Television and On-Demand Audiovisual Services. The ERC concluded that broadcasting bullfights is therefore an editorial decision for RTP to make.
For that reason, ERC states that it "will follow the conclusion of the legislative process under way and, in due course, will assess the issue in light of the powers conferred on it by law".
Last live bullfight in 2020
According to data from Portugal's Inspectorate General for Cultural Activities, 147 bullfighting events (source in Portuguese) were held in mainland Portugal in 2025, more than half of them in Alentejo, in the south of the country.
RTP stopped broadcasting bullfights after the 2020 season. In that year, marked by the COVID-19 pandemic, it broadcast only two bullfights (source in Portuguese): one at the Monforte bullring on 28 August, and the Harvest Bullfight at the Almeirim Arena on 11 September.
In 2021, the public broadcaster dropped bullfighting from its schedule altogether, in line with other public service broadcasters abroad.
The Spanish public broadcaster RTVE had already taken a similar decision several years earlier, although it carried out occasional broadcasts during the process that led to these programmes being removed from the broadcaster's schedule.
From 2006 onwards, RTVE stopped regular broadcasts of bullfights because of the high cost of television rights, low audience figures and clashes with the time slot reserved for protecting children.
Then, in 2011, the broadcaster published a new stylebook (source in Spanish) that expressly excluded bullfight broadcasts because they involve violence against animals and clash with the protection of minors.
Between 2012 and 2016, after a change in legislation and management (source in Spanish), RTVE broadcast a handful of bullfights, including in Valladolid, Spain, in September 2012, in Cáceres in 2015, and a charity bullfight for Asprona in Albacete. It has had no regular bullfight broadcasts since, although it still shows the encierros (bull runs) during the San Fermín festival in Pamplona.
Today, bullfights are broadcast via specialist platforms and pay services. Even so, bullfighting still has an occasional presence on the public television channels of five Spanish regions (autonomous communities) (source in Spanish), as well as on private broadcaster Castilla y León TV. Bullfights are shown on Telemadrid, Canal Sur, Castilla-La Mancha Media, Aragón TV and Canal Extremadura.

noticias.titulo: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' - Fincher with fries?
noticias.resumen: Nostalgia and nihilism collide in David Fincher's gritty but edgeless follow-up to Quentin Tarantino's 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood'.
noticias.texto:
Nostalgia and nihilism collide in David Fincher's gritty but edgeless follow-up to Quentin Tarantino's 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood'.
The year is 1977, and the movies ain’t what they used to be.
Over the last decade, a New Wave of young filmmakers have taken over, moving from indoor sets to city streets to film grittier, meaner, counter-cultural stories that reflect the disillusionment of the times.
In the process, Hollywood’s prior artifice has been shattered; no longer a glossy, well-oiled machine solely controlled by big studios.
But nothing lasts forever — and something is about to come along (as it always does) that once again changes everything: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope.
As screenwriter and filmmaker Paul Schrader told film historian Peter Biskind for his book "Easy Riders and Raging Bulls": “Star Wars was the film that ate the heart and the soul of Hollywood. It created the big-budget comic book mentality.”
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (TFMCB) takes place in the summer of ‘77, right at the height of Star Wars mania. While only glimpsed on cinema marquees in passing shots, its background presence sets the tone for a movie that’s not only wrestling with shifting attitudes and the violent tug of time, but also itself.
A follow up to Quentin Tarantino’s Oscar-winning Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019), TFMCB focuses on its character Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt), the former stuntman to actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) who once kicked Bruce Lee’s a** and took down a bunch of Manson Family members while high on an acid soaked cigarette.
In other words, Cliff is cool. That's kind of his whole thing.
Eight years later, he’s living with his dad (Peter Weller) and working multiple jobs in Los Angeles: a projectionist at the New Beverley Cinema, a cocktail maker at a bar with mud fighting contests, and a “fixer” for celebrities being blackmailed by criminals.
Oh, and he also sometimes acts in porno movies under the stag name Randy.
The plot mostly hinges around Cliff’s relationship with an excitable TV actor named Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), who finds himself in a spot of trouble with some Filipino gangsters that are now threatening to kill his wife (Carla Gugino).
But mis-adventures aside,TFMCB is primarily a hangout movie.
Similar to George Lucas's American Graffiti, it excels at immersing viewers in retro Americana — albeit a crumpled and nonchalant version. As we ride with Cliff through the streets of LA, the staticky sounds of KRLA radio station a near-constant presence, you can almost smell the tobacco smoke wafting through the screen and it's just fun soaking up the atmosphere, slouching into it like a weathered chair.
Booth himself is as engaging as ever and manages to maintain some of his enigma despite being front and centre. This is thanks to Pitt's endearing performance, which once again leans into the character's effortless bad-a**ery — part surfer-dude, part grindhouse hunk.
But if Once upon a Time was Tarantino’s ode to a golden age of cinema - a re-writing of history with a fairy tale ending - TFMCB is a cynical reckoning with reality and the inevitability of change.
While Cliff confronts this by coasting on his own legends and clinging to the fringes of an increasingly loose-moralled industry, he knows no happy ending is coming — and who cares? None of it “means sh**” to him anyway.
Director David Fincher (Seven, Gone Girl) was the perfect choice for capturing such apathy, dipping Tarantino’s script in a vat of slick gloom that sharpens and darkens the mood. And it is at points very dark — both in its on-screen brutalities, and its visuals, which swap Once upon a Time's vibrant 35mm film for the dirge of desaturated digital.
Still, the nostalgic vibes of its predecessor remain, and anyone with an interest in this particular era of Hollywood filmmaking history will find themselves drawn to its niche cultural references and rich world building; scenes bathed in neon sleaze and analogue media ASMR.
Beyond the movie’s cool persona, however, there’s not much substance to hold onto.
Cliff Booth is a great character, but what made him so beloved in Once upon a Time was his bond with Rick specifically and his interactions with other equally-charismatic characters. In TFMCB, there are very few interesting characters to anchor him in the same way. The criminals are bothersome but bland, Peter Weller as Gus Booth is woefully underused, and TV star Charlie Peters is eccentric in an oddly underwhelming way.
The most compelling on-screen dynamic is between Cliff and the glamazonian Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), who share a memorable scene on a balcony discussing the terms and conditions of Cliff’s slapping kink. But the chemistry between the two tends to simmer more than sizzle, and Crosby, outside of a fun speech about movies being like cheeseburgers, is mostly relegated to solemn looks and the occasional burst of sass.
Meanwhile, a lack of overall narrative purpose means that Cliff meanders from moment to moment, which can be compelling in its own way, but lessens the impact of any actual action. Even the tensest plot points, like a violent home invasion, start to feel like disruptive filler (can't we just get back to making banana daiquiris?)
TFMCB alsomarks the final movie to be made as part of Fincher’s exclusive partnership with Netflix (following Mank and The Killer), with only a brief two-week theatrical release in select cinemas before streaming. This, along with Fincher’s admitted use of some artificial intelligence in post-production, create a notable flatness to its aesthetic; one that also examples the very thing it laments: the slow degradation of creative spirit to time.
This appears on screen like a literal push-pull between nostalgia and nihilism that ultimately flicks a lit cigarette on Tarantino's celluloid romanticisms.
It once again raises questions about the current state of cinema. About its profit-driven and streamer-led decision making that has created a more homogenised and sanitised media landscape where original, renegade ideas (like those of New Hollywood) are stifled and pre-existing ones mined of their spark.
But if we take Crosley's view that movies are "just meant to be fun", TFMCB works as an entertaining couple of hours spent with a former stuntman in a Hawaiian shirt — the Fincher with fries and a side of Tarantino dipping sauce.
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is out at select European cinemas now ahead of its Netflix release on 23 December 2027.

noticias.titulo: Marseille stadium violence escalates into diplomatic affair between France and Bulgaria
noticias.resumen: Clashes between Marseille and Bulgarian fans broke out on Thursday evening before the Europa League match OM–Levski Sofia; eleven Bulgarians were injured, five hospitalised.
noticias.texto:
Clashes between Marseille and Bulgarian fans broke out on Thursday evening before the Europa League match OM–Levski Sofia; eleven Bulgarians were injured, five hospitalised.
The violence that broke out on Thursday evening at the Vélodrome stadium has taken on a diplomatic dimension. French President Emmanuel Macron and Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova reacted from Brussels, where they were attending the European summit. Eleven Bulgarian supporters were injured in the clashes, five of whom had to be taken to hospital.
Emmanuel Macron condemned with "the greatest firmness" the violence against Bulgarian supporters. He spoke with the Bulgarian president and assured her that the incidents "would not go unpunished".
Iliana Iotova spoke of "horrifying" images and "unacceptable" violence. She called on the French authorities to fully clarify the attacks and on UEFA to check the security conditions in the stadium.
The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs also condemned "firmly the assaults committed against Bulgarian nationals in Marseille".
What happened at the Vélodrome?
The causes of the incidents are still unclear, with the facts still being established. According to the newspaper L'Equipe (source in French), around ten minutes before kick-off, scheduled for 18:45, Bulgarian fans seated in the side stand Jean-Bouin, outside the visitors' section, are said to have repeatedly provoked the Marseille ultras.
Nazi salutes were among the gestures observed. A video shared on social networks (source in French) shows one of these supporters making such a gesture before being restrained by a security guard.
The situation quickly escalated. Several dozen OM supporters, mainly from the Virage Sud, left their stand to move towards the Jean-Bouin and confront the roughly 500 Bulgarians who had taken their seats to watch the match.
Blows were exchanged, sometimes using flagpoles, along with missiles and flares being thrown. Some Marseille supporters were wearing balaclavas. Security staff and riot police eventually intervened to separate the two sides. Tear gas was also used to disperse those involved.
According to the Bouches-du-Rhône police prefecture, eleven Bulgarians were injured. Five were taken to hospital, notably for eye and head trauma. No arrests were initially reported.
Olympique de Marseille also condemned the incidents and announced that it wanted to establish the circumstances precisely. The team eventually won 1-0, in a match that was also marked by further tensions at half-time.

noticias.titulo: Does Europe have a cybersecurity problem? | Password
noticias.resumen: According to experts, the cybersecurity incidents Europe experienced in November should not come as a surprise. But how much do we know about these attacks? And what can Europe do to improve its cybersecurity?
noticias.texto:
According to experts, the cybersecurity incidents Europe experienced in November should not come as a surprise. But how much do we know about these attacks? And what can Europe do to improve its cybersecurity?
From cyberattacks on fridges to bomb threats at schools, November 2026 has been marked by a series of incidents that have unsettled Europe and brought the state of the bloc’s cybersecurity back into the spotlight.
In the second episode of Password, Euronews Tech Talks’ monthly miniseries on the major tech events shaping Europe, we dive into hacking attacks and technical outages with Euronews’ journalists Jonathan Benton and Roselyne Min.
What happened?
On 2 November, supermarket refrigeration systems in Belgium and several other European countries were targeted in cyberattacks, resulting in food waste and raising concerns across the continent.
Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin later said Iran was “very likely” behind the attacks, while Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot stated there was not enough evidence to draw conclusions.
Regardless of who was behind the issue, it was not the first time supermarkets were targeted. Already in October, similar attacks had taken place in France.
“We don't exactly know what the hackers wanted, but if they wanted people to notice, they certainly achieved that visibility,” Min said. “If someone gets into a government database, it can take months for you to find out. But if you walk into a local supermarket and the staff is emptying the freezers, you see that impact right away,” she continued.
A cyberattack, this time directed at a political institution, targeted the European Commission, which confirmed the incident on 19 November.
“Several Commission applications were temporarily taken offline, including HR tools such as the EU Academy,” Benton explained. “Email addresses were among the data exposed, but there was no money that was stolen,” he continued.
The European Commission suspects a China-backed hacking group is behind the attack. Yet, Beijing has consistently denied supporting hacking groups accused of conducting cyberattacks on foreign actors.
The bomb threats, which paralysed flights across the continent and schools, were also a major concern for Europe. In Italy, on 11 November, around 6,000 schools were targeted, and students evacuated, spreading chaos all over the country.
“This is the main advice: that this should have been caught by spam filters. Although they [experts] have warned that this wasn't necessarily enough, that people should have been a bit more careful scrutinising and checking their emails, checking for phishing approaches, this kind of thing, to find suspicious activity,” Benton said.
Hybrid warfare of Europe unpreparedness?
Following these disruptions, the concept of hybrid warfare once again featured in public debates and newspaper headlines, with commentators linking the recent attacks to a broader strategy of destabilising Europe for political reasons.
Yet, Min prefers a more guarded approach. “I’d be cautious calling every incident hybrid warfare. (...) A government can also back hackers simply to raise money even if there’s no geopolitical tension per se with Europe,” she said, bringing the example of North Korea, where hackers are employed to steal cryptocurrencies.
Regarding Europe’s readiness to face cybersecurity threats, experts seem to agree that Europe is on the right path, but more investment and better implementation of current frameworks are needed to improve Europe's cybersecurity systems.
“Europe does not lack cybersecurity companies; we have huge growth in that. Our problem is the scalable market,” Cecilia Bonefield-Dahl, director-general of DigitalEurope, the trade association for Europe's digital technology industries, told Euronews Next.
“If Europe is all about that, making us competitive and making us safer in Europe, that is exactly how we should spend our time and our money,” she continued.
AI and quantum computing, the new threats to cybersecurity
According to the European Commission, the cyberattack it suffered was conducted with the help of artificial intelligence, a technology that is believed to be already enhancing hackers’ capabilities, helping them find vulnerabilities in their targeted systems.
Quantum computing is another technology that can further threaten cybersecurity.
“It (quantum computing) will only massively expand the capacity for the system to find vulnerabilities, but not only that, but to also break down conventional cryptography, which means normal passwords and security systems that would have taken, for example, millions of years to break, would now take hours,” Benton explained.
For these reasons, according to Joyce Hackmayer, associate fellow in the international security programme at Chatham House, Europe needs to act faster.
“The threats are familiar and so are the fixes. AI adds urgency because it is helping attackers move faster, but it can also help defenders. But the time Europe has to act is shrinking,” she told Euronews Next.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

noticias.titulo: Feijóo vows to quit if he loses Spanish election and dares Sánchez to do the same
noticias.resumen: Feijóo dared Sánchez to give up his seat and his legal protection if he loses. The prime minister declined.
noticias.texto:
Feijóo dared Sánchez to give up his seat and his legal protection if he loses. The prime minister declined.
One pair acted as if they were perfectly in sync, while the other behaved as if they did not know each other. The leaders of the two right-wing parties chose to ignore each other completely in a final election debate that reflected a reality in which, apparently, all four candidates to become Spain's prime minister feel comfortable: in the elections on 29 November, what really seems to be on offer is two different models of the country.
The four-way showdown began with Ada Colau, the leader of Frente Amplio, wearing an LGBT pin on her lapel. The former mayor of Barcelona used her opening remarks to ask her rivals to condemn killings linked to gender-based violence. The International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women was marked on Wednesday. Only Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, ignored her request.
Buoyed by the previous debate with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, which the media consensus said he had won, a visibly self-assured Alberto Núñez Feijóo even dared to nod to the meme culture of millennials, the most progressive demographic group in the population pyramid. The candidate of the conservative People's Party (PP) made references to the Luna Rossa pizzeria and used a phrase that would make any Gen Z voter cringe: "Amiga, date cuenta" (roughly, "Girl, wake up").
Feijóo had one main challenge in this debate: to avoid mistakes after his earlier win, in a campaign in which the polls, as in 2023, make him the favourite. One exchange in the public services segment did not help him. Colau accused him of hypocrisy for not demanding the resignation of Carlos Mazón, the former head of the Valencia regional government, who was widely criticised over his handling of the deadly floods of October 2024. She also criticised Feijóo for not asking Mazón to give up his status as an aforado, an office-holder who can only be tried by a higher court.
"Good management is taking charge in a national emergency, not running away from Paiporta while you stay quiet," Feijóo replied. Paiporta is the town near Valencia, in eastern Spain, that was worst hit by the 2024 floods. The reply provided another viral clip in a campaign that seems to be followed more on live streams than on traditional broadcasts. The candidate, who was not quick enough to respond immediately, returned to the remark during the final segment of the night.
The synergy between Sánchez and Colau was almost complete throughout the programme, recalling the July 2023 campaign, when Yolanda Díaz was in the spotlight. Díaz was then the candidate of Sumar, the left-wing platform allied with Sánchez's Socialists. Only in the closing moments of each segment – housing, the economy, public services, corruption, foreign policy and immigration – did the Barcelona politician gently criticise certain policies of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE).
Abascal, who used the far-from-casual term Reconquista in his closing statement, focused his contributions on three common enemies of the country: immigration, environmental policies and corruption. Reconquista refers to the medieval Christian campaigns to retake the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule. At no point in the debate did Abascal address his hypothetical coalition partner, whether inside or outside government, and he directed most of his attacks at Sánchez.
The Vox leader also tried to reach out to working-class voters. He attacked the profits of IBEX 35 companies, the firms in Spain's benchmark stock index, and contrasted them with the economic conditions that, he claimed, the rest of society has to endure.
Sánchez had a better night than in his previous head-to-head with Feijóo, but he was slow to go on the offensive, leaving several awkward silences after attacks from his two rivals on the right. At the outset he again tried to strike a conciliatory tone, a strategy that had already failed him in the previous debate. Although he adjusted as the debate went on, he appeared much more comfortable taking on the far-right leader than the conservative one.
In the last segment of the debate, the opposition leader laid down a challenge to the prime minister. Feijóo said he would resign from his post, give up his seat in parliament and renounce his legal protection if he did not become prime minister, and he demanded that Sánchez commit to doing the same. Sánchez did not accept the challenge.

noticias.texto:
Javier Martínez-Cantó, political scientist at the Institute of Public Goods and Policies (IPP–CSIC), says corruption scandals "have been hindering the popularity" of Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as he seeks to remain in power ahead of Sunday's snap elections.

noticias.titulo: A travel guide to Calvià – a 2027 European Capital of Tourism
noticias.resumen: Recognised as one of the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism, Calvià is an ideal destination for travellers looking for more than sun and sand. Here’s what you can discover.
noticias.texto:
Recognised as one of the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism, Calvià is an ideal destination for travellers looking for more than sun and sand. Here’s what you can discover.
Calvià, a Mallorcan setting of cliffs, bays, beaches and islets, has been named the 2027 European Capital of Tourism in the cities with between 25,000 and 100,000 inhabitants category.
The coastal destination was awarded the designation for its “ambition to transform its tourism model, moving away from high-volume mass tourism towards a more sustainable and year around approach”, the European Commission said.
Jury members also recognised its work to have tourism contribute to long-term economic, environmental and social wellbeing, while also “creating a more balanced relationship between visitors, residents and the local environment”.
But what makes this Balearic municipality worth a visit in 2027? From historic landmarks, hiking trails and its coastal cuisine, here's where to go and experience Calvià.
Must-see attractions
Sprawled over 145 square kilometres and surrounded by the mountains of Sierra de Tramuntana, this Spanish municipality’s history dates back to the 13th century, with estates still standing from the 16th and 17th centuries.
Can Verger, which now hosts a library and facilities for young people, and Can Ros are among the best known old Mallorcan manors still standing.
There is also a selection of markets to visit. The traditional market in Calvià village is the city’s oldest and takes place every Monday morning, where more than 60 stalls offer visitors food, clothes and handicrafts.
Calvià has also frequently been the destination of choice for both national and international film productions, including the 2019 comedy “The Hustle”, starring Anne Hathaway and Rebel Wilson. Filming took place across various locations, including Puerto Portals.
There is also a dedicated “Calvià, Film Set” route where set-jetters can explore other locations that have graced silver screens.
Adventures on land and water
Several certified hiking trails are ideal for exploring Calvià on foot.
The PR-MA 1 route connects the town of Peguera and the village of Es Capdellà. Landscapes of pine forests, farmland and views of the Torrent des Gorg mountain range are part of the itinerary. While for history buffs, the ancient medieval tower-house, Torre d’En Boira, which dates back to the 14th-century, can also be seen along the way.
Other certified routes include PR-MA 2: La Vall Verda, PR-MA3: Sa Vinya, and PR-MA 4: Sa Font de Sa Cometa.
Away from dry land, the Mediterranean waters are great for activities like motor and jet boating, windsurfing, as well as for banana boat rides, scuba diving and surfing.
Coastal cuisine
Unsurprisingly for an island destination, dining in this Mallorcan municipality features plenty of fresh sea catches alongside traditional fayre.
Leña Mallorca, Spanish steakhouse at the Mandarin Oriental Punta Negra, is inspired by local culinary traditions. With open-fire cooking and a display of dry aged meats, guests can sample an array of vegetable, seafood and meat dishes, as well as Spanish-Japanese fusion “yakipinchos” grilled skewers.
Matsuhisa, the restaurant by Chef Nobu Matsuhisa, is also located in the Mandarin Oriental Punta Negra. Set against sea views, it offers diners sushi paired with coastal ambience.
For paella, Paco’s Santa Ponsa offers authentic Spanish cuisine, alongside tapas, fresh fish as well as steak, pizza and sweet treats – all within easy reach from beaches like Platja de Santa Ponça.
Meanwhile, Lucy Wang in Portal Nous blends Japanese with French and Mediterranean cuisine. Dishes on offer range from edamame to ceviche, alongside sushi and sashimi.
Where to stay
After a day packed with hiking, water activities and dining, a luxurious stay awaits at the five-star Hotel Golf Santa Ponsa. The property offers views of the Puig de Galatzó peak and is nestled in a golf club surrounded by six kilometres of coastline, beaches and a marina.
Indoors, the hotel offers an array of rooms and suites, including some with terraces or balconies. Guests can choose to unwind in its dedicated space for wellness, which includes private massage cabins. There is also a restaurant serving guests seasonal Mediterranean cuisine.

noticias.titulo: NATO jets scrambled after drone briefly enters Latvian airspace
noticias.resumen: Latvia's army hasn't said where the drone came from, and it warns more incursions are likely.
noticias.texto:
Latvia's army hasn't said where the drone came from, and it warns more incursions are likely.
NATO fighter jets and a Latvian interceptor drone were deployed overnight after an unidentified drone briefly entered the country's airspace near the Russian border, Latvia's National Armed Forces (NBS) said on Friday.
The drone was detected moving close to the border in Ludza municipality, eastern Latvia, and "briefly flew over Latvian territory", the army said in a statement.
According to the NBS, an air threat was declared in Ludza at 2.30am local time (00.30 GMT) and residents were sent an orange alert. That level signals a confirmed threat that requires immediate action.
The alert was lifted at 2.55am, when a lower-level yellow warning was issued for neighbouring Balvi municipality in Latvia's north-east. That warning ended at about 3.30am, public broadcaster LSM reported, citing the armed forces.
"Fighter jets from NATO's air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed," the army said. The interceptor returned to its launch site after the flight, and air defence units were ready to respond immediately.
The NBS did not say where the drone came from. It said it had sent extra air defence units to the eastern border, and warned that foreign drones could again enter Latvian airspace while Russia's war in Ukraine continues.
Several countries near the war have reported drone incursions or crashes since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Drones have been shot down over Latvia twice this year, the NBS said at the time. French jets on NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission downed one in June, and allied fighters shot down another over Balvi in August.

noticias.titulo: German sofware giant SAP weighs at least 10,000 job cuts amid AI shift, reports say
noticias.resumen: If confirmed, the cuts could affect about 9% of the company's global workforce. SAP's shares in Frankfurt were down on Friday morning.
noticias.texto:
If confirmed, the cuts could affect about 9% of the company's global workforce. SAP's shares in Frankfurt were down on Friday morning.
In a move to prepare for the AI era, Europe's most valuable software company, SAP, is drawing up plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs, Bloomberg first reported on Thursday, citing unnamed sources. The number could change after talks with employee representatives, the report added.
SAP told Euronews that "the business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful". The company said it expected roles and functions to change over time, but "no decisions have been made regarding any further measures". It added, "We do not comment on speculation."
SAP makes software that helps companies manage their finances, supply chains and payroll. Chief executive Christian Klein is pushing to build AI into those tools, after some customers questioned whether earlier AI products were worth the cost.
According to Bloomberg, SAP was looking at changing how it develops and sells its software and had asked all departments to identify possible cuts, with a particular focus on product development, engineering and sales.
SAP has also bought several companies to support its AI push. In July, it completed the purchase of Prior Labs, which develops AI models for business data, and Dremio, which helps companies bring data from different systems together. This month it completed its purchase of TechWolf, a Belgian company that uses AI to map the skills employees have and the work they do. SAP also bought data management firm Reltio in May.
Other major software companies are reshaping their workforces as they invest in AI and look to cut costs. Oracle's workforce shrank by about 21,000 in the year to May as it restructured its business, partly in response to AI adoption. In October, Microsoft said it was offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees as it sought to contain costs and help fund its AI investments.
The potential cuts are coming at a time when SAP's cloud business continues to grow. Cloud revenue rose 25% in 2024 and 23% in 2025, or 26% in both years once currency effects are stripped out. In the third quarter of 2026, cloud revenue rose 26% year on year to €6.67 billion, while profit after tax rose 11% to €2.27bn.
SAP shares were down about 0.5% at €193.18 at 10:55 CET on Friday.

He still needs to be formally appointed after the European Parliament and the bank's top officials give their views

noticias.titulo: Iran denies responsibility for Kuwait drone strike that killed two Italians
noticias.resumen: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the accusations baseless and the incident "suspicious" and offered to cooperate on a joint investigation. Kuwait called it "a heinous Iranian aggression". Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE condemned the attack.
noticias.texto:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the accusations baseless and the incident "suspicious" and offered to cooperate on a joint investigation. Kuwait called it "a heinous Iranian aggression". Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE condemned the attack.
Iran denied responsibility on Thursday for drone strikes on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the accusations baseless and proposing a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City.
Araghchi spoke by telephone with his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts, Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Antonio Tajani, and later wrote on X that the incident was "suspicious and looks like a preecooked recipe for war."
"We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.
Tajani had earlier told the Italian Senate that several Iranian drones struck Kuwaiti military facilities at around 2 pm local time (12 pm CET), including an air defence radar centre where two Italian specialists employed by arms company Rheinmetall were working.
Kuwait's Al-Sabah condemned the attack as "a heinous Iranian aggression" and offered condolences to Italy.
Senior spokesperson for Iran's armed forces Abolfazl Shekarchi flatly denied any Iranian military operation in the region and accused the US and Israel of staging a false flag attack to destabilise the area.
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency went further, citing an unnamed security source who alleged that Ukraine had deployed a network of thousands of drones across the region, including in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. It provided no evidence.
The Iran embassy in Rome separately issued a statement categorically rejecting any Iranian role and warning against attempts to widen the war.
Gulf states condemn Tehran
Saudi Arabia called for an immediate halt to Iranian attacks and said it held Tehran responsible for the consequences of its actions. Bahrain asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable and demanded compensation for the damage.
Qatar warned that repeated strikes on Kuwait risked undermining diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions. The UAE, Syria and Jordan also condemned the attack.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Tehran and said Gulf security was directly linked to Europe's security.
Iran has repeatedly struck Arab Gulf states with drones and missiles since the start of the war, saying it has targeted military bases and US-linked facilities, with Kuwait and Bahrain among the most frequently targeted countries.
Tehran has urged its neighbours not to allow their territory to be used for attacks against Iran.
Iran's army confirmed a separate drone attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base earlier in November.
Tajani had informed the Italian parliament on 8 October of a decision to relocate most of its troops from Kuwait, with only around 10 military personnel remaining in the country at the time of the attack.

noticias.titulo: Video shows Levski fan caught giving Nazi salute before Marseille match
noticias.resumen: Violent clashes marred Marseille’s Europa League win over Levski Sofia, with a filmed Nazi salute, flares, injuries and condemnation from both presidents.
noticias.texto:
A Levski Sofia supporter has been filmed appearing to perform a Nazi salute in the stands during Marseille’s Europa League tie against the Bulgarian side, in footage that has circulated widely online. The clip emerged amid chaotic scenes at the Stade Vélodrome, where flares and other projectiles were thrown and rival supporters clashed before and during Thursday’s match.
Around 500 Levski fans were housed in the away section. About ten minutes before kick-off, several Marseille supporters ran from a home stand and breached the away enclosure, apparently targeting the Bulgarian fans. Projectiles and flares were thrown between the two groups, and further disturbances broke out during the half-time break.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital with injuries including eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder, according to the Marseille police prefecture. Around a dozen Bulgarian fans were reportedly injured in total. Despite the disturbances, the match kicked off as scheduled, with Marseille securing a 1-0 victory over the Bulgarian side.
The violence drew condemnation from French President Emmanuel Macron and his Bulgarian counterpart, Iliana Iotova. Levski Sofia coach Julio Velázquez also condemned the incidents, describing the scenes as “unacceptable for football”. The disturbances overshadowed the European fixture and renewed concerns over spectator safety at international club matches.

noticias.titulo: France's inflation slows to 2.9% in November as energy prices fall
noticias.resumen: Consumer prices fell by 0.7% in November 2026, after rising by 0.4% in October, according to the latest figures from Insee, published this Friday.
noticias.texto:
Consumer prices fell by 0.7% in November 2026, after rising by 0.4% in October, according to the latest figures from Insee, published this Friday.
Prices fell by 0.7% in November after rising by 0.4% in October, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) said on Friday.
This slowdown in inflation is largely explained by the movement in energy prices. While they are still showing a sharp increase compared with last year, they rose at a less rapid pace in November than in October, moving from +24,1 % to +19,2 %.
Insee particularly highlights the marked fall in prices of petroleum products, even though gas tariffs continue to rise.
Service inflation also fell back to 2,3 % year-on-year, after 2,6 % in October, a drop that Insee attributes to a "sharp slowdown" in prices for accommodation and transport.
By contrast, Insee records a slight increase in food prices (up 1,3 % over one year after 1,2 % in October), driven by a sharp rise in the fresh products sector (+9,4 % over one year compared with 8 % in October).
Consumption and unemployment stable
Meanwhile, French household spending on goods stabilised this month, after falling in September and August, according to Insee.
The drop in energy consumption (-2,9%) is offset by a rebound in consumption of manufactured goods (+1,3%), while food consumption remains stable (-0,1%).
The report also highlights the stability of salaried employment (0,0 %, that is -12 200 jobs, compared with -0,1 %, or -26 100 jobs, in the previous quarter). However, employment figures continue to fall year-on-year for the fifth consecutive quarter.
Salaried employment nonetheless clearly exceeds its level before the health crisis at the end of 2019 (+4,8 %, that is +1,2 million jobs), the national statistics institute notes.
However, France's gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 0,2 % in volume in the third quarter of 2026, after remaining stable in the previous quarter, Insee says, adding that the growth carry-over for 2026 stands at +0,1 %.
The purchasing power of households' gross disposable income (RDB) per consumption unit rose by 0,2 % (after a fall of 0,5 %), while the household saving rate stabilised in the third quarter at 17,4 % of their RDB.

noticias.titulo: What the ECB’s new leadership could mean for interest rates
noticias.resumen: Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde with eurozone inflation at twice the ECB’s target. Analysts expect broad policy continuity, but say he could take a more direct role in shaping interest-rate decisions.
noticias.texto:
Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde with eurozone inflation at twice the ECB’s target. Analysts expect broad policy continuity, but say he could take a more direct role in shaping interest-rate decisions.
European leaders have backed Spain’s former central bank chief, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, home to 359 million people.
This comes as the eurozone faces high inflation driven by the Iran war, and concerns over high government debt and borrowing costs across Europe.
Leaders from the 21 EU countries that use the euro also backed candidates for two other top posts at the ECB.
Hernández de Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, which is dubbed the central bank of central banks, in Basel, Switzerland. He served on the ECB’s rate-setting Governing Council from 2018 to 2024 as head of Spain’s central bank and has a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus.
Hernández de Cos built a reputation in Spain as a consensus builder. Analysts expect him to bring that approach to the ECB while taking a more active role than Lagarde in shaping monetary policy.
Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, told Euronews Business that "Pablo Hernández de Cos is an economists’ economist". He described him as "technically highly competent and respected" and said he takes an interest in the details of monetary policy.
Kenningham does not expect him to change the course of monetary policy much in the near term, "but he will be more likely to challenge advice from the Chief Economist than his predecessor".
Kenningham sees Hernández de Cos as leaning towards lower rates, in line with Capital Economics' forecast that the ECB may raise rates by just another quarter of a percentage point before starting to cut them by the end of 2027.
Eurozone inflation was 4% in October, above the bank’s 2% target. The ECB could still raise rates on 17 December, when Christine Lagarde will chair the meeting.
How Hernández de Cos might steer the ECB
ING's global head of macro, Carsten Brezski, told Euronews Business that he expected Hernández de Cos to play a more hands-on role. "We will now get a president (again) who will leave a clearer personal mark on monetary policy than his predecessor."
Brezski said he expected Hernández de Cos to continue building consensus on the Governing Council, as Lagarde had, while taking a more active role in shaping policy. He said investors would pay closer attention to the president’s speeches for clues about where interest rates were headed.
A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.
In 2020, Hernández de Cos backed the ECB’s pandemic bond-buying programme, which was expanded to €1.85 trillion. It helped keep borrowing costs down as closures and travel restrictions hit the economy. In a speech that year, he said the programme “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” and had lowered borrowing costs for eurozone governments and companies.
Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and rising interest costs.
Brezski sees Hernández de Cos as a pragmatist. "It’s hard to put De Cos into the dove-hawk category. In my view, he will simply be a very pragmatic central banker."
Two other seats on the ECB board
Hernández de Cos won out over another leading contender, former Dutch central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favours higher rates to ward off inflation.
The European Council also put forward France’s Laurence Boone, who heads Santander’s corporate and investment banking business in France, and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, for two seats on the ECB’s six-member executive board.
Brezski said France appeared to have played a key role in securing backing for Hernández de Cos. "It seems as if the French were key, shifting their support from Knot to De Cos." He suggested France may have put more weight on securing the role held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, including the implementation of any future bond purchases.
The ECB can buy bonds in certain circumstances to bring down government borrowing costs when it judges that market turmoil is unwarranted and threatens the way monetary policy works across the eurozone. Analysts say the bank is unlikely to step in if France’s borrowing costs rise because its politicians cannot agree on how to cut the deficit.
Kenningham sees Boone as more likely to favour lower rates than Isabel Schnabel, whom she would replace. He sees Brunnermeier as more likely to favour higher rates than Philip Lane, whom he would replace.
"The net impact on policy will probably therefore be small, though it remains to be seen what positions they take up when they are in post", he said.
The European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council will be consulted on all three candidates before EU leaders make the formal appointments.
Lagarde is leaving before her term ends
Lagarde, 70, announced on 29 October that she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to leave early so she could speak more freely about issues beyond monetary policy.
As for her plans, in an exclusive interview with Euronews, Lagarde said in July that she was "not a candidate for anything", playing down speculation that she might run in France’s presidential election.
In October, she declined to say whether she would back a candidate or what job she would take next. However, in November, Lagarde said a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was “one of the options” after she leaves the ECB. She already sits on the forum’s board of trustees.
Lagarde is regarded as having taken a pragmatic approach, building consensus among the national central bank governors who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being labelled a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.
She congratulated Hernández de Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.
“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Estonia prepares to close all five road border crossings with Russia
noticias.resumen: Long queues have formed at Estonia's border with Russia ahead of its planned closure on 1 December. The decision, prompted by security concerns, threatens to separate families and disrupt local businesses.
noticias.texto:
For families living on either side of the Estonian-Russian border, the impending closure threatens months of separation. People carrying suitcases queued at the Friendship Bridge linking Narva and Ivangorod, rushing to visit relatives before restrictions take effect. Some had given up their jobs in Estonia to be closer to elderly parents in Russia.
The closure follows sabotage attacks targeting Estonia’s defence industry, attributed by its security services to Russian intelligence. Moscow dismisses the allegations as unfounded and accuses Tallinn of seeking to erect a new “Iron Curtain”.
Beyond the human cost, the decision threatens businesses dependent on cross-border travel. Local authorities estimate annual revenue losses of between €500,000 and €600,000 for Narva and Setomaa, while the government is preparing a €2 million support package over six months.
All five road crossings will shut at 7am on 1 December for an initial six months, with rail freight through Narva continuing subject to sanctions. Around 3,000 people have signed a petition calling for exemptions on family grounds, particularly for those with sick or elderly relatives. The government will review the situation after six months.

noticias.titulo: Shanghai named the world's best shopping city – and Europe has just six entries in the top 20
noticias.resumen: Europe may be home to three of the world’s fashion capitals, but it has just six cities in Time Out’s top 20 shopping destinations ranking, with only London and Copenhagen making the top 10.
noticias.texto:
Europe may be home to three of the world’s fashion capitals, but it has just six cities in Time Out’s top 20 shopping destinations ranking, with only London and Copenhagen making the top 10.
For many of us, a trip to a new place isn’t complete without a little shopping. Around the world, tourists love to snap up a bargain which provides a long-lasting memory after the holiday is over.
Now, Time Out has ranked the best global shopping destinations, with Shanghai in China taking the top spot.
Despite being the home to three out of the “big four” fashion capitals, Europe only has six entries in the top 20, and just two – London and Copenhagen – are in the top 10.
That was decided by a combination of Time Out’s global network of editors, local experts and data from the publication’s annual Best Cities survey, which gathered the views of more than 24,000 local residents across 150 cities worldwide.
The scoring model combines 70% local sentiment and 30% expert evaluation, based on five key pillars:
- quality and variety of shopping, affordability, city vibe
- how safe and welcoming locals consider their city
- wider city experience
- the quality of restaurants, public transport and walkability
- expert evaluation, which is made up of Time Out editors’ assessment of each city’s shopping offering in 2026
These are the best cities for shopaholics to add to their bucket list.
Shanghai, China
Shanghai’s shopping scene is a mix of international names and a growing crop of homegrown fashion and lifestyle brands.
From rummaging for antiques at Juqi Antique City to browsing beauty boutiques along Anfu Road and exploring immersive retail spaces on Middle Huaihai Road, there’s plenty to discover.
Local labels including An Ko Rau, The Beast, Pane and Short Sentence are among Time Out’s recommendations.
London, United Kingdom
One of the four main fashion capitals – alongside Paris, New York and Milan – London is world-renowned for a hugely varied shopping scene.
It certainly caters to all tastes, from the famous department stores of Harrods, Liberty and Selfridges to the vintage shops of Brick Lane, designer boutiques on Bond Street and independent record stores in Soho.
For something quintessentially British, Time Out recommends stopping by the original Daunt Books in Marylebone, just north of shopping paradise Oxford Street.
Tokyo, Japan
It seems like Japan is on everyone’s must-visit list, judging by the number of viral shopping haul videos on social media.
That’s no surprise as Tokyo’s shopping districts offer everything from high-end fashion and vintage designer finds to quirky stationery, manga, cute trinkets and traditional crafts.
Ginza is the place for luxury labels and grand department stores, while Harajuku, Shibuya and Omotesando have a mix of independent boutiques and trend-led brands.
For vintage shopping, head to Shimokitazawa or Koenji, or visit Beams Japan for a curated selection of Japanese fashion, design and crafts.
New York City, United States
New York is the only non-European fashion capital, and its shopping credentials are legendary, far beyond Fifth Avenue and its iconic department stores.
Across the five boroughs, shoppers can discover independent designers, rare vinyl, vintage fashion, antiques, artisan goods and specialist retailers.
Time Out recommends Grand Bazaar on the Upper West Side, the city’s longest-running market, for discovering local makers and taking home a unique piece of the Big Apple.
Melbourne, Australia
Melbourne’s shops reflect the city’s creative, independent spirit, with everything from international labels and luxury fashion in the Central Business District (CBD) and Chadstone to vintage finds and emerging designers in Fitzroy and Collingwood.
Armadale’s High Street is a good place to discover Australian fashion, while beauty fans should make a beeline for Mecca’s flagship on Bourke Street.
