noticias.titulo: Germany and Austria push for European ownership of TikTok
noticias.resumen: The two countries want TikTok’s European business and key technology, including its recommendation algorithm, to come under European control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address security concerns.
noticias.texto:
The two countries want TikTok’s European business and key technology, including its recommendation algorithm, to come under European control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address security concerns.
Germany and Austria on Thursday called for TikTok's European business to be placed under European ownership and control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address concerns over data access and algorithms.
The Chinese-owned social media platform poses "fundamental security policy risks for Europe", German culture and media minister Wolfram Weimer said after meeting Austrian digital state secretary Alexander Proell in Vienna.
In a joint statement, the two politicians called for "a European ownership structure for TikTok's European business and European responsibility for the key technological infrastructure — from the recommendation algorithm to data access".
Germany and Austria will seek to build EU-wide support for their proposal at a meeting of the Telecommunications and Energy (TTE) Council in Brussels on December 2, the statement said.
On November 6, TikTok was preliminarily found to be in breach of Europe's Digital Services Act (DSA) over how its recommender system exposes users to potentially harmful content.
But Weimer and Proell said regulation did not answer "the basic question of who actually controls the platform".
"TikTok is no longer a toy, but part of the infrastructure of our democracy. This infrastructure must not remain in the hands of a geopolitical systemic rival," Proell said.
ByteDance, the Chinese parent company of TikTok, in January ceded control of the platform's US operations to a majority American-owned joint venture, in response to a threatened ban in the United States.
Weimer in May said he was "firmly convinced that Europe should follow the American example and that the company's ownership structure must be put up for discussion".
TikTok rejected the proposal as having "zero merit", saying it ignored existing European laws including the Digital Services Act and GDPR as well as the company's 12-billion-euro Project Clover data security programme.
TikTok also said its European operations are run by companies incorporated in Ireland and Britain and are subject to European law, while parent company ByteDance is majority-owned by global institutional investors and has no Chinese government ownership stake.

noticias.titulo: Thanksgiving turkeys fall from the sky for families in remote Alaska
noticias.resumen: Two friends in Alaska take to the skies each year to deliver Thanksgiving turkeys to families living in isolated wilderness communities, some completely off the grid and around 50 miles from the nearest road.
noticias.texto:
In south-central Alaska, two friends are taking to the skies to deliver the traditional holiday meal to families living in remote wilderness communities.
For the past few years, pilot Heidi Hastings and her friend Esther Keim have carried out the annual operation. While Hastings flies the aircraft, Keim drops the turkeys through the plane's window.
Some of the communities they reach are completely off the grid, around 50 miles from the nearest road. With snow and ice making access difficult, residents can struggle to get supplies, including a turkey for Thanksgiving.
Known as the “turkey bombers”, the two women have turned the flights into a yearly tradition, making sure families in some of Alaska's most remote areas can also enjoy a Thanksgiving meal.

noticias.titulo: Denmark arrests teenager over data breach affecting 11,000 people
noticias.resumen: An 18-year-old has been detained over the latest breach of Denmark’s national civil registry, two months after a separate cyberattack exposed data linked to 8.8 million people.
noticias.texto:
An 18-year-old has been detained over the latest breach of Denmark’s national civil registry, two months after a separate cyberattack exposed data linked to 8.8 million people.
An 18-year-old has been arrested in connection to a cyber-attack that leaked the personal information of 11,000 people from Denmark's national registry, authorities said Thursday, two months after another huge data hack.
Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised security systems since the early October attack, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed.
Despite that "the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach," the digital affairs ministry said.
"Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people," it said, adding that the breach was detected on November 23.
The incident "was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident."
An 18-year-old man has been arrested and remanded in custody "for having, without authorisation, accessed the Civil Registration System, where he managed to retrieve 11,000 identification numbers," police said in a statement.
The perpetrators of the October hack have not been identified yet.
But in October, an unidentified person contacted Danish newspaper Politiken in English via an encrypted messaging service and claimed responsibility.
The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company.
They said the employee's password was 123456.
In September, the Civil Security Agency raised the threat level for cyberattacks against Denmark to "high".
There has been a surge in cyberattacks, notably targeting supermarket refrigeration systems.
There has also been a series of false bomb threats against schools and planes across Europe, which could potentially be part of a hybrid warfare campaign.
That theory has not been confirmed, however, due to a lack of evidence.

noticias.titulo: Russia: Moscow's iconic Soviet-era expo park opens its 20,000-square-metre outdoor ice rink
noticias.resumen: Moscow's iconic VDNKh exhibition park has opened its vast outdoor ice rink for the winter season on Thursday 26 November 2026, welcoming skaters to 20,000 square metres of ice winding around the complex's landmark Soviet-era fountains.
noticias.texto:
Skaters glide past monumental Soviet-era pavilions and ornate fountains at Moscow’s largest ice rink, where a leisurely circuit feels more like a winter promenade than a sporting exercise. Stretching across more than 20,000 square metres, the rink can accommodate almost 5,000 people at once. Its route follows the exhibition park’s main avenue, passing Pavilion No. 1 and winding around the Friendship of Peoples and Stone Flower fountains.
First opened in 2015 and billed as Europe’s largest artificial ice rink, the complex covers some 68,300 square metres when its surrounding facilities are included. After nightfall, floodlit buildings and fountains transform the setting, accompanied by music drifting across the ice. Adult admission starts at 500 roubles (around €4.70), skate hire costs around 800 roubles (around €7.50), and the season continues until 28 February.
Beyond its architectural splendour, the rink has become a meeting place for generations of Muscovites. Some return each winter to reconnect with friends, while others enjoy the physical challenge of perfecting their technique.

noticias.titulo: Italian brand Armani to expand its luxury hotel empire in Egypt and Saudi Arabia
noticias.resumen: The Italian fashion house is expanding beyond its existing hotels in Dubai and Milan, with a new Red Sea resort planned for 2030 and a Riyadh opening expected next year.
noticias.texto:
The Italian fashion house is expanding beyond its existing hotels in Dubai and Milan, with a new Red Sea resort planned for 2030 and a Riyadh opening expected next year.
Fashion house Armani is stepping up its hospitality ambitions, with new luxury hotels planned in Saudi Arabia and Egypt.
Currently, the Italian luxury brand has properties in Dubai and Milan – where it was founded – but it’s decided to expand some distance from Italy’s fashion capital.
Instead, it has announced plans for its first hotel in Egypt, a beachfront development on the Red Sea scheduled to open in 2030. That announcement follows the ongoing construction of Armani Hotel Diriyah in Riyadh, which is expected to welcome its first guests in 2027.
The upcoming openings are part of a much bigger plan to grow Armani's presence in the luxury hospitality market.
At present, the brand operates two hotels: Armani Hotel Dubai, which occupies several floors of the Burj Khalifa, and Armani Hotel Milano.
The Dubai property opened in 2010, followed by the Milan hotel in 2011. Both were developed through Armani's long-standing partnership with businessman Mohamed Alabbar, founder of real estate development company Emaar.
In January 2026, the two parties announced a new joint venture through Alabbar's private investment company, Symphony Global, giving the partnership worldwide exclusivity to develop future Armani Hotels & Resorts in selected international destinations.
The agreement runs for 20 years, with an option to extend it by a further decade.
There have been rumours of potential future destinations for hotels and resorts, including London, Paris, New York, Miami, Bangkok, Singapore, Tokyo and the Maldives.
Here’s what we know so far about the confirmed upcoming openings.
Expansion into Saudi Arabia amid a tourism boom
Currently under construction in Diriyah, a historic area on the outskirts of Riyadh, Armani Hotel Diriyah is scheduled to open sometime in 2027.
The development forms part of the wider Diriyah project, one of Saudi Arabia's major tourism and cultural regeneration schemes, which is centred around the historic At-Turaif District, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The district’s traditional Najdi architecture, mud-brick buildings and narrow streets are a world away from Riyadh's modern skyscrapers.
The new hotel will bring Armani's design-led approach to this historic setting, adding another luxury accommodation option, among many already existing and soon to be opened, for visitors exploring the area.
Armani Hotels to make Egyptian debut on the Red Sea
Scheduled to open in 2030, Armani is planning a new hotel and residential development at Marassi Red Sea, a coastal resort and residential development near Hurghada International Airport.
The beachfront property will overlook both the Red Sea and the marina, bringing together hotel accommodation, serviced apartments and a limited collection of private residences carrying the Armani name.
Interiors will follow the aesthetic of Armani/Casa, the fashion house's furniture and interior design arm, with the brand promising its signature understated style and attention to detail throughout.
Wellness will also be a major part of the offering here. Plans include a dedicated sanctuary focused on health, restoration and longevity, with personalised treatments, fitness facilities and relaxation experiences.

noticias.titulo: Half of new HIV diagnoses in Greece are made late, early data shows
noticias.resumen: The number of new HIV diagnoses has fallen over the past year, but late diagnoses remain a challenge in Greece.
noticias.texto:
The number of new HIV diagnoses has fallen over the past year, but late diagnoses remain a challenge in Greece.
New HIV diagnoses in Greece have fallen year-over-year, but challenges remain, preliminary health data shows.
As of October, 490 new cases were recorded this year in the National HIV Registry, corresponding to 4.7 diagnoses per 100,000 population.
New diagnoses are at lower levels than in the same period of 2025, according to data from the National Public Health Organisation (EODY).
Despite the decline, there are significant challenges for timely diagnosis and epidemiological surveillance. Roughly half of the cases for which data were available were diagnosed at a late stage, and authorities don't know how the infection spread in a significant proportion of cases.
According to EODY data, 22,408 HIV infection cases have been recorded through October 2026. Among those cases, 5,200 people developed AIDS and 3,980 died. Meanwhile, 11,891 HIV patients received antiretroviral therapy (ART) to suppress their viral loads.
As for the new diagnoses, 84.1% were among men and 15.9% were among women.
Unprotected sexual contact continues to be the main way HIV spreads in Greece. Among the 490 new diagnoses, 41.6% concerned men who had unprotected sexual contact with men. Another 12.7% were linked to unprotected heterosexual sex, while 10.6% were linked to shared needles and other intravenous drug use.
However, the number of cases for which the transmission route is undefined or has not been filled in remains particularly high. This concerns 169 diagnoses, which represent 34.5% of the total.
One of the most important findings of the epidemiological report concerns late diagnosis of HIV infection. Among 281 new diagnoses that could be assessed, roughly half were made in a later stage.
Among people aged 40-49 the rate of late diagnosis reached 57.3%, while in the 50-and-over age group it rose to 62.5%. By contrast, lower rates were recorded among men who had sexual contact with men (41%) and among people aged 30-39 (34.7%).
The report also records a shift in the age distribution of new cases. While up to 2024 the 30-39 age group predominated, over the past two years people in their 40s have been the most frequent diagnoses. At the same time, in recent years there has been an increase in the proportion of diagnoses among people over 50.
Overall, 30.2% of new diagnoses were made among people in their 40s, followed by people in their 30s at 25.9% and people aged 50 and over at 22.9%.
Among the positive findings of the report is the decrease in new cases linked to the shared use of intravenous drugs.
Specifically, in 2026 a reduction of 22.4% was recorded compared with 2025. However, EODY emphasises that levels have not yet returned to those before the epidemic surge that occurred in the period 2011-2013.

noticias.titulo: Europe Today: EU leaders unable to find an agreement on EU's budget
noticias.resumen: The European Union’s 27 leaders met in Brussels yesterday with the aim of trying to find common ground on finalising the bloc’s budget. But red lines seemed to have deepened between the budget’s main opposing camps, we debrief the summit with our correspondents Angela Skujins and Sasha Vakulina.
noticias.texto:
The European Union’s 27 leaders met in Brussels yesterday with the aim of trying to find common ground on finalising the bloc’s budget. But red lines seemed to have deepened between the budget’s main opposing camps, we debrief the summit with our correspondents Angela Skujins and Sasha Vakulina.
On today’s show
An EU summit specifically convened to find a breakthrough on the European Union's next budget ended in disarray. The 27 heads of state and government, split in opposing camps, refused to abandon their red lines and openly questioned whether a deal could be reached by December. Our correspondent Angela Skujins brings us the latest news.
During the summit, EU leaders did found an agreement: over who will be the next European Central Bank president. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos, former governor of the Bank of Spain and current head of the Bank for International Settlements, is set to take over from Christine Lagarde in February. We speak with Francesco Papadia, senior fellow at the economic think tank Bruegel.
Hosuk Lee-Makiyama, director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, explains the impact of Trump's tariffs.
Javier Martínez-Cantó, Spanish political scientist, brings us the latest news on the Spanish election campaign ahead of Sunday's vote.
When and where to watch Europe Today?
You can join Euronews’ Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am, 9 am and 10 am Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter.

noticias.titulo: Germany's IG Metall reaches pay deal amid industrial crisis
noticias.resumen: A pay deal that could cover 3.7 million workers across Germany raises wages in two stages and lets struggling manufacturers seek labour cost savings in return for binding pledges to invest and protect jobs in Germany.
noticias.texto:
A pay deal that could cover 3.7 million workers across Germany raises wages in two stages and lets struggling manufacturers seek labour cost savings in return for binding pledges to invest and protect jobs in Germany.
Germany's largest trade union, IG Metall, and employers in the metal and electrical industries agreed a pay deal on Thursday after 26 hours of talks. The deal initially covers two German regions. If adopted nationwide, it could extend to 3.7 million workers in industries including carmaking, electrical equipment and electronics, aerospace, defence and mechanical engineering.
Employees covered by the agreement will receive a 2% pay rise from 1 May 2027, followed by a further rise of 2.3% from 1 April 2028.
They will also receive a one-off payment of €150, €300 or €450 in March 2027, depending on their employer's net return on sales, IG Metall said in a statement.
The agreement will run for 25 months, until 30 November 2028, Gesamtmetall, the umbrella organisation for the sector's employers' associations, said in a separate statement.
Trade unions and employers have also agreed on a mechanism which, according to Gesamtmetall, permits the "use of collective bargaining measures to reduce costs in return for commitments regarding investment, products or technologies which offer long-term employment prospects" in Germany.
The deal followed two waves of warning strikes involving more than 956,000 workers, according to IG Metall. Walkouts earlier this week hit plants operated by Mercedes-Benz and BMW.
IG Metall had sought a 5% pay rise over one year. Its president, Christiane Benner, called the deal "a solid agreement in turbulent times".
Gesamtmetall described it as a "painful compromise on pay".
"We are pushing the limits of what is possible and, for some of our companies, perhaps even going beyond them," said Gesamtmetall's president, Udo Dinglreiter.
Dinglreiter said the deal looked ahead and would "help to secure jobs and sites".
The pay talks came as German industry struggled, with the car sector under pressure from Chinese competition.
Germany’s economy grew by just 0.1% in the third quarter from the previous quarter, down from 0.3% in the second quarter. The federal statistics office had initially estimated third-quarter growth of 0.2%.

noticias.titulo: Why European households are rushing to buy solar panels ahead of a dark, cold winter
noticias.resumen: Changes to solar incentives and long installation processes mean European homeowners could benefit from planning now.
noticias.texto:
Changes to solar incentives and long installation processes mean European homeowners could benefit from planning now.
Winter is cold, dark and grey. Yet for many Europeans, it’s a great time to switch to solar power.
While many are focused on the holiday season, industry experts are urging homeowners considering a switch to solar to contact suppliers before Christmas – although not to take advantage of the winter sun.
Several European countries are making changes to solar energy subsidies and tax breaks in 2027, meaning homeowners might want to fast-track their plans to enjoy the financial benefits.
But even without changes to government incentives, there are good reasons to get ahead of the spring sunshine.
How long does it take to install solar panels?
Although a typical rooftop solar installation takes just one or two days, getting building permits and, in some cases, approval to connect to electricity grids can take weeks. Sometimes months.
Last year, an OECD report citing earlier research found that permit times for rooftop solar projects ranged from six weeks in Malta to as many as 10 months in Bulgaria.
The country has since made it easier for homeowners, scrapping permit requirements for solar systems up to 20 kilowatts intended for personal use, but delays are still common across Europe.
In Germany, a consumer watchdog warned last year that homeowners in Saxony were waiting months to have their solar panels connected to the grid – and, in extreme cases, more than a year.
And Edward Gurney, the founding director of the UK-based Solar and Battery Company, says getting approval from electricity providers can take four to five weeks even under normal circumstances.
“A lot of solar equipment is manufactured in China, and getting replacement stock delivered can take around six weeks,” he says.
Winter weather can also disrupt installation schedules, as icy roofs make working conditions unsafe.
“When you’ve already got a busy installation schedule, losing even a few days to bad weather can push subsequent installations back,” Gurney says.
Why it pays to install solar panels before spring
Waiting until the weather warms up could mean missing out on a prime period for solar production, too.
Solar power generated less than five per cent of the EU’s electricity in January last year, but by May, it was supplying more than 20 per cent, according to the European Environment Agency.
In Germany alone, 74 per cent of the solar electricity fed into the grid last year was generated between April and September.
The sooner homeowners have their panels installed, the sooner they can start benefitting from this springtime bump.
In the meantime, Gurney recommends using winter to assess how much electricity you might use and compare quotations from different installers.
“The number of panels, battery capacity and how much electricity your household uses will all affect the long-term value of the installation,” he says.
Solar subsidies are changing across Europe
Homeowners in several European countries could face changes to the cost of installing solar panels in 2027. Since April 2022, homeowners in England, Scotland and Wales have been able to have solar panels installed without paying value-added tax. From 1 April 2027, the tax rate will return to five per cent.
In Germany, people who install solar panels from January onward could miss out on government support unless new energy laws are approved before the end of the year, the German Solar Industry Association warns.
Although German lawmakers have tentatively agreed to continue paying homeowners for surplus electricity they sell to the grid from solar systems up to 25 kilowatts, they have yet to strike a final deal.
And in Austria, the government plans to stop offering grants for solar panels in 2027 and instead help homeowners buy batteries to store the electricity they generate.
In the UK, at least, the looming tax hike appears to be prompting consumers to act. The Solar and Battery Company reported a 37 per cent bump in enquiries about solar installations in early November as UK residents seek to beat the April deadline.
Gurney expects demand to continue growing as the deadline nears, but he also warns that booking an installation before April doesn’t guarantee homeowners will avoid having to pay the tax.

noticias.titulo: Mixing drugs is now the norm, EU drugs agency warns
noticias.resumen: Most drug-related ER visits in a new survey involved people who had taken more than one drug or mixed drugs with alcohol.
noticias.texto:
Most drug-related ER visits in a new survey involved people who had taken more than one drug or mixed drugs with alcohol.
Cocaine sent more people to the emergency room than any other drug in 2025, according to a new analysis of select hospitals from the European Union Drugs Agency.
Nearly 14,700 people sought emergency medical help for drug overdoses or other “acute drug-toxicity” at surveyed hospitals in 2025, the agency said. That includes both illegal drugs and misused prescription medications. The analysis dug into about 7,400 of these cases at 45 hospitals across 18 EU member states and Norway.
Cocaine was involved in 32% of ER visits, followed by cannabis (24%) and amphetamine (11%). In all, 39% of visits involved a single drug, while 23% involved a drug and alcohol and 38% involved multiple substances.
For example, 72% of patients who visited the ER about ketamine had also been drinking or used another drug, the report found. The most common combination was cannabis, cocaine and alcohol.
“Polysubstance use is more the norm than the exception,” said Isabelle Giraudon, the EUDA’s principal scientist on the health consequences of drug use.
That is worrisome because some drugs interact in ways that “cause additional problems and increase the risk of severe outcomes,” Giraudon told Euronews.
For example, she said people who take opioids or GHB/GBL (gamma-hydroxybutyrate/gamma-butyrolactone) — sometimes called “G” or “liquid ecstasy” — along with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other depressants may be at higher risk of respiratory slowdown, which can become life-threatening.
Patients who took a single drug, or a single drug and alcohol, spent a median of five hours in the hospital, compared with seven hours for people who took at least two drugs, the analysis found.
Overall, 66% of patients were medically discharged directly from the ER — but that varied depending on the drug they had used. Patients who used methamphetamine or amphetamines were more likely to be referred to a psychiatric ward than people who took other drugs.
Meanwhile, people on heroin or GHB/GBL were more likely to be sent to a critical care unit.
Younger people were more likely to visit the ER for ecstasy or nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas, while the median age was 38 for visits involving heroin and 36 for crack cocaine.
Men accounted for 72% of hospital visits, which peaked on weekends. Two-thirds of patients arrived by ambulance.
While there were big differences across European hospitals, this type of data can help “inform the local policy and responses, based on the local situation and needs, and improve preparedness,” Giraudon said.
Notably, the analysis only included drug poisoning patients who made it to the ER, not those who died of an overdose or were treated on site and did not go to the hospital. It also did not track health complications from regular drug use, such as infected injection sites or hepatitis B, a liver infection that spreads through blood and bodily fluids.
“This data represent only a fraction of drug-related harms,” Giraudon said.

noticias.titulo: These are Europe’s best attractions for families to visit in 2027, according to travellers
noticias.resumen: Trip.com has ranked Europe’s best family-friendly attractions for 2027, with Disneyland Paris at number one and London landmarks dominating the top 10.
noticias.texto:
Trip.com has ranked Europe’s best family-friendly attractions for 2027, with Disneyland Paris at number one and London landmarks dominating the top 10.
Keeping the whole family entertained while on holiday is no easy feat. Fortunately, there is no shortage of attractions in Europe that cater to travellers of all ages.
For families already planning where to go in the year ahead, Trip.com has compiled its 2027 Europe 50 Family-friendly Attractions ranking, which is based on “genuine customer reviews, year-round sales popularity, consistent quality assurance and distinctive themes”.
The best attractions were chosen for search popularity, thematic relevance, duration on the rankings and ranking position, with the family-friendly attractions being defined as those that offer “facilities and services, ensuring a safe, fun and educational experience”.
Disneyland Paris, which scored 4.7/5 across 4,177 reviews, has been recognised as Trip’s top family-friendly attraction for 2027. Having achieved a four-year streak on the platform’s annual lists, it offers families a getaway with parades and performances for children, alongside services for parents within its parks and hotels.
UK destinations dominated the list, with half of the entries within the top 10, including the iconic London Eye and Warner Bros Studio Tour London on the outskirts of the capital.
In the Netherlands, the water village of Giethoorn emerged in fifth place and offers families a quiet getaway known for its historic canals, narrow waterways and being car-free. Visitors can hop on a kayak, board a canal cruise or hire a “sloop”, which is a small electric boat ideal for sailing across the canals.
Ranked seventh, City Park in Budapest, Hungary, is a green escape that’s home to many species of plants and animals. Across 13,000 square metres, the main playground offers children ample space for play.
Pena Park in Sintra, Portugal, makes its first appearance on Trip’s annual lists. It ranked ninth overall and features winding, labyrinthine paths that weave beneath its dense woodland before arriving at the National Palace of Pena.
Rounding off the top 10 is Kalemegdan Park in Belgrade, Serbia. The cultural monument covers more than 60 hectares and features archaeological sites for history buffs.
Europe's best family friendly attractions to visit in 2027
- 1. Disneyland Paris, Chessy, France
- 2. London Eye, London, UK
- 3. Warner Bros. Studio Tour London, Watford, UK
- 4. Royal Observatory Greenwich, London, UK
- 5. Giethoorn, the Netherlands
- 6. The Natural History Museum, London, UK
- 7. City Park, Budapest, Hungary
- 8. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London, UK
- 9. Pena Park, Sintra, Portugal
- 10. Kalemegdan, Belgrade, Serbia
- 11. University of Cambridge, UK
- 12. The Lion King musical, London, UK
- 13. Siam Park, Costa Adeje, Spain
- 14. Tivoli Gardens, Copenhagen, Denmark
- 15. Santa Claus Village, Rovaniemi, Finland
The top three family-friendly attractions
Disneyland Paris
Topping the list of where families ought to visit in 2027 is a holiday destination where visitors, young and old can “hold court with Disney princess characters" and team up with Marvel super heroes.
The “magic” is split across two parks: Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World.
Disneyland Park is home to the iconic Sleeping Beauty Castle and five "lands" which families can explore. Throughout the park, it’s common to bump into characters such as Mickey Mouse and his pals.
Meanwhile, Disney Adventure World is home to worlds inspired by the family musical Frozen, as well as Marvel and Pixar films. There are themed attractions and visitors can also enjoy shows and more character encounters.
Trip recommends sightseeing for about one to two days, with a dated one-day ticket starting from €87 in January 2027, while children under the age of three can go for free.
London Eye
On the other side of the English Channel, the London Eye towers 135 metres over the UK’s capital. Built in 2000 to celebrate the millennium, this family-friendly destination is located on the South Bank and takes around 30 minutes for each rotation.
From such a height, visitors see iconic landmarks, including Elizabeth’s Tower which houses Big Ben, the architectural marvel of St. Paul’s Cathedral, the Houses of Parliament and Buckingham Palace. On a clear day from the top of the Eye, it is even possible to see Windsor Castle, 40 kilometres away.
The panoramic views will cost adults and children £29 (€34.52) for a ticket online, however, infants’ entry is free.
Warner Bros Studio Tour London
For set-jetters, rounding off the top three is Warner Bros Studio Tour London. This family-friendly attraction is adjacent to the working studio where all eight Harry Potter films were made. Here, visitors can explore two soundstages and a backlot of original sets, animatronic creatures and costumes, including Quidditch uniforms.
The themed fun continues into the dining hall where the menu at The Hogwarts Table is inspired by the films’ characters and recognisable locations. There’s also the Dragon Roasted Café where coffee is “brewed beneath the watchful gaze of the Ukrainian Ironbelly Dragon”.
Tickets in 2027 will start from £61 (€72.69), while children under four-years-old can go for free.

noticias.titulo: New Zealand election: newcomer centrist party to decide as Luxon scrambles for a majority
noticias.resumen: The final count showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.
noticias.texto:
The final count showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.
New Zealand's final vote count has left neither bloc with a majority, handing a brand-new centrist party the power to decide who governs.
The Electoral Commission's final tally showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.
The tally on Friday, after 400,000 special votes including ballots from New Zealanders abroad, showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National party dropping two seats to finish on 40.
The right-wing bloc now holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, one short of the 66 needed. The left, led by Labour's Chris Hipkins, has 58, with Labour on 36.
That leaves the Opportunity party, an unaligned centrist newcomer with seven seats, as kingmaker. Its support would not be enough to put the left in power, Hipkins conceded on Friday, in an apparent admission of defeat.
Luxon, who ruled out working with Opportunity before the 7 November vote, reversed course saying he was confident of forming a government with Opportunity and his usual partners, the libertarian ACT (13 seats) and the populist NZ First (12).
All three minor parties would need to back him.
"These negotiations may be challenging and they could take some time," he said. "But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly."
Qiulae Wong, the 38-year-old newcomer
Opportunity is led by 38-year-old business consultant Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either side. Her party's five "bottom line" policies include tougher climate action and an end to bottom-trawling, both at odds with ACT and NZ First.
Wong also repeated that she will not join a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters is foreign minister, citing his past remarks in parliament about Asian people. She said she would consider either a full coalition or a "confidence and supply" deal, under which her MPs would back key legislation and decide other bills case by case.
Both major parties took under 30% of the party vote: Labour 29.88% and National 28.35%. Analysts pointed to anger over the cost of living and little enthusiasm for either leader.
PM Luxon survived two confidence votes among his own MPs this year, while Hipkins led Labour to defeat in 2023. Minor parties on both flanks gained ground, with the Greens on 17 seats and Te Pati Māori on five.
Opportunity's rise is striking: it failed three times to enter parliament before Wong took over less than a year ago, and none of its new MPs has served before. If no government can be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh election.

noticias.titulo: Asia-Pacific trade bloc opens accession talks with UAE, Philippines and Indonesia
noticias.resumen: It could mark the start of the CPTPP alliance’s biggest expansion to date.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Trade ministers from the Trans-Pacific Partnership launched accession talks with the UAE, Philippines and Indonesia on Friday. The 12-nation trade alliance, also known as the CPTPP, agreed to establish three working groups to handle the negotiations, which could lead to its biggest expansion to date. Countries joining the alliance must commit to sweeping tariff liberalization as well as opening up digital trade. Accession talks with Uruguay, which have been running since early this year , are well advanced and could “potentially” be concluded early next year, a diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the plans told POLITICO. Trade ministers are meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, for the 11th CPTPP Commission meeting, hosted annually by a rotating chair. The U.K. became the first country without a Pacific coastline to join the bloc in 2024. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico and Singapore were among its founding members in 2018. Decisions are taken by consensus. The U.K. is expected to sign a trade deal soon with the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE. But London has yet to strike trade deals with the fast-growing Indonesian and Philippine economies. Negotiations with the three nations “are all complicated and will require serious effort to get across the line,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation think tank. “This includes capacity building for some applicants to make certain that everyone is clear on what the CPTPP requires, as well as careful work to ensure that member concerns are addressed.” The bloc is emerging as a “Plan B” as efforts to reform the World Trade Organization falter. China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Ukraine, Cambodia and Argentina have also applied to join.

noticias.titulo: The man who coined ‘Brexit’ likes the sound of ‘Breturn’ and ‘Brejoin’
noticias.resumen: Peter Wilding - credited by Oxford English Dictionary with first using the term Brexit - says having a snappy new shorthand will bring the arguments into the present.
noticias.texto: LONDON — The political strategist credited with first using the term Brexit says it’s too early to predict slogans for a future referendum — but rates Breturn and Brejoin as potential portmanteaux. Peter Wilding, a consultant based in Brussels, told POLITICO that the political landscape has shifted since 2016 when Brits voted to leave the EU and that pro-EU campaign rhetoric will have to change to keep up. His comments come as U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reopens the conversation on Britain’s relationship with Europe, and campaigners on both sides of the debate regroup in preparation for a potential second fight over bloc membership. Since arriving in Downing Street, Burnham has argued that Brexit “has not worked” as he tees up tighter ties with the EU. He has said that he hopes to rejoin within his lifetime — but insisted Monday that it would be “unthinkable” to do so without a referendum. “If you’re looking for something catchy, there’s a couple of options: Let’s Breturn or Brejoin,” Wilding said when asked what the moniker for a future campaign should be. “But really, Burnham doesn’t want to go back to the past, he wants to go to the future, and the faces and arguments of 2016 will be dumped.” “There will be a tonal change where Burnham caters his argument towards the younger vote and the business vote — seizing these cohorts will be vital to electoral success,” the strategist added. Wilding coined Brexit in 2012 when he penned an article on Britain’s place in Europe. “Unless a clear view is pushed that Britain must lead in Europe at the very least to achieve the completion of the single market, then the portmanteau for Greek euro exit might be followed by another sad word, Brexit,” he wrote for news outlet Euractiv , now known as Rapporteur. His writing is cited as the earliest evidence of the word Brexit in the Oxford English Dictionary. The term was subsequently adopted as the accepted shorthand for the U.K. leaving Europe and was plastered on buses and billboards during the 2016 referendum campaign on Britain’s membership. Having a snappy way of encapsulating the Vote Leave argument — and catchy slogans to go alongside — was crucial in building the campaign in the public imagination, Wilding said. “The Take Back Control control slogan was an absolute winner.” As Burnham gears up to set out different options for the U.K.-EU relationship, Wilding argued that the British prime minister has already got the upper hand on the opposition by co-opting the winning slogans of the past. “Burnham has found the two best weapons from the 2016 campaign: take back control and immigration, and he has occupied that territory,” he said, pointing to the Labour leader’s party conference speech in September . The PM told supporters in Liverpool: “The British Right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place.” Wilding said that Burnham’s gradual approach to deepening Britain’s ties with Brussels is “flushing out” the opposition — who he claimed look “splutteringly indignant” when they trot out 2016-era arguments that have been disproved. “Burnham is tackling the immigration argument head on,” Wilding said. “He can say you won that referendum on immigration and the Boriswave threw your credibility away and because of that you don’t have an argument to make” — a term coined by the online right to describe the increase in migration under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s Conservative government following the pandemic. Nigel Farage, a key architect of the campaign to pull the U.K. out of the EU, announced Wednesday that he is launching a new effort Keep Britain Out. “There will be a lot of online battling,” Wilding said. “But the only leader is Burnham himself, and what he says and does will affect the development of the Get In and Stay Out campaigns.” On the question of whether the public is ready for another full-blown campaign, the Brexit-coiner said: “I don’t think they are. I think we are in the team talk period before the match begins and anything can happen in the next year.”

noticias.titulo: Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ?
noticias.resumen: Plus de 78% des sites des services publics maltais reposent sur de la technologie américaine, contre moins de 3% en Allemagne. Qu'en est-il en France ?
noticias.texto:
Dépendance aux Big Tech américaines : où en est la France par rapport à ses voisins européens ?
Plus de 78% des sites des services publics maltais reposent sur de la technologie américaine, contre moins de 3% en Allemagne. Qu’en est-il en France ?
BRUXELLES — Même si l'UE est unie dans sa volonté de réduire sa dépendance aux technologies américaines, chaque Etat membre devra se débrancher de son côté — et certains auront bien plus d'efforts à fournir que d'autres.
Une étude menée par des chercheurs finlandais a mis en évidence de grandes disparités dans le degré de dépendance des Etats européens envers Amazon, Microsoft et Google pour les services publics numériques destinés aux citoyens.
"Cette variation n’est pas aléatoire, elle est systématique", explique Vili Lehdonvirta, professeur de politique technologique à l’université finlandaise Aalto et coauteur du rapport.
Advertisement
Les chercheurs ont analysé les sites web gouvernementaux de 158 pays — notamment les portails permettant aux citoyens de trouver des informations, de déposer des demandes et d'effectuer des démarches administratives — afin d'évaluer dans quelle mesure ceux-ci dépendent des trois géants de la tech américaine.
Au sein de l'UE, Malte, la Finlande et l'Irlande affichent les parts les plus élevées de services publics nationaux hébergés par des hyperscalers américains : respectivement 78,5%, 56,1% et 45,8%.
En revanche, le taux estimé pour la France est de 9,3%, comparé à 2,9% pour l'Allemagne.
La publication de cette étude intervient alors que l'UE négocie actuellement un projet de législation qui obligerait les administrations publiques à revoir leurs achats de solutions digitales américaines, dans un contexte marqué par les menaces répétées de Washington contre les politiques numériques de Bruxelles, de tentatives locales de se passer des services américains et les récentes pannes ayant affecté des outils informatiques très répandus.
Selon l'étude, Bahreïn présente le plus fort degré de dépendance au monde, les services américains hébergeant 81% des sites étudiés, tandis que la Russie et la Chine ne comptent aucun site public lié aux trois géants de la tech.
Les chercheurs ont constaté que les disparités dans le recours aux Big Tech tendent à être liées à la taille d'un pays et au coût du travail.
Advertisement
"L'explication est d'ordre économique : dans un grand pays, le marché domestique est mieux à même de soutenir des alternatives ou des technologies nationales, qui impliquent des investissements importants et des économies d'échelle élevées", a détaillé Vili Lehdonvirta.
Pourquoi la taille compte
En Europe, la carte de la dépendance aux technologies américaines suit des tendances similaires, reflétant la taille du marché et le niveau de revenu. Cependant, elle est également plus contrastée en raison d'un ensemble hétéroclite de choix nationaux qui complique les efforts de l'UE visant à réduire ces dépendances stratégiques.
"Dans l’ensemble, on a cette configuration où les petits Etats membres ont recours au cloud américain et pas les grands Etats membres", a décrit Vili Lehdonvirta. "Le cloud est un exemple de technologie qui nécessite un investissement initial important, et ensuite, plus on opère à grande échelle, plus elle est efficace."
La méthodologie de l’étude présente certaines limites pour évaluer le degré de dépendance globale, car elle se concentre uniquement sur l’hébergement des services nationaux destinés au grand public, et non sur les systèmes locaux ni sur l’utilisation plus large de la technologie au sein de l’administration. Par exemple, Vili Lehdonvirta indique que les entités municipales — tels que les conseils d'école ou les systèmes de billetterie des piscines — sont plus susceptibles de recourir à des technologies américaines, la souveraineté numérique ne relevant pas de leurs compétences.
La taille et les revenus ne font pas tout non plus : les choix politiques déterminent également si les pays développent ou non des fournisseurs nationaux.
Au Royaume-Uni — la cinquième puissance mondiale —, 50,9% des sites gouvernementaux dépendent de technologies américaines, selon l'étude. Vili Lehdonvirta rappelle que l'exécutif britannique "a décidé, il y a environ quinze ans, de mettre le paquet sur le cloud dans le cadre d’une directive du gouvernement s’appliquant à tous les ministères et agences gouvernementales". En l’absence d’alternatives nationales, "très rapidement, tout a migré vers le cloud américain. Aujourd’hui, il serait difficile de revenir en arrière, même s’ils le souhaitaient", souligne-t-il.
Advertisement
De nouvelles règles à venir
La publication de cette étude intervient alors que les responsables politiques à Bruxelles débattent pour savoir où fixer les limites : les nouvelles règles proposées — dans le Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) — devraient-elles obliger les administrations publiques à réaliser des tests de souveraineté et à se tourner vers des alternatives européennes pour les secteurs les plus sensibles, ce qui pourrait évincer les géants américains de la tech ?
Rien que dans le secteur privé, les entreprises européennes dépensent environ 330 milliards d'euros par an en services cloud et logiciels américains, ce qui confère à la tech américaine une part de marché estimée à 83% selon une étude de 2025.
Mais les Etats membres n'ont pas tous intérêt à des règles strictes en la matière. Cela dépend en partie s'ils ont ou non des fournisseurs nationaux prêts à rivaliser.
Josh Kallmer, directeur des affaires internationales chez Zoom, dont le siège est aux Etats-Unis, estime pour sa part que l'échelon européen est le bon niveau pour agir, car il permettrait d’éviter des règles différentes dans chaque pays. "Cette divergence supplémentaire affecte une entreprise comme la nôtre", a-t-il déclaré lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO. "Chaque restriction supplémentaire mise en place a un impact beaucoup plus important sur la liberté de choix dans les pays de taille moyenne et les petits pays."
Les négociateurs du CADA en sont pleinement conscients. "Nous devons essayer de mettre en place un cadre clair afin que les 27 pays aient la même interprétation de la loi, car, en fin de compte, le but est de faciliter la tâche des PME en Europe", dit Diego Solier, eurodéputé membre des Conservateurs et réformistes européens, qui est l'un des principaux négociateurs sur ce dossier.
Pour le coauteur de l'étude, Vili Lehdonvirta, ce texte risque de rater sa cible s'il ne répartit pas plus équitablement les coûts et avantages au sein de l'UE.
"Le coût de la mise en conformité de cette politique pèse principalement sur les petits Etats membres, tandis que ses avantages, à savoir l’augmentation de l’activité économique, profitent surtout aux grands Etats membres", développe-t-il. "Si nous ne disposons d’aucun mécanisme de partage des charges, le résultat final sera similaire à ce que nous observons actuellement, c’est-à-dire une sorte de tentative timide qui n’oblige pas vraiment qui que ce soit à agir."
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

noticias.titulo: ‘Islam is Sharia’: Germany’s far-right leader attacks Le Pen on Muslims and Europe
noticias.resumen: AfD’s Alice Weidel talks mass deportations, the right to Israel’s existence and peace with Russia.
noticias.texto: BERLIN — Alice Weidel sees her far-right Alternative for Germany as the country’s new mainstream party. That doesn’t mean she’s moderating her message. In a wide-ranging interview, the co-leader of the AfD — Germany’s most popular party — called for the departure of millions of migrants and accused Germany’s Central Council of Jews of taking its marching orders from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats. She also took aim at Marine Le Pen, accusing the far-right French presidential candidate of isolating her own party on the European right by bashing Germany. “Yes, I’m keeping my fingers crossed for Ms. Le Pen,” Weidel said during an interview with a new weekly video podcast from WELT published Friday. WELT, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. But Weidel bristled at Le Pen’s call this week for a “Europe of nations” to replace a “German Europe.” The leader of France’s far-right National Rally party had “perhaps misunderstood something, or doesn’t see how the money flows,” Weidel said, referring to Germany paying the largest portion of the EU budget. The relationship between the two parties has been cold since Le Pen cut ties with the AfD in 2024, after one of the AfD’s leading politicians told an Italian newspaper that not every SS member was automatically a criminal. Among Europe’s “patriotic” parties, “it is not the AfD that is isolated, but increasingly the National Rally, if it carries on like this,” she added. Weidel also rejected Le Pen’s contention in a television appearance in October that Islam, unlike Sharia, is compatible with the French Republic: “Islam is Sharia and Sharia is Islam.” Le Pen has worked to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust. On the subject of expelling migrants from Germany, Weidel outbid her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, who recently put the number of people who should leave Germany at 2.6 million. “Frankly, the number is much larger,” she said, and listed whom she meant: the roughly 250,000 people already obliged to leave the country as well as violent offenders, Islamists and others who “hang around in our social hammock, live an easy life here and don’t integrate.” She added those whose protection she would revoke once the reason for fleeing no longer applies — “completely, entirely, all” 900,000 Syrians, all Afghans and, after a peace deal, 1.1 million Ukrainians. On Ukraine, Weidel doubled down on her claim that Kyiv had already lost the war. If she were in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s shoes, she would recommend “immediately flying to Russia and sitting down at the table with Putin.” She added: “I would do it.” Weidel dismissed the suggestion that a Russian victory would trigger another wave of refugees heading west. “There will be no refugee movement. Quite the opposite,” she said, arguing that Ukrainians in Germany would return home once peace was established “because they are needed there.” Weidel was more evasive on the subject of Israel. Asked about a now-deleted post by AfD lawmaker Kay Gottschalk stating there is no “right to exist” for any nation, Weidel called it “botched.” Asked directly whether Israel has a right to exist, she said, “As a German party, what befits us first and foremost is defending Germany’s sovereignty. That is in our national interest.” Then, “to answer your question directly”: anyone who looks at the AfD’s motions in the Bundestag over the past ten years “will see who stands at Israel’s side.” The AfD, she added, is “the only and last protective power of Jewish life in Germany.” Asked why, then, the Central Council of Jews in Germany warns against her party, Weidel claimed the organization had been politicized by the CDU. “It is permanently being used as a weapon against the AfD,” she said, offering no evidence. Council President Josef Schuster has repeatedly warned that an AfD government would endanger Jewish life in Germany, citing the party’s positions on religious practices and its politicians’ remarks about the Nazi era. The Council did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement provided to POLITICO after publication, Schuster described Weidel’s allegation as “absurd.” “For years, the AfD has been searching for a fig leaf for its resentment-laden politics, while at the same time seeking to restrict freedom of religion and to destroy the consensus on the politics of remembrance,” he said. “The Jewish community in Germany will not provide it with that fig leaf.” In September, Weidel declared that the AfD had supplanted the Christian Democrats as Germany’s traditional people’s party — meaning a party with broad appeal across society . For all her attacks on the Christian Democrats, Weidel made clear she was still open to working with them. The CDU, which she no longer considers a center-right party, was “destroying itself behind the firewall,” she said, referring to the longstanding agreement by Germany’s establishment parties not to work with the far right. Her hand, she said, remains “outstretched.” UPDATED: This article was update on Nov. 11 with a comment from Schuster. Marc Felix Serra o is a Global Reporter with The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network and co-host of “Zur Wahrheit gehört” (“Part of the Truth”), a new weekly video podcast from WELT. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio .

noticias.resumen: Presented by Fusion for Energy.
noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Thursday’s European Council summit ended in disarray after frugal countries pushing for a smaller EU long-term budget walked out of planned negotiations led by European Council President António Costa. Some are even pushing for him to give up his role trying to broker a deal. While no one expected a final deal on the MFF at this summit, talks have been acrimonious. What went so wrong? Will Costa be pushed out as a negotiator? And why are EU diplomats booking extra hotel room nights for December’s Council meeting? Kathryn Carlson, covering Sarah Wheaton’s maternity leave, asks what’s next for the budget talks after the disastrous summit. And she digs into the challenges the next European Central Bank president, Pablo Hernández de Cos, will face when he succeeds Christine Lagarde. She’s joined by Chief Foreign Affairs Correspondent Nick Vinocur, finance reporter Gregorio Sorgi and Deputy Finance Editor Bjarke Smith-Meyer. noticias.titulo: Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans
noticias.resumen: Tech needs boundaries — "a bit like rearing children," says Andrew Bailey.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned governments need to reassure the public about the benefits of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models, amid rising fears the technology is advancing at a pace beyond human control. As the U.K. prepares to take over the G20 presidency, Bailey backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plan to put AI at the heart of the country’s plans. But the U.K. central banker said lawmakers, not regulators, would have to set the guardrails for the technology. “It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England. With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI. U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as “super intelligence.” Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency. The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system. With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves. But the governor argued it was reasonable for the public to ask what the benefit is from the rapid growth of a technology which could be used to blow holes in the financial system, but also order the Christmas shopping. “The public needs to trust this technology,” he said. “There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.” He added: “It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.” The U.K. central banker is acutely aware of the threats the new technology could bring to the financial system. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee report on Thursday spelled out risks including increasingly interconnected and opaque financing that could spread the pain should a potential stock market AI bubble burst. But Bailey said he would put himself in a camp of people who want AI to succeed to improve productivity and well-being. “But it has to be under human control,” he said. “We want AI to be used by humans, as it were.”

noticias.titulo: Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out
noticias.resumen: Kyiv is pushing for tougher checks on neutral status, a ban on Kremlin-linked symbols and funding cuts for sports bodies that let Russians compete.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Kyiv is stepping up its bid to keep Russian athletes out of global sports tournaments. “We cannot allow international sport to become the weak link in the democratic world,” Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi told POLITICO from Brussels, where he met EU sports ministers, as legal and political momentum builds for Russian competitors to return. International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry has said athletes should not pay for governmental actions ; top sporting organizations have eased restrictions instituted in 2022 after the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion began; and a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling overturned ice hockey’s ban on Russian teams. Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added. With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted. Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.” “I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position. No propaganda in sport On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries. In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals. The countries wanted the Commission’s guidelines on visa applications by Russians to prevent nonessential travel, including to sporting events, rather than wait for a revised Visa Code that is not expected before the first quarter of 2027. They also encouraged fellow EU countries not to grant visas to Russian or Belarusian athletes. Bidnyi said his three points are designed to stop Russia from using sport for propaganda, while Moscow maintains a relentless bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. The first measure is a ban on Russian symbols, such as flags or the national anthem. “It’s unacceptable that the anthem of a country that kills peaceful people in Europe today sounds in such a cheerful manner in European arenas,” he said. A photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik showing Vladimir Putin meeting young ice hockey players while visiting the VOLGA Arena multifunctional sports complex in Nizhny Novgorod on Aug. 28, 2026. | Kirill Zykov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images The second is to make “neutral athlete” status something that is actually verified. “The neutral status should be maintained by detailed checking,” Bidnyi said. “We must check all aspects.” The third is money. Bidnyi pointed to the new EU restriction on Erasmus+ funding — the bloc’s main program for education, training, youth and sport — for organizations that allow Russian state symbols, calling it a “first concrete result.” He wants the same model widened to organizations that let Russians use sport as a “tool of propaganda,” whether or not symbols are involved. Bidnyi also raised the issue of soldiers that have become athletes, which touches the EU’s newest migration measures. The Commission’s visa guidelines , published this week alongside the sanctions package, tell national authorities to refuse visas to anyone who has served in Russia’s armed forces and fought in the war. Bidnyi said the International Paralympic Committee has tolerated combatants taking part in its events, and that Russia is now trying to put soldiers who fought in Ukraine on its Paralympic teams. He called that “absolutely unacceptable.” Europe, he said, already refuses visas to combatants, and “it should be like this.” The IPC said it has no rules barring former soldiers from competing, pointing to the movement’s origins in rehabilitating injured war veterans after World War II. Nor is it its role, the IPC added, “to make moral judgments on which injured soldiers should or should not be allowed to compete.” It said former soldiers from countries including the U.S., Britain, Iraq, Bosnia and Iran have competed, and that it expects more at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. The IPC said its responsibility is to decide which national Paralympic committees and athletes are eligible and to enforce its conduct rules. It said accreditation for the Games is the final decision of the organizing committee and national authorities, which handle security and background checks. Their organization’s answer did not mention Russia or Ukraine. Russia’s sports minister, who the EU has also sanctioned, stated in September that more than 70 war veterans were already on national teams. Bidnyi also alleged that the Russian Union of Martial Arts recruits on behalf of units fighting in Ukraine and trains drone operators, and said that should be prohibited. The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Bidnyi’s assertions about Russia’s military recruitment and wider propaganda strategy. Ice hockey backlash Sporting institutions, however, are gradually moving toward Russian reinstatement. On one side of the confrontation, Bidnyi said, are governing bodies, courts and federations, which are “gradually opening the door to Russians hiding behind claims of neutrality.” His primary example is the Oct. 30 decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ban on Russian teams for the 2026-27 season. “The hockey case is the most outrageous example of Russian influence,” Bidnyi said. Russian Alexander Ovechkin celebrates during the charity hockey “Match of the Year” between Russian players of the National Hockey League and the Kontinental Hockey League at the CSKA arena in Moscow on July 13, 2025. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images Asked for comment, CAS said that the case, brought by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the IIHF, “was decided on a strictly legal basis” and that it is not aware of any circumstance that could have affected the panel’s independence. Ultimately, that ruling set off a backlash. Finland, Sweden, Czechia, Norway, Austria, Denmark and Latvia have said they will play at next May’s men’s world championship in Germany but not against Russia — which means almost half of the 16 teams are refusing to face Russia. Canada’s government said Russia will not be allowed to play at the world juniors there next month. Sponsors are also balking, with Skoda, the tournament’s main sponsor, saying it will reassess its backing. The IIHF says it still disagrees with the ruling. Sanctions have also been lifted in gymnastics, weightlifting and chess, and the international ski federation has cleared more than 400 Russian and Belarusian athletes and support staff to compete as neutrals this season. Bidnyi expects more of the same. The IOC’s decision to reinstate the Russian Olympic Committee, he said, “has set a dangerous precedent. International federations may now begin lifting restrictions one after another, hiding behind the autonomy of sport.” Moscow, Bidnyi said, will keep going back to CAS and present every readmission as a propaganda win, with Putin personally overseeing the effort. On the other side, he said, are governments, which can take a “principled stand” and refuse to let Russian representatives or the symbols of an aggressor state onto their territory. Russian participation “has long ceased to be merely a matter of sporting regulations,” he said. “It is a question of national security.” The next chance to build a common position is a meeting of sports ministers in Tallinn in January. Bidnyi said it could bring in non-EU countries such as Canada and Norway, which have already taken firm action.

noticias.titulo: Spain’s looming right-wing pivot on climate is already playing out in Valencia
noticias.resumen: The center-right People's Party and far-right Vox's record in the flood-hit region offers clues on how their climate-skeptic policies could play out at the national level.
noticias.texto: VALENCIA — Spain’s climate agenda could be in for a radical shake-up if conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo takes power alongside the far-right Vox party after Sunday’s election — a prospect already playing out in Valencia. Feijóo has pledged to scrap what he calls “unrealistic” timelines for climate goals, arguing that Spain must pursue decarbonization at a more pragmatic pace. His center-right People’s Party argues that climate ambitions must not come at the expense of economic competitiveness, industry or households. His likely coalition partners, the far-right Vox party, want to go further — promising to dismantle what they call “climate impositions” from Brussels, remove low-emission zones and reverse restrictions on combustion-engine cars and CO₂ emissions. The two parties’ dismantling of climate policy can already be seen in Spain’s Valencia region, where the PP has governed with Vox’s backing since 2023, coinciding with a rollback of environmental protections and the deadly floods of October 2024. “The dangerous climate skepticism that will define a PP-Vox government at the national level has been on display here in Valencia from the moment they took power,” warned Raül Camacho Segarra, a spokesperson for the Valencian grassroots movement working to rebuild flood-damaged areas responsibly . The floods put the government’s approach to land use, environmental regulation and climate adaptation under intense scrutiny. Yet shortly after, PP politician Juanfran Pérez Llorca was sworn in as the region’s new president and reaffirmed his opposition to parts of the climate agenda, describing the center-right European People’s Party’s Green Deal as a “threat” to Valencia’s farmers. Local critics like Camacho accuse the right-wing government of failing to learn the lessons of the disaster and endangering the region’s communities. “The policies they instituted ahead of the floods made us more vulnerable, and instead of recalibrating after the tragedy, they’ve actually doubled down since 2024,” he said, pointing to the allocation of public funds to bullfighting events instead of emergency response and promoting construction in areas needed for flood prevention. Ana Camarasa, a physical geographer and regional flood risk expert at the University of Valencia, questioned politicians’ ability to pursue effective long-term resilience strategies while casting doubt on the threat posed by climate change. “Governments that deny climate change ultimately aren’t obliged to take measures to address it, because it’s a problem that officially doesn’t exist,” she said. Controversial climate record With its millions of voters, Spain’s fourth-most-populous region is a coveted prize in the country’s political battle for power. After eight years of left-wing rule, in 2023 the PP teamed up with Vox to take control of Valencia, forming one of its first regional coalition governments with the far right. Under regional president Carlos Mazón, the new administration moved to scrap plans for a regional emergency response unit , dismantled key elements of Valencia’s climate law and emissions taxes , and disbanded a newly created agency to monitor climate change . His government also eased rules governing development on flood-prone coastlines and protected agricultural land. Those decisions came under renewed scrutiny on Oct. 29, 2024, when Valencia was hit by one of the deadliest floods in modern Spanish history . The regional government downplayed the threat posed by a powerful storm that swept through the region, unleashing torrential rain that inundated towns and killed 229 people. President of Valencia’s Region Carlos Mazón gives a press conference to announce his resignation at Valencia’s Palau de la Generalitat on November 3, 2025. | Jose Jordan/ AFP via Getty Images For months after the disaster, Mazón — who controversially remained at an hours-long private lunch as the floodwaters rose — refused to take responsibility for his government’s handling of the catastrophe. Although crisis management is a regional responsibility, the PP shifted blame onto the national government and then-Deputy Prime Minister Teresa Ribera. But Spanish courts exonerated both national authorities and Ribera, noting the regional government was the only entity authorized to manage the crisis. After being denounced as an “assassin” by victims’ relatives one year on, Mazón finally stepped down . His successor, Pérez Llorca, took office promising to rebuild the region and leave it better prepared for future disasters. Yet key climate-protection measures have been further weakened since the floods. Weeks after the disaster, the government pressed ahead with legislative changes to allow construction closer to shorelines. More recently, other controversial proposals have surfaced, including a plan to build more than 1,200 homes on farmland that critics say is instrumental to absorbing water during torrential rainstorms. In an interview, Raúl Mérida, the technocrat appointed to oversee the region’s recovery, defended its reconstruction and adaptation efforts while playing down the significance of the Valencian government’s climate-skeptic statements. “Our actions are based on science,” he said, adding that politicians across the political spectrum had backed his proposals to build floodable parks and carry out environmentally conscious river-restoration schemes that aim to better protect communities against future storms. According to Mérida, 98% of infrastructure damaged in the disaster has been rebuilt. But he acknowledged that rebuilding did not necessarily mean the region was now better protected against flooding. “The emergency contracts only allowed us to restore the infrastructure that was there, not improve it,” he said, citing roads and bridges. “We had to rebuild some infrastructure that had proved inadequate in reducing the severity of the floods in the same way.” He added that the government had reinforced foundations and added protective stone embankments . When it came to private homes, he said, things were more complicated: Residents often had deep family roots and longstanding ties to the communities where they lived. Like other rapidly growing Spanish regions, Mérida said Valencia was under pressure to build more housing and had enough land to do so as long as flood-zone regulations were respected. But he insisted that the priority would be ensuring “regulations governing flood-prone areas are respected” and that “citizens and territory are protected.” “Adaptation measures work just as well in a left-wing municipality as they do in a right-wing one,” he said, adding that protecting communities from extreme weather should transcend party lines. The limits of green consensus In a September POLITICO poll carried out by PF Global, 60% of Spanish respondents described climate change as either the most important or one of the most important issues of our time. But the poll also suggests Spaniards are wary of climate action overshadowing other national priorities. Nearly half — 49.2% — said the country’s energy and environmental policies were diverting resources from other pressing issues, including the cost-of-living crisis, healthcare and housing. Just over half — 50.3% — said Spain should act on climate change but not more than other countries. That national ambivalence could give the PP and Vox room to argue for a slower, less costly green transition — even as voters continue to regard climate change as a major concern. Widespread anger over the deadly 2024 floods doesn’t seem to have weakened the right-wing bloc’s electoral prospects in the region: A range of polls project the PP and Vox could win 19 of the region’s 33 seats in Spain’s 350-seat parliament. Cars are piled in the street with other debris after flash floods hit the region on October 30, 2024 in the Sedaví area of Valencia, Spain. | David Ramos/Getty Images In Valencia’s central province (excluding Castellón and Alicante), where 16 seats are up for grabs, Vox is projected to double its representation, from two seats in 2023 to four in 2026. David Ribó, a candidate for the left-wing regionalist Compromís-Front Valencià coalition, said he was dismayed by the polling: “It boggles the mind that in a region that is the epicenter of climate change, political options that are openly denialist are still attracting votes.” Ribó argued that Vox’s success did not reflect public apathy to climate change, but rather frustration with mainstream parties, as seen in the immediate aftermath of the floods, when the populist slogan “sólo el pueblo salva el pueblo” (“only the people can save the people”) was directed at political leaders and institutions perceived to have abandoned the region. “People are struggling to make ends meet — especially because of the insane prices they’re having to pay for housing — and naturally, there is a sense of discontent,” he said. The “inequality crisis,” he argued, is pushing disillusioned voters toward populist leaders. The University of Valencia’s Camarasa expressed concern over the increasing climate skepticism in Spanish politics, arguing certain topics “shouldn’t be treated as an ideological matter: The data is there, and we’ve also seen the consequences that come when you ignore it.” The issue, she added, was particularly relevant amid the country’s housing crisis , which has put politicians under pressure to fast-track construction. Pointing to the deadly consequences of homes being built in flood-prone areas, she warned that leaders’ dismissive attitude toward the climate threat could lead to further “deficient and ineffective land management.” But she conceded that Spain’s political system was perhaps not built to address the threat the country faces. “A government lasts as long as it lasts, but the solutions have to last longer,” she said.

noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music MPs in Westminster have spent the week chewing over yet another review of how to reform the U.K.’s welfare system. But with questions over whether the Milburn or Timms reviews will ever lead to meaningful change, Westminster Insider went on a mission to find out why so many government reviews end up kicked into the long grass or, worse still, completely ignored. Carol Black, who has chaired four separate reviews, spills her secrets on how to actually get politicians to act on your recommendations. But she admits it’s “pretty awful when … nothing happens.” Sascha also speaks to Jill Rutter, senior fellow at the Institute for Government, who explains how to avoid the dreaded “graveyard of landmark reviews.” Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who lost the whip in July 2025 after taking part in a rebellion against Keir Starmer’s welfare proposals, says she is “Team Timms” and warns of the potential tensions between the two welfare reviews that could be coming down the track.
