noticias.titulo: Manchester United trigger Bruno Fernandes contract extension to 2028
noticias.resumen: The captain had said that a long-term contract renewal was on hold, but Premier League club exercised one-year option.
noticias.texto:
Manchester United trigger Bruno Fernandes contract extension to 2028
The captain had said that a long-term contract renewal was on hold, but Premier League club exercised one-year option.
Manchester United are understood to have extended Bruno Fernandes’ existing contract by 12 months, ending speculation about a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club.
The Professional Football Association’s Player of the Year was in the final year of his existing contract, which would have allowed him to speak with clubs outside the Premier League from January 1 about a move next summer.
Fernandes had revealed that negotiations about a new contract had been put on hold, adding to speculation that he could seek a move away from a team that are currently in the league relegation zone.
United, however, are understood to have triggered a clause in the current deal to make Fernandes stay with the Old Trafford club until the end of the 2027-2028 season.
Fernandes joined United in January 2020 from Sporting Lisbon, against whom he scored twice in the two sides’ midweek Champions League 2-2 draw.
The attacking midfielder quickly became the club’s most important player and last season recorded a record number of assists in a Premier League season, helping secure the return to Europe’s elite competition for this campaign.
A team source said the move suited both parties and left the door open to future talks over a new contract, although the immediate priority was improving results.
United are languishing in 19th place in the Premier League after their worst start to a top-flight season in 40 years.
Fernandes a doubt for Manchester United against Brenford
United entertain Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday, marking new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first home game in charge of the club.
Fernandes, however, is a doubt for the match after missing training on Friday due to illness.
“We don’t know,” Pochettino said on Friday when asked if Fernandes will play. “He’s affected by a virus from Portugal. He finished the game a little bit with a problem and today he could not be part of the training session.
“We’ll see during the day and [Saturday] how he wakes up. We’re not going to take any risks. When this type of situation happens, you don’t feel right. We are going to pay attention, but still we have decided nothing.”
Pochettino is still searching for his first victory after the dramatic draw in Lisbon and a 4-0 Premier League thrashing by Liverpool last weekend, although United were encouraged by their improved display in Portugal.
“We arrive full of energy, positive, but it’s difficult for the players when the results haven’t been up to scratch. We try to help them as best we can,” Pochettino said of his first week in charge.
“This is a group of players who want to do well, who want to perform. Our ‌job is to build confidence.”
On the speculation that had been swirling around Fernandes’ future in Manchester, following reports he had turned down two new contract offer, the Portugal midfielder said on Tuesday ‌that ‌talks could wait until results improve.
“I’m more worried about getting results, trying to bring the club back in a position to be proud of,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Haaland ‘happy’ at Man City despite outburst that led to transfer talk
noticias.resumen: Erling Haaland blasted beleaguered City's form, but ahead of Arsenal test, manager Enzo Maresca says striker is happy.
noticias.texto:
Haaland ‘happy’ at Man City despite outburst that led to transfer talk
Erling Haaland blasted beleaguered City’s form, but ahead of Arsenal test, manager Enzo Maresca says striker is happy.
Enzo Maresca insisted on Friday that Erling Haaland is “happy” at Manchester City after the striker expressed frustration over his side’s recent struggles.
Haaland gave a candid assessment of City’s malaise following Tuesday’s 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League, which came on the back of a Premier League draw at home with Fulham.
After winning 10 of their first 11 matches in all competitions this season, Maresca’s men have won just two of their last seven.
With a crucial trip to Premier League leaders Arsenal looming on Sunday, Haaland’s criticism added to the growing sense that City’s season is in danger of spiralling out of control.
“We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way,” Haaland said.
“I have no idea what we were missing but you could feel it in the last few games that something was not clicking fully.”
Haaland has scored just once in his last five games for City and is without a league goal in his past three matches.
The Norway star’s body language has been noticeably angst-ridden in recent weeks, prompting suggestions that he is growing disillusioned with life at the Etihad Stadium.
City are also awaiting the result of their appeal against a guilty verdict over breaches of Premier League financial rules, with the punishment potentially including a huge points deduction.
Despite City’s woes, Maresca is adamant Haaland remains committed to the cause regardless of speculation that he could seek a move at the end of the season.
“Erling is a nine; they live for goals and winning games. If they don’t score, they are upset. I think he gesticulates in the same way when we are winning games,” Maresca told reporters on Friday.
“For sure he is not happy because we are not winning games. But it is not just Erling. Everyone is on the same page.
“He has been good. He has been normal since day one. Two or three weeks ago, he was dancing inside the pitch and in the training sessions.
“He is happy. It is normal that results affect the mood a little bit but I don’t see any problem with Erling. He is a winner.”
Maresca will need Haaland back to his best against Arsenal if third-placed City are to earn a vital victory over the champions.
Already trailing six points behind Arsenal, a defeat in north London would be a huge blow to their title hopes.
Maresca has come under fire during City’s slump in his first season after replacing Pep Guardiola.
The former Chelsea boss claimed teething problems were inevitable during the transition from Guardiola’s dynastic reign.
“Transition requires time. It’s probably because we won seven games in a row, everyone was thinking at City there’s no transition,” Maresca said.
“But I’ve said many times I’m not a magician. There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new.
“For sure, when you don’t win games, it’s not the ideal situation. For me, it’s completely normal, I’m completely relaxed, no panic at all.”

noticias.titulo: Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
noticias.resumen: Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
noticias.texto:
Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.
Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.
Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.
Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.
Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.
“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here,” Badilla continued without elaborating. “Our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system.”
While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.
On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.
Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the university has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.
Why would Israel celebrate a UN figure not being allowed entry to Costa Rica?
As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide, for which she received numerous threats, Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.
Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.
She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.
In her July 2025 report, she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google, alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.
On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”
Who is Francesca Albanese?
Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.
After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.
Is this the first time Israel and its allies have targeted Albanese?
No.
Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.
The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.
In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.
The most significant escalation came in July 2025, when the Trump administration imposed sanctions against Albanese, accusing her of pursuing a campaign of political and economic warfare against Israel and the United States.
The measures included restrictions on Albanese entering the US, blocking her property and financial interests subject to US jurisdiction and prohibiting US nationals from engaging in transactions with her, effectively isolating her from much of the US financial system.
The US decision was roundly condemned by the UN and various rights groups.
A committee of the UN’s Human Rights Council characterised it as just one aspect of the “continued assault of the current US administration on the entire UN system and its core values of human rights, justice, accountability and the rule of law”. Rights groups, including Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International, also criticised the decision, with the latter slamming the US measures as a “disgraceful affront to international justice”.

noticias.titulo: Why did Georgian police clash with Turkish football fans over Palestine?
noticias.resumen: Georgia's Interior Ministry says 16 people were detained and three employees injured during clashes.
noticias.texto:
Why did Georgian police clash with Turkish football fans over Palestine?
Georgia’s Interior Ministry says 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured during clashes.
Police in Georgia have detained at least 16 people following clashes between football fans at a game between Turkish and Israeli clubs.
The Europa League fifth round match between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva was hosted in Georgia instead of Turkiye.
The coastal Georgian city of Batumi was selected last month as a neutral territory to host the game for “safety and security reasons” because of fears of protests over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the European football association, UEFA.
Despite the precaution, tensions between fans spilled over into the stadium and the match was suspended for 30 minutes. Once play resumed, Besiktas won the game 2-1.
It is not the first time violent clashes have marred football matches involving Israeli clubs since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Here’s what we know about the latest unrest:
What happened?
Tensions between fans had already been rising before kickoff in Batumi on Thursday.
According to the Georgian news outlet Civil Georgia, videos on social media showed groups of Besiktas fans marching through Batumi and physical confrontations between fans and police officers.
Turkiye’s Anadolu Agency reported that the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel opposition.
In the 26th minute, the game was temporarily suspended when clashes broke out between Georgian police and Besiktas supporters. Turkish media outlets reported that police entered the stands and used pepper spray against Turkish fans.
According to reports, the police involvement came after a fan displayed a Palestinian flag and banner.
Turkiye’s TRT World reported that police surrounded the fan and used pepper spray, adding that video later showed a Besiktas fan being carried out on a stretcher and others being injured during the intervention.
What have Turkiye and Georgia said?
Omer Celik, spokesperson and deputy chairman of Turkiye’s ruling AK party, posted on X that the “intervention and violence” against the Besiktas fans who unfurled a ‘FREEDOM FOR PALESTINE’ banner and held a Palestine flag was “unacceptable”.
“Besiktas fans spoke on behalf of the alliance of humanity and became the voice of humanity. We strongly condemn the Israeli team’s provocations on the pitch. We extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to our fans who were injured in the incidents and taken to hospital. We are closely monitoring the condition of our citizens,” Celik said.
But Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters that UEFA officials confiscated the fans’ Palestine flags and Georgian state authorities played no role in the confiscation.
Tamazashvili said that 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured.
“While marching from European Square towards Batumi Arena, some of the fans of the football club ‘Besiktas’ stood out by their aggressive actions,” the ministry said in a statement.
“They violated the public order by making indecent shouting and shooting of various objects, disobeyed the legal demands of the police, resisted law enforcement and physically confronted them.”
Police took appropriate measures to curb the violence, de-escalate incidents and ensure public safety, including the use of what it called “special means”, the ministry added.
It denied that the use of force was related to the display of pro-Palestine banners and flags.
“We categorically deny this information and emphasise that violent actions by fans and physical confrontation with law enforcers prior to the display of flags and banners have just begun while marching towards the stadium.”
How have Besiktas and other Turkish clubs responded?
Besiktas said it condemned the use of “disproportionate force”.
“We have initiated formal inquiries with our Consulate General in Batumi and with UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security personnel against our supporters; we will continue to monitor the situation closely until every single one of our supporters has returned home safely,” read a club statement.
In a post on X congratulating the Besiktas victory, the Turkish Football Federation said it would “closely monitor the unacceptable behaviour directed at our club, Besiktas and our supporters in Batumi tonight, and that we will take action with the relevant authorities to ensure that these incidents are fully investigated and the necessary steps are taken.”
Other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, also condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.
Why was Georgia hosting a match between Israeli and Turkish teams?
Since the onset of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, Turkish clubs have not hosted Israeli opposition at home because of security concerns, with matches played in neutral territories instead.
Turkish-Israeli relations have taken a downturn since the war began, with Turkish authorities taking a hard line against the military policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the occupied Palestinian territories.
However, Georgia and Israel have good relations with close ties maintained amid the war.
Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was in the capital Tbilisi for a diplomatic visit last year.
What’s Europe’s track record when dealing with pro-Palestine fans?
Not great.
Last year, English club Aston Villa hosted a Europa League game against Maccabi Tel Aviv, but security concerns prompted West Midlands Police to recommend the banning of Israeli fans from the game.
The decision was taken following violence after a match in Amsterdam between Maccabi and Dutch side Ajax. Police intervened against protesters and Israeli media framed the clashes as a “violent, anti-Semitic pogrom”.
In 2024, another match between Ajax and Maccabi Tel Aviv led to clashes between fans of the Israeli team and pro-Palestine protesters, as Maccabi fans burned Palestinian flags and attacked homes displaying them.

noticias.titulo: Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
noticias.resumen: Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.
noticias.texto:
Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.
The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons.
For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions.
Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman, promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel.
This, despite the fact that Lieberman himself became chair of the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee thanks to those same votes. That contradiction was pointed out by Mohamed Majadli, the chief editor of AlNas Radio in Israel and an analyst on the country’s Channel 12.
In such a limited space for political manoeuvres, Eisenkot embarked on forming a coalition, holding talks with his partners, while also trying to open channels of communication with ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly the United Torah Judaism party. At the same time, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett led efforts to form a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party and succeeded in convincing Eisenkot’s Yashar party to open formal talks with Likud.
The prospect of reneging on the change bloc’s central promise to oust Netanyahu looms large over these talks. Bennett and others are advocating for that outcome in light of the lack of a clear Zionist majority against Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
Meanwhile, leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, has publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu and has called out Bennett for his efforts to reach it. The Yashar-Likud talks are complex and overshadowed by, among other issues, accusations between the two sides.
Netanyahu accuses the change bloc of working to undermine Israel by working with Arab-led parties, which he has referred to as “the enemy”. Eisenkot has gone on the record saying that Netanyahu endangers the security of Israel and is willing to ignite war for his personal gain.
From Likud’s perspective, a unity government would require a rotation agreement on the premiership. That means that rather than getting rid of Netanyahu, Eisenkot would have to agree to Netanyahu staying on as prime minister for two years, or agreeing to serve second in the rotation.
This scenario gained traction after judges presiding over Netanyahu corruption trials recommended dropping the most serious charge of bribery, as well as reconsidering the charges or reaching a plea bargain in the others. This development has strengthened Netanyahu’s negotiating position and prompted him to call for an end to the political boycott against him.
Against this backdrop, Eisenkot is manoeuvring through dangerous political waters. If he fails to form a government, voters may be forced to return to the polls again while Netanyahu remains at the helm. This scenario could translate into a loss of support for the change bloc and hand Netanyahu a renewed mandate, while simultaneously ending the political careers of some leaders such as Eisenkot.
If Eisenkot chooses unity with Netanyahu over the promises he made to his voters, he will lose credibility among supporters. Additionally, Eisenkot could be outmanoeuvred by Netanyahu.
Many point to the coalition agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020, which included a rotating premiership. The government collapsed before Benny Gantz assumed his position and his political career never recovered.
In political terms, forming a unity government with Netanyahu would represent a reversal of election promises on fundamental issues such as transparency, judicial reform, and the influence of religion on the state, because unlike the change bloc, Netanyahu’s allies are already embedded in the state bureaucracy and able to entrench these policies.
More strategically, it reflects the knee-jerk reaction of Israel’s body politic to Palestinian citizens of Israel. This is what leading sociologist and researcher Honaida Ghanem calls Israel’s structural problem: its inability to reconcile that part of Israel’s political and leadership crisis is that in today’s Israel, anti-Arab sentiment is one of the few policies most Jewish Israelis can agree on, while they no longer agree on the nature of the state, the influence of religion over the state, or many other fundamental issues of identity and governance.
The prospect of a unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu remains possible, though not likely, primarily because of the personal and political risks such an unholy political marriage would entail for the change bloc leaders.

noticias.titulo: Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UN
noticias.resumen: El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.
noticias.texto:
Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UN
El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.
Hunger ‌is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme climate events, two United Nations agencies said in a new report.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen faced the gravest threats of famine, driven by violence, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather, including the El Nino phenomenon.
Listings in the report, released twice a year through the Global Network Against Food Crises, have risen from 13 hotspots in June, with Chad, Uganda and parts of both Southern Africa and Central America added, while Lebanon was removed.
Armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, the report said, as soaring food, energy and transport costs were eroding people’s ability to feed themselves.
El Nino, which is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots: Southern Africa, the Central American Dry Corridor and northeastern Uganda.
Covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was affecting efforts to avert catastrophe.
In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1bn to $2bn.
“While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote the FAO and WFP.
While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks – including risk of famine – re-emerged within a few years.”
In Sudan, famine remains a risk in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, as fighting disrupts food production, markets and aid deliveries.
The agencies also identified famine risks in parts of Somalia and South ‌Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation.
Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Gaza were also classified as areas of very great concern.
Gaza was ‌downgraded ‌from the highest level of concern after small improvements in food security following the October 2025 “ceasefire”. But agencies warned that conditions remained fragile in Gaza, while in the occupied West Bank, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen.

noticias.titulo: England’s Overton takes 5-12 as Australia bowled out for record low in T20
noticias.resumen: Australia are bowled out for 108 as Jamie Overton claims career-best figures in England's seven-wicket win in Brisbane.
noticias.texto:
England’s Overton takes 5-12 as Australia bowled out for record low in T20
Australia are bowled out for 108 as Jamie Overton claims career-best figures in England’s seven-wicket win in Brisbane.
Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as England thrashed Australia by seven wickets in the third T20 international in Brisbane on Friday.
Overton’s figures were the best by an Englishman against Australia in T20s as the home side were bundled out for 108, their lowest score on Australian soil.
“I thought Jamie Overton was outstanding tonight,” England captain Harry Brook said.
“He’s worked hard and put in some extra graft at training.
“He simplified his game and reaped the rewards tonight – he had it on a string and it felt like we could change the field and make them make a mistake.”
Brook won the toss and sent Australia in to bat, and off-spinner Liam Dawson struck early when he had Australian skipper Mitch Marsh caught at mid-on.
Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper attacked during the powerplay, taking the score to 55 after five overs.
Harper raced to 26 off 14 balls before Dawson grabbed his second when the Australian wicketkeeper got a top edge to Overton at mid-on.
Overton then swung into action with the ball, claiming the next five wickets as Australia slumped from 65-2 to 92-7 and then collapsed to 108 all out when Sam Curran clean-bowled Billy Stanlake.
Aneurin Donald, who smashed 85 off 32 on the Gold Coast on Tuesday, got the run chase off to a spectacular start, belting 31 from just 11 balls.
But a rain delay seemed to help the Australians, as Brook holed out for nine after play resumed, before Donald fell for 32, leaving England 49-3.
Another rain break threatened to stop England’s momentum again, but Jordan Cox blasted 33 in quick time to give the visitors an easy win and go ahead in the five-game series 2-1.
Marsh conceded that Australia were outplayed by a better team.
“No excuses, we’ve got to be better,” he said.
“We’ve all played Big Bash games here (at the Gabba).
“You have to give yourself the chance to cash in at the back end (of the innings), but we didn’t get near that tonight.”
The two teams head to Sydney for the fourth game on Sunday night.

noticias.titulo: Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan?
noticias.resumen: US president's new tariff regime targets China hardest, just weeks before Trump and Xi meet again in Miami.
noticias.texto:
Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan?
US president’s new tariff regime targets China hardest, just weeks before Trump and Xi meet again at the G20 in Miami.
In February 2025, US President Donald Trump marked his return to office by kick-starting a trade war with China.
New tariffs, amid accusations that China was failing to prevent the flow of drugs into the United States, set the stage for an escalating economic confrontation between the world’s two largest economies, which stands to reshape global trade.
While Trump’s new trade tariffs regime hit allies and rivals alike, China took the fight head-on.
Washington first put a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods, citing fentanyl and immigration concerns, and Beijing responded by curbing exports of five rare earth metals key to defence, clean energy and tech products.
Then it came to a showdown with Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April, including 34 percent for Chinese products. A tit-for-tat exercise ensued as headline US tariffs on China climbed to 145 percent, while US goods entering China were slapped with tariffs of 125 percent, alongside restrictions on rare earth exports.
The tariff war seesawed for much of that year before the two leaders sat at a table in October, on the sidelines of the 2025 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea, to call a truce.
The limited-time pause in hostilities paved the way for a diplomatic thaw.
Trump then travelled to Beijing last May for talks with Xi, who then visited Washington in September for the first time in more than a decade. Trump embraced the Chinese president when he arrived in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, earlier this month for this year’s APEC summit.
But then Trump returned to Washington and, in less than a week, his administration had announced a new tariff regime – its second attempt at reshaping its trade war after the Supreme Court declared his Liberation Day tariffs of April last year illegal.
“The practical purpose is simple: rebuild [the] tariff leverage the Supreme Court stripped away and force Beijing to the table before the next summit,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, the chief economist for Asia Pacific at investment bank Natixis.
‘Purpose changed somewhat’
This time, the Trump administration has announced plans to impose new tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods through unfair government subsidies, policies and suppressed wages.
China is subject to the highest rates – a new 20 percent levy that is still within the bounds of the trade truce that is set to expire in January. Washington has, however, threatened a 40 percent levy if trade talks break down.
Instead of the emergency powers it used the first time – and which the Supreme Court struck down – the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleging that targeted countries are making use of “structural excess capacity”. It has identified these 14 specific economies during an investigation it launched in March, but views China as the biggest offender, particularly in its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, a trade policy think tank in Singapore, said the “original intention” of the investigation “was to provide a more durable way to get back to the tariff levels” announced on Liberation Day.
“Over that time, I think the purpose changed somewhat,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Originally a means to apply tariffs, it seems clear that the White House wants a more sweeping use of Section 301, which allows a broad range of activities to be subject to possible negotiations and future punishment like tariffs,” she added.
Elms argued that Trump’s announcement coming in “now is rather interesting”, given he is due to meet with Xi next month, in Miami, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit. “This announcement adds another layer of possible tensions,” she said.
‘Right to retaliate’
Just before Trump landed in Shenzhen, where he was greeted by Xi on the tarmac, earlier this month, the Chinese leader had opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.
Xi also portrayed Beijing as a stable trade partner in contrast with the US, where Trump’s tariff war had already rattled global economic equations.
Responding to the latest round of tariffs this week, Beijing warned that it “reserves the right” to retaliate with steeper tariffs.
“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said, adding that Beijing “will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.
Referring to the eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity” practices undertaken by Jamieson Greer, Trump’s trade representative, China said it was “a typical act of unilateralism that severely disrupts the international economic order and seriously violates WTO rules”.
Under the latest measures, Washington is seeking to take its economic confrontation with Beijing beyond bilateral trade, targeting the industrial policies of countries emerging as alternative manufacturing hubs but whose supply chains remain closely intertwined with China’s.
Hinrich Foundation’s Elms told Al Jazeera that while Beijing “is probably ok with a 20 percent tariff, they are undoubtedly less comfortable with the attempt to hold all other trade partners accountable to the US for engagement with China”.
‘China can blunt this’
Investment bank Natixis’s Herrero said that Trump’s latest tariffs “are less a grand strategy than a familiar negotiating ploy: keep the pressure on after a friendly photo-op”, referring to the meeting in Shenzhen.
“The stated rationale is Chinese overcapacity,” she said, adding that, however, the aim is to “rebuild tariff leverage” and “force Beijing to the table before the next summit”.
Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore (NUS), said the new measures are a substitute for the struck-down reciprocal tariffs, with “the same kind of inherent reasons or motivations”.
Bo argued that the US government “needs to raise money to keep its many activities going, including the war on Iran”. Furthermore, “it cannot rely on the bond market due to high interest rates – and consumer inflation already hit them hard in midterm election results”.
“Tariff money is one of the easiest ways to finance itself, rather than asking for more from Congress,” Bo told Al Jazeera.
Despite nearly a decade of the ongoing trade tensions between the US and China, Beijing’s global goods trade surplus reached a record $1.19 trillion last year, underscoring the scale of its export dominance. By comparison, the US ran a $1.24 trillion goods trade deficit over the same period.
“Nothing has changed substantially over the years,” he said, adding that “no new tariff will be effective to reduce the Chinese overcapacity at all, or in a significant way.”
Bo said he believes both China and the US are “working hard on the trade negotiations to de-escalate or mitigate” before the two leaders meet again next month, where they want to discuss issues like AI, nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. “That’s a much bigger picture for them than a trade relationship,” Bo said.
For Beijing’s part, Herrero said that “China can still blunt” these new measures by the US.
“Rare earths remain its sharpest tool,” she added.
“The risk for Trump is the same as always: higher prices land on American consumers, and the wider trade system frays further,” Herrero said. “Whether that counts as a feature or a bug depends on how much pain Washington is willing to absorb.”

noticias.titulo: European football violence causes concern with far-right claim in UEFA game
noticias.resumen: Claims of Nazi salutes at UEFA Europa League game in Marseille headline night of further violence in European football.
noticias.texto:
European football violence causes concern with far-right claim in UEFA game
Claims of Nazi salutes at UEFA Europa League game in Marseille headline night of further violence in European football.
Violent clashes at two European football matches have stoked concerns about fan violence and prompted the leaders of France and Bulgaria to condemn behaviour that had “no place in civilized Europe”.
Images showed masked and bloodied fans wielding improvised weapons and metal pipes during a brawl at a UEFA Europa League match on Wednesday evening between Marseille and Levski Sofia, which the Bulgarian club said began when their fans were attacked by supporters of the French side.
A photographer working for the Reuters news agency said the clashes at the Stade Velodrome in Marseille had started after a supporter from the visitors’ stand made a Nazi salute.
Clashes also broke out at a Europa League match in the Georgian city of Batumi between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva, forcing the referee to suspend the match for 30 minutes.
European football’s governing body UEFA told Reuters its disciplinary body “would assess the match reports before considering any potential ‌next steps”.
What was the reaction to the Marseille and Levski Sofia game?
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he and French President Emmanuel Macron spoke by phone and condemned the violence at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match, in which Marseille police said 11 Bulgarian fans were hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilized Europe,” Radev said on Facebook.
“I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Macron said he had condemned “with the utmost force” acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans, which he said had “no place in sport or in public space”, and told Radev they would not go unpunished.
A protest was planned in front of the French embassy in Sofia later on Friday.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said: “Violence, racial hatred and provocation have no place in our stadiums.”
Manuel Bompard, a French lawmaker for the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party in the Marseille department, commented on a video on social media appearing to show a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.
“Congrats to the Marseille fans who responded with an antifascist chant,” Bompard wrote on X. “The far-right has no place in our stadiums!”
Batons fly, flares lit in Marseille and Levski Sofia clash
Levski Sofia, which lost the match 1-0, said masked fans had attacked its supporters with batons and flares. Some had let off flares and tried to get through the barrier as security staff tried to hold them back.
Images showed fans attacking each other through a netted fence separating sections of the stadium.
Before Thursday’s match, French authorities had introduced a sevenfold reduction of ticket sales to Levski supporters and imposed additional restrictions on their movement to and around the stadium, aiming to curb risks of violence.
The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would request a thorough investigation. Marseille said it would conduct its own analysis and was working closely with law enforcement.
What happened in the Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva match?
The match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva had been moved from Istanbul for what UEFA said were safety and security reasons.
Clashes in the stands led referee Morten Krogh to suspend the match in the 26th minute, and it resumed after a 30-minute delay. Georgian police entered the stands, and television footage showed one ‌fan being carried out on a stretcher.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that police used pepper spray. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said a number of fans had been denied entry. Besiktas went on to win 2-1.
Turkish Football Federation chair Ibrahim Haciosmanoglu defended the ‌decision ‌to keep Israeli clubs out of Turkiye following Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023 after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

noticias.titulo: Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
noticias.resumen: Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.
noticias.texto:
Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.
Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group.
The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz.
The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
A local source said that a residential building was struck and that “most” of the victims were children, according to the media report.
Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, the report said. Three people remain missing beneath the rubble.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting the internationally-recognised Yemen government did not immediately comment.
The coalition said later on Friday that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region.
Humanitarian crisis
Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, as the United States’ war on Iran escalated hostilities and the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.
Some 13,343 people have been killed or injured since August, according to the World Health Organization, while the country is sliding into a humanitarian crisis.
The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme said on Friday that Yemen is among conflict hotspots that face severe food insecurity.
The Norwegian Refugee Council warned this week that the renewed fighting has displaced thousands and piled pressure onto dangerously underfunded aid efforts.
Aid from the US, Germany and others has shrunk considerably in recent years, the nongovernmental organisation noted, saying it has received only 12 percent of funding for emergency shelter support in Yemen so far this year.
“Fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices,” NRC Secretary-General Jan Egeland said, warning that families across Yemen are being pushed deeper into need.
“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here,” Egeland stated.
Calling for better humanitarian access and civilian protection, he demanded that “the powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality”.

noticias.titulo: Arsenic in the water: Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution
noticias.resumen: Thailand is seeking to tackle river pollution stemming from rare earth mines in neighboring Myanmar. The two countries held joint talks this week as a "first step towards agreeing on the evidence."
noticias.texto:
Thailand presses Myanmar over mining pollution
November 27, 2026
Thailand is pushing its neighbor Myanmar to take on unregulated mining.
A toxic border river is putting lives and livelihoods at risk in northern Thailand. The Kok River, once rich in fish, is now polluted with arsenic, mercury, and other hazardous contaminants.
The reason is the mining activity in the militia-controlled regions of Myanmar. Most of these mines are located in Shan state, where civil war has raged since the 2021 military coup.
The mining activity is driven in part by China's dominant rare earth industry.
Two sides agreed to joint water sampling
Bangkok this week hosted the first Thai-Myanmar working group where it said tests proved rare-earth and gold mines in Myanmar were the reason of the pollution downstream. China was also present in the talks.
The two sides agreed to joint water sampling on the Kok and Sai rivers. This will cover 12 water sampling locations and is expected to begin between December and January.
But no public agreement was made about Thailand's request for a six-month suspension of mining operations.
The talks follow the suspension of tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district earlier this month, near the Myanmar border, after arsenic levels were found to be nearly 30 times higher than government limits.
Bangkok is also seeking China's help in pressuring private Chinese operators, given its position as the main importer of rare-earth materials from Myanmar, as the issue grows increasingly urgent after months of concern.
Authorities this week urged residents to avoid eating certain shellfish and other river species after tests detected dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in northern and northeastern Thailand.
Myanmar intervention to stop mining faces obstacles
"Arsenic does not come from nature, it came from mining sites. The source was from (Myanmar's) Shan state, no-one disagrees," Thai Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan Wongsawat said at the joint talks.
However, finding a solution remains a challenge.
Thanapon Piman, senior research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI), told AFP, "This is going to be a first step to agree on the evidence, otherwise you cannot move to the next step, like stopping mining activity.”
But Myanmar intervening to stop mining would be "really difficult," he added.
Several ethnic armed groups have been active in the region for decades, while the civil war is still ongoing.
Thai authorities point to two gold mines across the border from Mae Sai as the main contributors to elevated arsenic levels in the Sai River.
The broader region is divided among various groups, including Myanmar's military and the United Wa State Army, an ethnic armed group closely aligned with China.
The main mining belts are currently outside the control of Myanmar's military-backed government, including sites in Shan State.
Thailand might ask China's help, PM says
Thai authorities are also seeking to assess whether pollutant mines are under the control of Myanmar's government or other entities, Deputy Prime Minister Yodchanan told Reuters.
"We also would like them to check whether they can control every mine or they cannot. If they cannot, we will ask China to help,” he said.
A spokesperson from China's foreign ministry told AFP that Beijing "pays close attention" to the pollution issue and would provide technical support.

noticias.titulo: Georgia: Police clash with Besiktas fans at Israel club game
noticias.resumen: Turkey's Besiktas accused Georgian police of using "disproportionate" force during the game with Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva, which saw Besiktas fans unfurl a banner supporting Palestine.
noticias.texto:
Georgia: Police clash with Besiktas fans at Israel club game
November 27, 2026
A football game between a Turkish and an Israeli team in Georgia's Batumi was disrupted by violence, with UEFA due to assess the events on Friday.
Georgian police said 16 people were detained and three officers "sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions" during the match.
The police also accused some supporters of hurling stadium seats at security forces.
Turkey's Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were originally set to meet in Istanbul, but with the tensions between the two countries running high due to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, UEFA decided to move the match to Georgia for safety reasons.
Georgia denies police were deployed over Palestine support
During the Thursday game, Besiktas fans unfurled a banner, "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine," waved Palestinian flags and chanted anti-Israel slogans.
However, Georgian authorities insisted they did not intervene due to the fans expressing their support for the Palestinians.
"We categorically deny these reports and emphasize that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," said the Georgian Interior Ministry.
In turn, Besiktas accused the authorities of using "disproportionate force" against the fans, and Turkey's football federation condemned "the unacceptable attitudes, behavior and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium."
A Besiktas club employee told the AFP news agency that five Turkish fans were taken to a hospital for medical treatment.
The match was suspended for over half an hour due to the violence in the stands. Eventually, Danish referee Morten Krogh continued the game, which ended with Besiktas winning 2 to 1.
The Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
Turkish government ministers close ranks with Besiktas
The unrest has prompted a diplomatic incident between Turkey and Georgia.
Turkish sources indicated Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the clashes with his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili.
Meanwhile, Turkish Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak and Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci echoed Besiktas' accusations of "disproportionate" force used by the Georgian police.
In an online post, Bak pledged to continue "resolutely defend the rights of Turkish sport and our fans."
Turkish news agency IHA reported that the 16 detained Besiktas fans have been released due to diplomatic and legal steps ordered by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
According to Besiktas, Erdogan also spoke to the club chairman, telling the sports official he was closely monitoring the situation.

noticias.titulo: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
noticias.resumen: The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.
noticias.texto:
Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy amid rising fuel costs
November 27, 2026
Norwegian low-cost, long-haul airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.
The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.
Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.
What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?
Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.
But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.
"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.
Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.
"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.
The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."
Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.
Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?
Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.
In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.
It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.
This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

noticias.titulo: German lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
noticias.resumen: German lawmakers voted on a federal budget which foresees €556 billion in spending. Elsewhere, the Left Party is hosting a summit on femicide and the BSW party conference starts in Dresden. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Parliament approves €556 billion 2027 budget
Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
What you need to know
- German lawmakers to vote on 2027 federal budget
- Left Party hosts summit on femicide and violence against women
- BSW party conference starts in Dresden
- Rheinmetall lowers revenue forecasts
- Chancellor Merz to meet Pope Leo on Monday
Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.
German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans
German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63."
At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.
In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.
From 2029 onwards, however, only periods of employment, child-rearing, and the care of relatives will count toward the 45-year contribution requirement.
Periods during which an insured person received unemployment benefits, sickness benefits or transitional allowances – or held only a low-wage, part-time "mini-job" – will no longer be credited.
For weeks, Germany's coalition government partners, the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and Schweitzer's center-left Social Democrats have been struggling to reach a compromise on this issue.
A pension commission had proposed abolishing this popular type of pension, a proposal opposed by the SPD.
A group of leading coalition politicians, including Schweitzer, reportedly held final discussions regarding the plans as recently as Wednesday evening.
German parliament approves 2027 budget
Germany's ‌lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, voted in favor of a €556 billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost defense and infrastructure spending.
Total new borrowing will reach €210 billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in 2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild its military after decades of underinvestment.
"It is right that we invest in the railways and in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday, defending his budget. "It is right... that we invest in our security."
German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.
"We are putting up the money for defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil said. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again."
But there was criticism of the budget from the opposition Left Party, with party leader Ines Schwerdtner accusing the government only ever talking about emergency and war.
"But for millions of people in this country, the emergency comes every month when money gets tight," she said. "But you're not interested in these emergencies."
317 members of parliament voted in favor of the budget and 260 against it. There were no abstentions.
Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will have a private audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Monday before meeting Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome later, a government spokesman confirmed on Friday.
Merz, himself a Catholic, had a brief encounter with Pope Leo at the pontiff's inauguration in May 2025, but this will be the pair's first private meeting.
According to Politico, who first reported on the planned meeting earlier this week, officials expect the discussion to focus on "human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine."
Afterwards, Merz will be received with military honors by Italian Prime Minister Meloni, with whom he will hold talks on Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, economic cooperation and, "with certainty," the European Union budget for the period 2028-2034, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF).
Negotiations over the MFF in Brussels this week ended without agreement, with Germany leading a group of more fiscally conservative member states which also includes Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Italy, on the other hand, along with countries like Poland and Spain, would like to see a more ambitious EU budget.
Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast
German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has revised its medium-term revenue forecast for 2030 down from around €45 billion to between €33 billion and €37 billion, with an expected profit margin of around 20%.
The announcement, made on Friday at a market event in Hamburg, comes after the Düsseldorf-based company also lowered its forecast for the current year following delays in major orders notably from the German government.
In July, the German defense ministry canceled a multi-billion-euro contract to produce six new type-F126 naval frigates and there are now reportedly delays in an expected large-scale order of Boxer armored fighting vehicles (AFV).
Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger said the government was negotiating hard on price and that he would only sign off on the deal once "sufficient profitability" was guaranteed.
Meanwhile, Rheinmetall is set to deliver 66 additional Lynx AFVs to Romania, part of an order which now totals 298 such vehicles.
The deliveries to the European Union and NATO member state are set to begin in 2028 and be completed by 2030.
Rheinmetall is also manufacturing four battleships for the Romanian navy and has increased its production capacities in the eastern European country which borders Ukraine.
Rheinmetall 'grieving' for employees killed in Kuwait attack
German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has confirmed that two of its employees had been killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.
"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, providing technical support for air-defense systems," the Düsseldorf-based company said in a statement.
"Protecting the people of that country was a matter of deep personal importance to them. Both the company's leadership and the entire workforce are devastated by the loss of our colleagues. We share in the grief of those they have left behind."
The two victims were Italian citizens who worked as technicians for subsidiary Rheinmetall Italia, Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirmed in Rome.
Tajani said the pair had been at an air surveillance station in Kuwait when it was attacked by two Iranian drones. Two other people, a Pakistani national and Kuwaiti army captain, were also injured.
The Iranian foreign ministry has denied any involvement in the deadly attack.
Rheinmetall secured a contract to supply the Kuwaiti navy with defense systems in July.
BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference
Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.
The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.
After initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.
BSW split over stance on AfD
Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — with which it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.
Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain issues which an AfD minority government would want to implement.
The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.
The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy."
"We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but said: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media."
Wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority."
But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.
"Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term."
They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier."
Left Party hosts international femicide summit
Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is on Friday hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.
Under the title "Voices Against Femicide," the summit in Berlin brings together activists, politicians and researchers from around the world, including Kenya, Nigeria, Kurdistan, India, Afghanistan, Syria, Mexico, Argentina, Spain and Germany.
Across three panel discussions, the speakers will highlight women's rights, feminist struggles and legal perspectives and debate political measures which are urgently needed in Germany to effectively combat femicides and patriarchal violence.
The summit comes just two days after Germany's parliament, the Bundestag, marked Orange Day, the United Nations' officially named day for the elimination of violence against women, with a minute's silence and a series of speeches.
Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office reported a total of 1,176 female victims of attempted and completed homicide in 2025, up from 859 in 2024.
The number of female victims of domestic violence in Germany in 2025 rose by 2.8% to 197,667.
German parliament to vote on €556 billion budget for 2027
German lawmakers will on Friday vote on a federal budget for 2027 which foresees €556 billion ($610 billion) in government spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.
The largest chunk of expenditure (just over €200 billion) will go on federal contributions to the statutory pension system, while €110 billion is to be allocated to defense – a 32.7% increase.
The plans call for around €210 billion in fresh borrowing, a figure which is only expected to increase between now and 2030, while €2.7 billion are also expected to be shifted away from Germany's climate protection and transformation fund.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and their Social Democrat (SPD) coalition partners have spent an unusually long time wrangling over the budget, with Merz finally clinching a deal last week after more than eight hours of talks at the Chancellery.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Morgen! Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germanyis talking about on Friday, 27 November.
The German parliament, the Bundestag, is set to vote on a 2027 federal budget that foresees around €556 billion ($610 billion) in spending, around €31 billion more than in 2026.
Also in Berlin, Germany's socialist Left Party (Die Linke) is hosting an international summit on femicide and violence against women.
Meanwhile, the left-wing populist BSW party is holding its party convention in Dresden as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats.

noticias.titulo: As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
noticias.resumen: President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.
noticias.texto:
As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
November 27, 2026
Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.
President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.
Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and four other candidates.
The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.
What matters to voters
Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.
A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.
Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.
"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."
Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.
Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.
"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.
Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.
"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.
"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.
Jobs, cost of living top of mind
Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.
The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.
The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.
The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.
Alhagie Sama, a voter in Banjul, said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.
"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.
Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.
"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.
"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."
Election under observation
The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.
The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.
International observers are also monitoring the process.
Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.
The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.
"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.
Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."
The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

noticias.titulo: On the arrest of Informer TV owner and editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
noticias.resumen: The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable or whether this is another political power struggle.
noticias.texto:
Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
November 27, 2026
"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.
The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June last year.
On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by the police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching" and he labelled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures" and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted political opponents of the previous government, activists and independent journalists.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.
Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.
Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.
"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.
Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.
"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.
