"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.
"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."
On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?
According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.
Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.
Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.
Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.
A reckoning or an internal power struggle?
Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.
The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.
Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.
"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

noticias.titulo: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
noticias.resumen: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.
noticias.texto:
Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
November 27, 2026
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.
It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.
Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.
With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.
Why is Duterte on trial?
Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.
During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.
However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.
His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.
"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.
After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.
A 'way of governing'
Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.
"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.
"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.
"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.
Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.
Former president remains popular
The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.
Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.
His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.
"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.
Why was Duterte arrested?
Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.
The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.
For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.
What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.
Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.
The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.
Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.
In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.
The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.
What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?
The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.
Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.
Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.
By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.
Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.
However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.
"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.
For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.
"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.
"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

noticias.titulo: Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
noticias.resumen: War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn.
noticias.texto:
Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
November 27, 2026
For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.
The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly last year.
Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the conflict's impact.
In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband.
Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRA), said she had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.
"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.
What the figures show
Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 in year measured roughly from March 2025 to March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.
The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.
Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.
But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.
"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.
When marriage becomes an economic calculation
The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.
In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.
Thompson told DW that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.
Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Canada, described a similar risk.
When families cannot meet a girl's living costs, and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her towards marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.
War and displacement
Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.
Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene
Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.
Few legal safeguards against child marriage
Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below 18.
"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.
Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.
The concerns also extend to the online space. An HRA investigation published in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted or whether the war increased them.
What can be done to protect girls?
Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.
"Education alone is not enough," he told DW. Families also need the means to support their children.
Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.
According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

noticias.titulo: Philippines: VP Duterte says father's ICC case 'not a fair trial'
noticias.resumen: Sara Duterte has said the ICC will not give her father a fair trial and that the Hague-based court wants to "make a statement." Duterte alleges the case against her father is politically motivated.
noticias.texto:
Philippines: VP Duterte says father's ICC case 'not a fair trial'
November 27, 2026
The Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Duterte, criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Thursday, saying it would not provide a fair trial for her ex-president father's crimes against humanity case.
She said the court would try to "make a statement."
Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
What is expected at Duterte's trial?
The trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in court.
"I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.
Duterte said "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.
BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why is Rodrigo Duterte at the ICC?
Prosecutors at the ICC accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.
He has been charged with three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.
Duterte is the first Asian former leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.
Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.
Duterte: ICC trial is politically motivated
The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.
She said both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.
"I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

noticias.titulo: The tiny BSW is a party in crisis, as it is set to hand the far-right AfD power in eastern Germany
noticias.resumen: Sahra Wagenknecht's BSW party is set to disrupt German politics yet again. Espousing a mix of left-wing economic policy and populist far-right anti-migration rhetoric, it now stands to play kingmaker to the far right AfD
noticias.texto:
BSW set to play major role in German politics once more
November 27, 2026
This fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession. Launched in January 2024, it was named the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) to capitalize on the high profile and momentum of its founder, a former communist who had just exited the socialist Left party.
Since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason. In the past 34 months the newcomer party celebrated election successes at the European Parliament level and in German state elections. In the eastern states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party even took part in governing coalitions; however, both of these collapsed relatively quickly.
Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the German general election in February 2025. The party failed to gain the 5% share of votes required to enter parliament, by less than 10,000 votes. With that, it was denied the country's most important political stage and took the matter to court, demanding a complete recount.
'Germany has the election scrutiny process of a banana republic'
But Germany's Constitutional Court dismissed the BSW's election challenge as inadmissible, pointing to a lack of evidence.
"Simply insinuating the possibility of voting errors or expressing an unproven assumption does not meet the requirements for claiming an electoral mistake," the court explained.
The court's decision was published about a week before the party's federal conference is due to be held in Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony.
"Germany's election scrutiny process resembles that of a 'banana republic'," was the angry reaction of former party leader Sahra Wagenknecht, who stepped back from frontline leadership of her eponymous party in December 2025. Since then, she has led its commission on fundamental values.
One of her successors at the top of the BSW is European Parliament lawmaker Fabio De Masi. In his view, the decision of the Constitutional Court was a "black day for democracy in Germany."
Fellow co-leader Amira Mohamed Ali did not want to accept the rejected recount.
"It remains unclear whether the Bundestag is correctly composed and whether the approximately 2.5 million BSW voters have unjustly been deprived of their parliamentary representation," she said.
The disappointment at the failure to enter the Bundestag runs deep. The party has not recovered from this setback. It again failed to win representation in 4 out of 5 state parliaments in elections this year, albeit narrowly.
In Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate, as well as in the city-state of Hamburg in 2025, the BSW received less than 2%. This clearly shows that it is politically irrelevant in the western German states.
Will the BSW help the AfD to power in Saxony-Anhalt?
They find themselves in the spotlight, however, because of the role they are set to play in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the BSW got 5.3% of the vote in September.
Despite being the smallest party in that state parliament, they are set to play a pivotal role. They are the only political party that has indicated a readiness to help the election winner, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), into power.
The AfD, which is classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, won the election with almost 44% of the vote. Although his party does not hold an absolute majority in parliament, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund wants to be voted Germany's first-ever AfD state premier in December.
The BSW has not indicated any intention to vote for Siegmund, but if he falls short of winning the absolute majority of 42 votes in the first two rounds of voting, a third round will be held in which a simple majority will suffice to win. The BSW has announced plans to abstain from that vote. Siegmund would then only need to pick up one more "yes" vote or abstention.
During the secret ballot for the state parliament speaker, AfD candidate Tobias Rausch received 9 votes more than his party has lawmakers. It is not known exactly who they came from. Alongside the AfD and BSW, there are 4 other parties in the state parliament: the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), environmentalist Greens, socialist Left Party and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Sahra Wagenknecht rejects a firewall against the AfD
The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will be at the center of the party's upcoming conference in Dresden, because the BSW's increasing closeness with the far-right party is highly controversial.
Several BSW members, including board member Christian Leye, criticized this path in a column published in the weekly Die Zeit.
Leye recalled their party's founding consensus: "The clear political demarcation from the AfD."
He quoted party founder Wagenknecht, who at that time had said: "Of course we will not collude with the AfD."
"We are starting a party so that all the people who are considering or have voted for the AfD out of anger or disappointment — but not because they are right-wing — have a credible political home," Wagenknecht had continued.
But Wagenknecht has also long argued that the so-called "firewall" policy of mainstream parties refusing to work with the AfD has failed. This is why she is rejecting the idea of entering a mathematically possible governing coalition with the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt.
"We are basically agreed that we neither want to go into coalition with the AfD, nor tolerate them, just as much as we do not want to participate in a firewall coalition," she told German news agency dpa.
How the BSW plans to make its way through this dilemma at its party conference is unclear. Fabio De Masi, who replaced Wagenknecht as co-chair in December 2025, seems well aware of this.
He told German media network RND that dealing with the AfD continued to be like "riding on the edge of a razor blade."
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback against Russian athletes
noticias.resumen: As European countries challenge Russia's sporting return, Ukrainian Olympian Vladyslav Heraskevych believes the IOC is facing a 'very big crisis.'
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback against Russian athletes
November 27, 2026
Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.
Heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.
On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union (EU) and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.
"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," von der Leyen said.
In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never."
"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the World Cup event in Altenberg, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.
"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform."
Europe pushes back
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also said Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.
Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.
"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych said.
However, in recent weeks, there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.
Among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, said withdrawing as host of next year's Men's World Championship was an option.
Putin wades into dispute
The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.
"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads towards the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.
"Sport, like art, should bring people together."
Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.
"The matter is too urgent to wait until [new visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very big crisis," Heraskevych said, referencing the European pushback. Blanket bans could have a huge effect on Los Angeles Olympic qualifying events in Europe.
Can sport be separated from politics?
Under its president Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.
However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.
"We are not living in a bubble," he said.
"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics."
Citics have accused Coventry of cosying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.
Degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.
Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.
"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.
"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine."

noticias.titulo: Russian drone strikes hit Ukraine's energy, rail and civilian infrastructure, causing deaths
noticias.resumen: After a series of Russian strikes and with the onset of winter cold, Ukraine was forced to halt all electricity exports, while imports reached their highest level since mid-June.
noticias.texto:
After a series of Russian strikes and with the onset of winter cold, Ukraine was forced to halt all electricity exports, while imports reached their highest level since mid-June.
Since the evening of Thursday 26 November, Russian forces have attacked Ukraine with 155 strike UAVs of various types (51 of them jet powered), as well as Parodiya-type decoy drones. Ukrainian air defences managed to shoot down (source in Russian) 110 drones, but impacts were recorded at several locations.
Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky said that during the night the Russian Armed Forces carried out strikes on civilian infrastructure in nine regions of Ukraine.
"Tonight Russia carried out strikes on the railway, the energy sector, civilian enterprises and residential buildings in nine regions," he wrote (source in Russian) on Telegram.
As a result of the Russian attacks, by morning part of consumers in Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kirovohrad, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson regions were left without electricity, according to Ukraine's First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov.
In particular, he said (source in Russian) that in Dnipropetrovsk region engineers have been forced to carry out emergency shutdowns because equipment has been damaged and voltage has fallen in the high-voltage grid.
According to the authors of the November economic overview (source in Russian) by the Centre for Economic Strategy (CES), after the Russian attack on 20 November Ukraine completely halted electricity exports, and imports reached their highest level since mid-June.
Since September, Russia has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on Ukraine's energy system, targeting not only generation facilities but also high-voltage substations through which electricity reaches consumers.
As a result of the overnight strikes, two people were killed at an enterprise in Nizhyn in Chernihiv region; people may be trapped under the rubble.
One woman, aged 86, was killed and another six people were injured after Russian Armed Forces attacks on Izium in the Kharkiv region. Blocks of flats and private houses, administrative buildings and vehicles were damaged, and fires broke out in various parts of the city.
One person was killed in Kryvyi Rih and another two were wounded after more than 20 UAV strikes on five districts of the Dnipropetrovsk region.
Three people were injured on the morning of 27 November as a result of strikes by Russian drones on the Shevchenkivskyi and Kyiv districts of Kharkiv.
Strike by Ukrainian forces on chemical plant producing fuel for Iskander missiles
On Friday night Ukrainian drones struck a combined heat and power plant that is part of the Rosatom state corporation, as well as a synthetic rubber plant involved in producing components of solid rocket fuel, in Yefremov in the Tula region.
This is at least the third strike on the chemical complex over the past year.
It produces polymers for the rubber industry, electrical engineering, adhesives, sealants and lubricants, as part of the enterprise's output is dual-use.
In September the General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces claimed (source in Russian) that the Yefremov plant is involved in producing components of solid rocket fuel, including for ballistic missiles of the Iskander operational-tactical complexes. The plant has been under Ukrainian sanctions since May 2023.
Also overnight there were reports (source in Russian) of a massive drone attack on Saint Petersburg and Leningrad region. The authorities of the northern city said that 45 drones had been shot down over the region.
In Novorossiysk three people were injured in a drone attack, the operational headquarters of Krasnodar region reported. Another two people were killed in Bryansk region by a drone strike and an explosive device that was dropped.
The Russian Defence Ministry reported that 318 Ukrainian UAVs had been shot down in 10 regions, as well as over illegally annexed Crimea.
Ukrainian troops also reported (source in Russian) destroying a camouflaged oil depot in occupied territory in Luhansk region, which Russian forces were using to supply fuel to their units.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky summed up the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and defence industry facilities, saying there were "results" in Samara, Nizhny Novgorod, Krasnodar, Rostov, Volgograd, Stavropol, Bryansk, Perm and Tula regions, as well as in Bashkortostan and Tatarstan, and in the Black Sea.
"Ukraine is absolutely right to respond to every Russian strike. And I thank our Ukrainian defence forces for ensuring that the responses are accurate."
"Russian oil facilities, enterprises involved in producing explosives and other sites that serve the needs of the war, military airfields and aircraft, our range covers all of this," the president said.

noticias.titulo: Social worker in Italy's 'family in the woods' case suspended for 70 days
noticias.resumen: The disciplinary council of Abruzzo's Order of Social Workers has sanctioned Veruska D'Angelo over her handling of the case involving the family living off-grid in Italy.
noticias.texto:
The disciplinary council of Abruzzo's Order of Social Workers has sanctioned Veruska D'Angelo over her handling of the case involving the family living off-grid in Italy.
The social worker who handled the case of the so-called "family in the woods" in Palmoli, in Italy's central Abruzzo region, has been suspended from practising for 70 days.
The regional Order of Social Workers' disciplinary council imposed the suspension on 44-year-old Veruska D'Angelo, finding that her professional conduct had caused "serious harm" to those receiving her services.
The decision follows controversy surrounding the handling of the case of Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion, a British-Australian couple whose three children were taken into care following a ruling by the juvenile court in L'Aquila, which ordered their placement in a protected facility.
Complaints and disciplinary proceedings
The disciplinary proceedings were launched following complaints from the regional Order of Social Workers' president and the couple's former lawyers.
The allegations against D'Angelo include breaches of professional standards relating to impartiality, respect for diversity and professional confidentiality, particularly in her dealings with the media. Her handling of the professional relationship with the family has also come under scrutiny.
The couple's former lawyers alleged that D'Angelo had displayed a hostile attitude towards the parents and failed to maintain the impartiality required of her role.
The social worker has consistently denied the allegations through her lawyer.
Calls for the children to return home
Lawyer Simone Pillon welcomed the suspension, saying in a statement that the decision confirmed his concerns that the information provided to the juvenile court in L'Aquila had not always been objective and that assessments of the family's suitability had been influenced by ideological considerations.
Pillon called for a review of the handling of the case and for the court to reconsider the children's placement in care.
"Now it is up to the court to acknowledge what has happened and decide on the children's definitive return to their family," he said.
Antonio Marziale, president of the Observatory on Children's Rights, also welcomed the decision, describing it as an important step towards protecting children's rights and preserving family ties.
Marziale stressed the need for impartiality, independence and careful consideration of the views of those involved in child protection cases, while ensuring that legal safeguards are respected.
Social worker has 60 days to appeal
The suspension does not take immediate effect. D'Angelo has 60 days to lodge an appeal with the national disciplinary council.
The written decision will detail which breaches of professional ethics the disciplinary panel found to have occurred.
The sanction concerns D'Angelo's professional conduct and does not automatically affect the L'Aquila juvenile court's rulings on the custody and placement of the three children.

noticias.titulo: UK: London's Cake and Bake Show honours David Attenborough's centenary
noticias.resumen: From lifelike gorillas to miniature sugar sculptures of David Attenborough, bakers in London are celebrating the legendary broadcaster's centenary with spectacular creations inspired by nature.
noticias.texto:
Visitors admired an extraordinary collection of wildlife-inspired cakes in London on 27 November 2026, featuring remarkably lifelike gorillas, snow leopards, hedgehogs, badgers and squirrels. Several creations depict Sir David Attenborough himself, sculpted in sugar alongside wild animals or dressed for a polar expedition. Among the most striking entries is a mother gorilla cradling her newborn, recreated with astonishing attention to detail.
The exhibition forms part of The Cake & Bake Show’s annual competition, which celebrates Attenborough’s centenary this year under the theme Inspired by Nature. Paying tribute to the broadcaster behind Planet Earth and The Blue Planet, the competition brings together amateur bakers and professionals competing forprizes including £1,000 in cash and Kenwood appliances.
Judges praised the artistic and technical expertise required to create elaborate cakes capable of retaining their shape for several days in a warm exhibition hall. Visitors can vote for their favourite creation, with the public vote contributing to the final result alongside the judges’ scores. The winner will be announced on Sunday 29 November, the closing day of the event at London’s Olympia exhibition centre.

noticias.titulo: Black Friday: Where in Europe are shoppers the gloomiest?
noticias.resumen: As Black Friday deals hit Europe, new European Commission data show consumer confidence ranging from cautious optimism in Malta and near-neutral sentiment in Spain to deep gloom in Greece, while Italians cut back sharply on plans for big purchases.
noticias.texto:
As Black Friday deals hit Europe, new European Commission data show consumer confidence ranging from cautious optimism in Malta and near-neutral sentiment in Spain to deep gloom in Greece, while Italians cut back sharply on plans for big purchases.
Shop windows across Europe are covered in discount signs today, from Lisbon to Warsaw. Whether people walk in and spend is another matter.
On the same day as Black Friday, the European Commission published its monthly survey of consumers, with a reading for each of the 27 EU countries. It asks households how they feel about their finances, what they expect for the wider economy and how much they plan to spend on big purchases over the next 12 months.
The confidence indicator averages the balances from four questions. A negative reading means negative answers carry more weight overall than positive ones.
For the euro area as a whole, confidence stood at -16.9 in November, confirming last week's early estimate. That is a one-point improvement on October, but still well below the historical average of -10.7.
The backdrop explains much of the caution. Prices in the euro area rose 4% in the year to October, according to Eurostat, the fastest pace since September 2023, driven by energy costs.
Averages hide a lot, though. Country by country, the mood ranges from cautious optimism in Malta to deep pessimism in Greece.
Greece stands alone at the bottom
Greek consumers are by far the gloomiest in the EU. Their confidence reading fell to -50.5 in November from -48.9 in October.
No other country comes close. Romania, the next most pessimistic, stands at -29.7.
Greek households have rarely been cheerful, with a historical average of -40.5. Even so, November's reading sits ten points below that already low bar.
Prices are part of the story. Annual inflation in Greece reached 5.7% in October, the fourth-highest rate in the EU, while Romania recorded the highest at 7%, Eurostat figures show.
After Greece and Romania come Estonia (-29.2), Bulgaria (-28.4), and Italy and Portugal, both at -24.9.
Estonia is the most striking case. Its reading is almost 18 points below the country's own historical average, the widest gap anywhere in the EU.
Italians are holding back on big purchases
For retailers counting on Black Friday, one question in the survey matters more than most. It asks whether households plan to spend more or less on major purchases, such as furniture, appliances or electronics, than they did over the past 12 months.
In Italy, the answer turned sharply more negative. The balance dropped to -46.5 in November from -40.4 in October, far below the country's historical average of -25.1.
Only Romanian households are more reluctant, at -47.4. Greece follows at -43.9.
Italy's overall confidence also slipped to -24.9, its weakest reading in at least a year.
At the other end of the scale, Lithuania (5.0) and Malta (3.4) are the only EU countries where, on balance, households plan to spend more on big purchases over the next 12 months than they did over the past year.
Malta, Spain and Lithuania lead the optimists
Malta is the only EU country with a positive consumer confidence reading, at 2.9.
Spain comes second at -1.1, its best level in at least a year and above its own historical average of -2.4. Lithuania follows closely at -1.4.
Hungary (-5.1) and Sweden (-7.7) complete the top five.
Hungarian consumers tell a different kind of story. Their reading is still negative, but it sits 17 points above the country's historical average of -22.1, the biggest positive gap in the bloc.
In total, eight of the 27 member states now show confidence above their own long-term norms: Malta, Spain, Lithuania, Hungary, Czechia, Luxembourg, Croatia and Poland. Many of them are in central and eastern Europe.
Slovenia sits exactly on its average, while the remaining 18 countries are below theirs.
The big economies sit in the middle
Germany, the EU's largest economy, scored -14.3, a touch better than in October. France improved to -20.2 from -21.9, while the Netherlands slipped to -16.6 from -19.0.
National surveys published earlier this week point to the same cautious mood.
"Lower taxes on fuel are doing little to lift spirits among German consumers," Melanie Debono, senior Europe economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note on Thursday, commenting on the GfK survey of German households.
In France, households grew less worried about their finances and jobs in November, but their willingness to spend on big items weakened further in the INSEE survey.
"The outlook for near-term spending is downbeat, based on these data," Claus Vistesen, chief eurozone economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note on Wednesday.
Saving rather than spending
Across the euro area, households are leaning towards putting money aside. The survey's balance on savings intentions over the next 12 months rose to 10.0 from 8.9, compared with a historical average of -2.9.
Luxembourg leads at 52.6, while in Germany the balance rose to 23.2 from 20.8.
There is one piece of better news for shops. Consumers' expectations for price rises eased. The balance on price expectations for the next 12 months eased to 30.0 from 33.8 in the euro area, although it remains well above its average of 21.4.
The wider picture is not one of collapse. The Commission's broader economic sentiment indicator, which also covers businesses, fell to 95.8 in the euro area, dragged down by industry.
"Down sharply, but recession risks remain low," Vistesen said in a note on Friday.
For Europe's retailers, that may be the real Black Friday problem. Consumers are not in crisis, but many of them are in no hurry to spend.

noticias.titulo: Trump tariffs brought EU and Indonesia closer on trade, minister tells Euronews
noticias.resumen: US tariffs brought the EU and Indonesia closer, Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said in an exclusive interview with Euronews. After a decade of talks, the two sides signed a deal last week, and the minister expects it to lift trade by 50% in three years.
noticias.texto:
US tariffs brought the EU and Indonesia closer, Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto said in an exclusive interview with Euronews. After a decade of talks, the two sides signed a deal last week, and the minister expects it to lift trade by 50% in three years.
US tariffs pushed the EU and Indonesia closer as they negotiated a trade deal, Indonesia's economy minister told Euronews in an exclusive interview.
Airlangga Hartarto expects the deal, signed in Brussels on Saturday after a decade of talks, to lift trade between the two sides by 50% within three years.
Asked whether US President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs had helped bring the talks to a close, Hartarto said: "I think there is an impact of the parallel negotiation with the US". Jakarta has been negotiating tariffs with Washington alongside its talks with Brussels.
The EU and Indonesia struck a political agreement in July 2025, two days before Trump announced a deal setting a 19% US tariff on Indonesian goods. On Wednesday, Washington proposed new tariffs on some goods from 14 trading partners, including the EU and Indonesia.
EU-Indonesia goods trade was worth €28.9 billion last year, according to the European Council. The minister said the 50% goal had been discussed with EU partners and business groups from both sides.
He called the two economies "not competing but compatible", since they make different products and can meet each other's needs.
Investor confidence
Hartarto also played down a downgrade warning from MSCI, whose stock indices are tracked by funds worldwide.
In October, the index provider proposed downgrading Indonesia from "emerging" to "standalone" status, which would remove Indonesian shares from its emerging markets indices. It plans to decide by the end of June 2027.
Jakarta's benchmark stock index, the IDX Composite, has fallen roughly 38% this year.
The minister likened the warning to a broken window. "So basically this is an issue of a window that is broken by somebody, right?" he said.
Asked whether he meant that everything looks broken to investors through that window, he agreed and said Indonesia's economy was in better shape than the MSCI warning suggested.
He described Indonesia's growth as "one of the highest" in the G20. The economy grew 5.45% in the first nine months of 2026 from a year earlier, according to Statistics Indonesia, the national statistics agency.
Jakarta is reforming its capital market to improve transparency, he added.
Hartarto also said next week's New Asia Forum, an investment conference in Bali, could yield deals worth up to $30 billion (€27.4bn). "I think the potential of $30 billion is there," he told Euronews.
That figure is the forum's target for the whole region. Danantara, the Indonesian sovereign wealth fund backing the forum, expects that about 40% to 50% will go to Indonesia.
Indonesia plans more of these events to promote investment, including one with the EU that the minister has discussed with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.
Chip ambitions
Mathias Cormann, Secretary-General of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), launched two reports in Jakarta this week as Indonesia aims to join the Paris-based group of mostly wealthy economies by 2028.
According to the minister, one report looks at how Indonesia can benefit from the digital economy by developing semiconductors. The other, the OECD's latest economic survey, found Indonesia would need growth averaging 5.8% a year for 20 years to become a high-income country by 2045.
On current productivity trends, though, growth would slow to about 3.5%, the OECD warned. The minister said the 5.8% figure was in line with the government's plans, in which chips play a big part.
"Indonesia has already made a contract with Arm," he told Euronews as an example of the moves the country is making to become a bigger player in the global AI economy.
Danantara signed a framework agreement with the British chip designer in London back in February.
Through the agreement, Indonesia is training up to 15,000 engineers in AI and semiconductors and will acquire six pieces of chip-design intellectual property, the minister said.
Year-end deadlines
Indonesian exporters face two deadlines at the turn of the year.
From 30 December, the EU's twice-delayed deforestation regulation (EUDR) will require large and medium-sized companies to prove that palm oil, coffee, cocoa, rubber and other goods they sell in the EU were not produced on land deforested after 2020.
According to the minister, the rules were discussed separately from the trade deal.
Indonesia is ready to comply, he said, but has asked for schemes such as its own national Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil (ISPO) certification to count towards compliance. That request is still being discussed, he added.
On 1 January, Indonesia also leaves the Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP), under which the EU cuts tariffs for developing countries. Exports that currently benefit from the scheme will then face standard EU duties until the trade deal applies.
Hartarto is confident the agreement will be in place in time. He said it was being brought to the European Parliament "so that on the first of January next year it will be implemented".
Indonesia's embassy in Brussels has been in contact with several MEPs, who have given strong support, according to the minister.
The Parliament's legislative tracker lists 14 December, the first day of its last plenary session of the year, as a provisional date for its vote. The file is still at the preparatory stage, and the Parliament said on signing day that the exact timeline had not yet been agreed. MEPs cannot amend the deal, only approve or reject it.
Once both sides have completed their internal procedures, the deal will apply provisionally, likely in early 2027, according to the European Commission.

noticias.titulo: 'Colourful and complicated': New London Museum promises to show city in all its glory
noticias.resumen: After a a decade-long transformation costing more than €500 million, London Museum reopens its doors this weekend at the former Victorian General Market at Smithfield and it's billing itself as the world's largest city museum.
noticias.texto:
After a a decade-long transformation costing more than €500 million, London Museum reopens its doors this weekend at the former Victorian General Market at Smithfield and it's billing itself as the world's largest city museum.
During the long and often torturous process of refurbishing the once derelict Smithfield meat market, the London Museum director Sharon Ament said her intention was to create a building that represented the city in all it's "colourful and complicated glory."
Her vision of the British capital's past is now ready for the public to render its verdict.
For starters, the €532 million building replaces the poorly located Museum of London which closed in 2002. The new version is much easier to find and reach by public transport. In fact, visitors to the historic site can even see passing trains, as it allows free and largely unfettered access to people living and working around the building.
"It has lots of entrances so unlike many museums, there are few barriers to getting in and out. And even if people just flow through the museum on their way to work, that is good enough for me," Ament says.
Moving an established museum to a new location was no small undertaking, but the attraction of Smithfield proved difficult to resist, according to Ament: "Museum leaders don't really think about moving a museum. It's not for the faint hearted, I would say, but the compelling attraction of Smithfield Market... You know, I could see its potential as a forum museum and to be a really great museum."
Past Time paradise
The museum draws on a collection of around seven million objects gathered from across London's boroughs, telling the story of the capital and its inhabitants across thousands of years.
Billing itself as the world's largest city museum, it features diverse items ranging from Roman mosaics, the swimming trunks of London Olympic hero Tom Daely, a bagel filled with barbecued pork, and a sewer-clogging chunk of fat.
The redevelopment has also restored Smithfield's historic General Market, preserving its sweeping dome, decorative ironwork and vaulted brick cellars while creating a new exhibition space.
The former meat market's architecture has also helped shape the museum's new approach. Its large trading floor and extensive underground spaces offer opportunities to bring London's history to life in different ways.
"So we found that a market makes a brilliant museum. It's made for public to come in and out, it's got deep basements, and then it's set in this historic area. So it's enabled us to tell the story of that area as well," explains Ament.
Ament's ambitions for the new museum extend beyond traditional expectations. She plans to use the now all too commonplace immersive projections and spatial sound to bring Roman London to life in its underground vaults. But, Ament also wants the new building to become a lively social space, with cultural events, storytelling activities and late-night openings featuring DJs on Friday and Saturday nights.
For Ament, it's crucial that museums today respond to changing expectations and become places where people can gather. "We've learnt that people need places to gather. We've learned that history is not something to be frightened of. And, you know, sometimes it's tough and sometimes it's glorious. Let's talk about that balance."
The permanent galleries will be free to enter, allowing visitors to explore London's history without paying an admission fee.
London Museum opens on 28 November, with further exhibition and learning spaces planned as part of a second phase of redevelopment in 2028.

noticias.titulo: A green valley with a circular twist: Austria´s shapes the sustainable tech of tomorrow
noticias.resumen: Austria´s Green Tech Valley Cluster hosts 300 companies — including 20 global tech leaders — shaping the innovative and circular technologies of the future. They are developing solutions in sectors like hydropower, solar thermal, wind, recycling, batteries or electro-mobility — all made in Europe.
noticias.texto:
Austria´s Green Tech Valley Cluster hosts 300 companies — including 20 global tech leaders — shaping the innovative and circular technologies of the future. They are developing solutions in sectors like hydropower, solar thermal, wind, recycling, batteries or electro-mobility — all made in Europe.
In southern Austria lies the nerve centre of a world-leading green technology provider.
Here and across 280 locations over 80 countries, 30,000 employees are developing new solutions for renewable energies — especially hydropower, but also in the pulp and paper, metal and energy storage sectors.
The company claims to be a key global actor in the green transition, helping industries worldwide to enhance efficiency, reduce waste, and minimise emissions.
We were granted special access to their manufacturing facilities — and an equally rare interview with their CEO, Dr. Joachim Schönbeck.
“We have a responsibility to develop the technologies we can because that is what we can provide to society”, he told us. “But our target is to make it economically viable, because we learned that if it's too costly, nobody can afford it; it will not fly. So that's where we see our part”.
The group´s latest available annual revenue hovered around €8 billion — and growing.
“The roadmap is definitely this drive to electricity”, Mr Schönbeck said. “So we have the renewable energy. We have the extension of the grids that will come. We will see much more applications into electrical motors, into batteries, into transformers. And this is where we all can supply technology into. We have about almost 40% of our revenue that is related to that area and we see that growing”.
Not far from there, we visit another big European actor in green solutions.
With 4,000 employees and active in 9 countries, Saubermacher AG company recycles all sorts of residues from 40,000 clients in 1,600 municipalities.
At its Graz site alone, around 10,000 tonnes of used textiles are recycled every year — currently manually, but soon, also automatically, according to CEO Andreas Opelt.
“Currently, just 1% of the textiles worldwide are recycled, and so the technology for textile recycling is not as advanced and upscaled as it should be”, Mr. Opelt says. “30 years ago, we started with plastic recycling, also in the similar stage that we started with manual sorting. Then we created our first pilot plants, and we have also our first pilot plant being set up here. And I'm sure in two, three years, we will have big plants fully automated, doing the job at a big scale because we want to reach much more than this 1% of recycling, but a degree that is really sustainable.”
A huge global provider of green technologies. A big European name in the recycling sector. What do they have in common?
They are both members of a green technology cluster headquartered at the futuristic Science Tower in Graz, a 60-meter-tall architectural and technological landmark in the city's Smart City district.
Under a strict public-private partnership, the Green Tech Valley Cluster gathers 300 companies shaping the innovative green and circular technologies of tomorrow.
This includes 20 global tech leaders, as well as many medium-sized companies and start-ups, all developing technical solutions in sectors like hydropower, solar thermal, wind, recycling, batteries, energy storage, charging devices or electromobility, explains Bernhard Puttinger, the cluster’s CEO.
“We see, of course, at the European Union, we have high wages, high energy costs, but we are very pioneers in these technologies, and we see, of course, that global competition sometimes is not a level playing field”, he acknowledges. “But to overcome these challenges, innovation and new ways of collaboration are the answer and this is what we as a cluster try to foster.”
The cluster claims that one seventh of the world's green electricity production is done through technologies developed by its members.
“It's about their needs, the opportunities they see. We bring together their joint strategies, their future business opportunities, and with that we start projects and programmes to initiate joint future projects”, Mr Bernhard tells us while driving around Graz. “At the end of the day, our key performance indicator is how many innovation projects have been started on an industrial level. Within the last five years, a quarter of a billion euro R&D investment budget was initiated starting from ideas from the cluster. So, we see there's a good impact from our side.”
A short tour around the region takes us to one of the clusters´ key members, a company combining tradition with engineering and innovative research to develop and mass-produce wood hybrids that replace classic materials for industry, mobility or logistics.
Aiming to increase its innovation drive, the company has heavily invested in a state-of-the-art research facility called Wood Vision Lab, due to begin operating by 2027.
“On the one hand, wood is a millennia-old raw material of mankind. But on the other hand, thanks to the digital twin (technology) that we have built, we can calculate and design it in such a way that we can really use it for current and future high-tech applications”, Martin F. Karner, CEO at Weitzer Woodsolutions, says. “In principle, it is about using the digital twin on really lightweight components; to maximize the advantages of wood as a raw material in the product component.”
The Green Tech Valley Cluster also hosts 2,300 specialised researchers working to shape future green solutions in different fields.
Martin Sagmeister, for example, leads a team working to develop technologically sustainable solutions across the whole value chain of hydrogen — from production, to storage, to transportation.
“The main thing about hydrogen is its versatility,” explains Martin Sagmeister, Senior Researcher and Project Manager at HyCentA Research GmbH.
“So, you can use it as a chemical compound, you can use it as an energy carrier, you can store it, you can transport it, you can use it for mobility. In Europe, we are using it now — hundreds of thousands of tonnes or millions of tonnes that we already need — and we need to replace this grey hydrogen with green hydrogen. That would be our first priority.”
Meanwhile, researchers at Graz University of Technology are developing paper-based solutions to replace chemical-loaden isolation membranes in batteries or fuel cells.
“Paper was already thought to be dead in the 80s. So, everybody was thinking about the paperless office and that paper wouldn't play a role anymore in the future”, explains Stefan Spirk, Associated Professor at the Institute of Bioproducts and Paper Technology at TU Graz.
“But paper can have applications that are basically never-ending. So, we have papers, not only like in here, when we use it in a separator as a membrane, in batteries, in fuel cells, in electrolysers. [But] we also have commodity products. We have packaging applications. We are replacing plastics with more and more paper products. And that's why I think this is a very important area of research for the future of Europe.”
Spirk is also CEO at Ecolyte GmbH, a start-up exploring new industrial applications for paper materials.
The Green Tech Valley Cluster claims 600 green tech solutions developed by its members are already in the world market.

noticias.titulo: EU budget summit collapses as row over money exposes clash over Europe's strategic tasks
noticias.resumen: The EU summit on the Union's common budget for 2028-2034 has initially failed. Some want to protect established spending, others to cut costs and mainly finance new strategic tasks, warns foreign policy expert Alexander Wolf of the Hanns Seidel Foundation in Berlin.
noticias.texto:
The EU summit on the Union's common budget for 2028-2034 has initially failed. Some want to protect established spending, others to cut costs and mainly finance new strategic tasks, warns foreign policy expert Alexander Wolf of the Hanns Seidel Foundation in Berlin.
Europe wants to become more independent, competitive and secure. Yet it is precisely the tasks that are crucial to this that face the deepest cuts in the draft for the next EU budget. Behind this lies a structural problem in European politics.
The special Brussels summit on the European budget for the years 2028 to 2034 ended without agreement. On 17 December, the heads of state and government will meet again. Until then, the main question will be how much Europe is prepared to spend.
Costa wants cuts above all in new strategic priorities
The European Commission has proposed a financial framework of just under €2 trillion. Council President António Costa has reduced this to around €1.78 trillion. Germany and other net contributors still consider that too high.
More revealing than the overall figure, however, is where Costa makes the cuts. Compared with the Commission’s draft, he removes around €95.5 billion from competitiveness, prosperity and security, and around €54 billion from agriculture, cohesion and related tasks. That amounts to reductions of 16 and 5% respectively. In defence industry, security and space, the cuts are almost 30%.
Costa’s draft does foresee substantial increases for defence and competitiveness compared with the current budget. Even so, the new strategic priorities are being cut disproportionately.
The logic of national interests
Germany and other net contributors want to limit their payments and focus the budget more strongly on competitiveness and security. Poland and other cohesion countries defend the funding for their regions. France wants an ambitious European budget while also protecting its agriculture. Italy takes a sceptical view of additional European levies.
Each of these positions is understandable from a national perspective. The problem arises from how they interact.
The European financial framework requires unanimity in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament. Every government can make its approval conditional on its own interests being safeguarded. This favours spending whose benefits can be clearly attributed to individual member states.
A French president can explain to farmers which subsidies he has secured in Brussels. A Polish prime minister can point to new roads and modernised regions. But which head of government can claim the benefit of a joint European air defence system purely for his or her own country?
Joint European tasks do have political advocates. But their benefits are less easily mapped onto the national balance sheet that underpins almost every budget negotiation in the end: how much did we pay in, and how much do we get back?
Agriculture or defence? A budget for a new world
About 60% of the current European financial framework is devoted to agriculture and cohesion. Both areas serve core purposes of European integration: food security, economic development and the reduction of regional disparities.
However, Europe now has additional tasks to tackle that did not carry anything like the same weight when this budget structure was created.
Russia is threatening Europe’s security order. China has built up significant technological and industrial capacity in strategic sectors. The United States is pursuing its own economic and security interests, which do not necessarily coincide with Europes.
The conditions under which the bloc has built its prosperity in recent decades are changing fundamentally.
That cannot be addressed simply through higher national defence spending. It is equally about joint defence research, industrial production capacity, secure supply chains, cross-border energy networks, military mobility and European expertise in key technologies.
In 2024 Mario Draghi set out what would be needed: catching up the innovation gap with the United States and China, combining decarbonisation with competitiveness, and strengthening Europe’s security by reducing strategic dependencies. He put the additional private and public investment required at €750 to 800 billion a year.
This sum cannot and should not be financed solely from the European budget. However, the budget can mobilise national and private investment and make joint projects possible where individual member states cannot achieve the necessary scale on their own.
The substance is shrinking: what Europe should finance jointly
I believe the European budget should be shaped much more by its tasks. The decisive factor should be what the member states can achieve better, more efficiently or more cheaply together than alone.
Agriculture and the less developed regions of Europe still need reliability. But their shares of the budget should, with appropriate transition periods, gradually yet clearly decline in order to create more scope for joint investment in the future.
Anyone who thinks Europe can simply carry on as before is living off a substance that is steadily shrinking. A Europe that wants to become more sovereign and more independent also has to get ahead of events.
That calls for honesty on the revenue side. Costa’s draft sets aside €158 billion solely for repaying the EU debt taken on during the pandemic. This money is not available for other tasks.
Costa therefore proposes additional European sources of revenue, including levies on digital services provided by large companies, on tobacco and on non-recycled electronic waste. Anyone who rejects additional own resources has to explain whether they prefer higher national contributions or corresponding cuts. And anyone who demands more European tasks has to say how they should be funded.
The contribution rebates also belong in this context. They are the expression of a budget logic that measures the success of European policy by national returns. As long as this calculation dominates, funding joint tasks will remain structurally more difficult.
The price of an agreement: established or new tasks?
Germany and France are pushing for an understanding before the end of the year. Given the French presidential election next spring, that is understandable.
One possible compromise would be an even smaller overall volume combined with concessions to the net contributors, agriculture and the cohesion countries. Particularly contentious sources of revenue could be postponed, and funding for further aid to Ukraine could be negotiated separately.
Such an agreement would carry weight. It would create planning certainty and show that 27 governments, despite differing interests, are capable of reaching a compromise.
The crucial question, however, would be the price at which it is achieved. If the main effect is to protect established spending while once again making the new strategic tasks bear most of the savings, the underlying problem would remain.
Europe would still have to tackle many of its new tasks largely through national budgets, loans and additional financing instruments. Especially for long term investment in security, infrastructure and technological competitiveness, a lack of joint planning can lead to higher costs and avoidable duplication.
We do not have to turn all our challenges into European ones. But we should organise and fund at European level those we can no longer adequately handle at national level.
Anyone who wants a more sovereign and more independent Europe must also be prepared to draw fiscal policy conclusions from that.
