noticias.titulo: North Korea halts Russia military aid over Seoul row, Kyiv says
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's military intelligence said Kim Jong-un personally ordered the suspension after Russia's deputy foreign minister said it would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's military intelligence said Kim Jong-un personally ordered the suspension after Russia's deputy foreign minister said it would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
North Korea has suspended military assistance to Russia following a diplomatic dispute over Moscow's statements on Seoul, Ukraine's military intelligence directorate said on Wednesday, in claims neither Moscow nor Pyongyang has confirmed or denied.
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry's Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) said North Korean leader Kim Jong-un personally made the decision after Pyongyang took offence at remarks by Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko, who said in October that the Kremlin would help de-escalate tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
North Korea's Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui characterised the statements as "not consistent with the spirit of the allied agreements between the two states" and announced a temporary suspension of military support, the HUR said.
The suspension includes a ban on Russian military transport aircraft using North Korean airspace, a halt to deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and a stop to further artillery munitions shipments, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
North Korea is also holding back from fulfilling a Russian request to expand its military contingent on Russian territory from 8,500 to 50,000 troops, the HUR added.
Rudenko made no public statement in those terms, but told Russian state media on 20 October that Moscow was ready for a "normalisation of relations" with Seoul.
"We do not link our relations with any country to what is happening with Ukraine. Therefore, if our South Korean partners take any practical steps, then of course they will be welcomed on our part," he said.
On 16 November, a senior aide to Kim, Politburo Presidium member Cho Yong Won, met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, on the eve of the APEC summit.
Moscow and Pyongyang had made no official statements in response to the HUR report at the time of publication.
Putin and Kim signed a mutual defence pact in June 2024, after which North Korea became one of Russia's closest military partners in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine. Russia deployed North Korean troops in an offensive later that year against Ukrainian forces in the Russian border region of Kursk.
Russia remains heavily dependent on North Korean weapons and materiel. In exchange, Pyongyang is understood to be seeking military technology, raw materials and financial assistance, as well as operational experience from Russia's war in Ukraine.
North Korea's army numbers more than 1 million personnel, making it one of the largest in the world.

noticias.titulo: No burqas at school and fewer foreign pupils: Italy passes controversial education law
noticias.resumen: The school decree, which includes new rules on digital transition, was finally approved in the Chamber on Thursday. During the vote, opposition MPs displayed signs saying "At school no one is a foreigner".
noticias.texto:
The school decree, which includes new rules on digital transition, was finally approved in the Chamber on Thursday. During the vote, opposition MPs displayed signs saying "At school no one is a foreigner".
Italy has approved a controversial education reform introducing a ban on face coverings in schools and a 30% cap on students of foreign origin in first-year classes, prompting accusations of discrimination from opposition parties.
The cap will not apply to students who have already achieved an adequate knowledge of the Italian language, while the ban on face coverings will prevent Muslim female students from wearing burqas and niqabs in class.
The legislation also introduces Italian language courses for foreign parents.
The Chamber of Deputies gave its final approval to the Decreto Scuola with 142 votes in favour, 112 against and four abstentions, following its approval by the Senate on 20 November.
Decree-law 170 of 30 September 2026, which introduces urgent provisions to ensure the regular start of the 2026/2027 school year, support measures under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and promote the integration of foreign students, had already secured the government's confidence.
The final vote was marked by protests from opposition MPs, who displayed a sign in the chamber reading "At school nobody is a foreigner".
Opposition accuses government of discrimination
Opposition parties sharply criticised the new restrictions, accusing the government of failing to address the real challenges facing Italy's education system.
"The problem is not how many foreign children there are in a class, but how many teachers and what tools we provide to guarantee everyone the right to learn. Everything else is discrimination and racism," Five Star Movement (M5S) MP Antonio Caso said.
"Alessandro Ingusci died because of indifference, while he was asserting the right to study and to housing. And this should be the real urgency for a government that issues decrees to address emergencies in schools. Yet this decree does not tackle any of the real urgent issues: not the safety of school buildings, not the low salaries of teachers, not the right to study," he added.
Irene Manzi, the Democratic Party's national head for schools and leader of its group on the education committee, also condemned the measures.
"A decree that divides girls and boys within classes and moves them from one school to another if the 30 per cent limit is exceeded, ignoring their stories, the contexts in which they live, the environment in which they grow up. It treats them like parcels," Manzi said.
"And it adds sanctions for parents and reports from educational institutions such as the CPIA, breaking that climate of trust on which the educational community should be based. As if foreign families had fewer rights."
"What has been approved is a decree without vision," she added.
Meanwhile, the governing majority expressed "maximum satisfaction" with the final approval of the legislation.
"Today's vote is also a significant show of unity of the majority around our government and its reforming action," Minister for Education and Merit Giuseppe Valditara said in a statement.
Digital textbooks divide governing coalition
Despite the controversy surrounding restrictions on foreign pupils, the fiercest clash between the majority and the opposition concerned a provision on school and university e-books, which also divided the governing centre-right coalition.
Under the new legislation, publishers of school and university textbooks will be required to offer digital versions of their publications at 50% of the price of their printed equivalents.
The measure aims to make educational materials more accessible and ease the financial burden on families.
However, the Italian Publishers Association (AIE) expressed strong opposition to the provision.
"Our deep opposition remains unchanged to a measure that does not bring real economic benefits to families and students but places on educational and academic publishing the burden of a support policy that should be a public responsibility," AIE President Innocenzo Cipolletta said.
"A provision that is not consistent with the results of countless international scientific studies, that interferes with copyright, opens the door to piracy, alters the economic value of the work, puts at risk the sustainability and jobs of companies and ultimately undermines the cultural value of books in the educational path."
Within the governing coalition, Forza Italia opposed the measure on e-books, while Brothers of Italy (Fratelli d'Italia) supported it. The majority subsequently closed ranks for the final vote.
Rosaria Tassinari, Forza Italia's group leader on the Culture Committee, welcomed the final approval of the decree.
"Forza Italia has expressed a clear and consistent position, opening a debate that led to the agenda item signed within the majority, which represents a point of balance between the different sensitivities that emerged," she said.
What else does the new school law introduce?
The legislation also introduces changes to teacher recruitment, including permanent appointments, and modifies specialisation pathways for support teachers.
It updates the timing and procedures for drafting Individual Education Plans and introduces additional funding for administrative, technical and auxiliary staff, as well as for the fund aimed at improving educational provision.

noticias.titulo: France's government faces mounting pressure from both sides of the barricades
noticias.resumen: Exhausted by weeks of street protests, French police officers are demanding better pay, more resources and greater protection. Meanwhile, students and trade unions are determined to maintain their mobilisation, despite what they deem as a strategy of repression aimed at stifling the movement.
noticias.texto:
Exhausted by weeks of street protests, French police officers are demanding better pay, more resources and greater protection. Meanwhile, students and trade unions are determined to maintain their mobilisation, despite what they deem as a strategy of repression aimed at stifling the movement.
Wrapped up against the November cold, several dozen men and women stand outside the police station in Paris's 12th arrondissement, blowing into their hands to keep warm. At a signal from their union representatives, the blue and white flags of the Alliance police union are raised in front of the cameras.
Legally barred from striking, these police officers were protesting during their break, as part of a nationwide mobilisation called by their main unions Alliance, Un1té and UNSA-Police.
Axhausted by weeks of successive demonstrations, police representatives call the government to urgently address longstanding grievances.
Police officers at breaking point
“We're demanding that our risk allowance be raised to 35%. It's currently at 28.5% and has been since 2019. It's non-negotiable.” Yannick Landreau, Paris regional representative of the Alliance police union, told Euronews.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, has offered to gradually raise the allowance to 33.5% of their basic salary by 2029.
Too late, and too little, say the unions, demanding immediate action
“More and more of our colleagues are being injured,” Landreau said. « In just the first seven days of the protests in Paris, we recorded 50 instances of injured colleagues per day. The reality now is that mortar rounds are being fired directly at law enforcement » said Landreau.
Intervention units, he said, still lack fire-resistant uniforms, while officers drafted in from local police stations to reinforce crowd-control operations do not always have adequate protective equipment.
Citing a toll of more than 2,600 injured officers, Landreau also pointed to the cancellation of leave and rest periods.
“My colleagues are exhausted and they're hurt in their flesh,” he said. “At some point, this will have to stop. Because we don't know how much longer we'll be able to ensure people's safety.”
The extent of the discontent became apparent last week when some 1,200 members of France's CRS riot police reportedly called in sick on a single day of protests, according to an internal police count.
Officers have complained of shifts lasting up to 15 hours and prolonged periods away from their families.
A decade of successive crises
The current unrest has compounded grievances that have been building for years.
From the 2015 terrorist attacks and the prolonged Yellow Vest protests of 2018 and 2019 to successive waves of social unrest, French police forces have been repeatedly mobilised on a large scale.
“Never any respite. But we've never given up,” said Landreau.
France relies on approximately 150,000 national police officers and 100,000 gendarmes, whose duties range from everyday policing and maintaining public order to criminal investigations and counterterrorism
Newly qualified police officers earn around €2,160 net a month, rising to approximately €2,340 in the Paris region, according to the National Police's official pay scale.
Discontent extends beyond frontline policing.
« We signed an agreement in 2022, and it hasn't even been fully implemented,” Georges Knecht, secretary general of SNIPAT, a union representing administrative, technical and scientific personnel at France's Interior Ministry, told Euronews.
“Some staff are now earning below the minimum wage and need a compensatory allowance just to reach it. This cannot go on.”
According to Knecht, administrative, technical and scientific personnel account for around 15% of police staff in France, compared with 25 to 30% in most European police forces.
He pointed in particular to the shortage of forensic police personnel, numbering just 3,300 nationwide, despite their increasingly important role in criminal investigations.
“We've moved from a culture of confession to a culture of evidence,” he said. “From minor burglaries to terrorist attacks, they're the ones on the front line.”
Knecht also warned that the lack of professional status for forensic personnel was prompting staff to seek transfers to other government departments.
“We feel we're being put off, that they're playing for time until the next elections.”
France's controversial approach to policing protests
While police officers are demanding greater protection, the methods used to police demonstrations have come under renewed scrutiny..
The use of rubber-ball launchers and explosive crowd-control grenades in France has long drawn criticism from human rights organisations, particularly since the Yellow Vest protests, during which a number of demonstrators suffered life-changing injuries.
The latest protests have reignited the debate over the proportionality of police responses and the right to demonstrate, further fuelled by Parliament's approval last Friday of controversial legislation presuming the lawful use of firearms by police officers and gendarmes unless proven otherwise.
Denounced by critics as a “licence to kill”, by opposition MPs, the legislation has been challenged before France's Constitutional Council.
In an opinion issued on 5 November, the human rights office of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) also warned that the measure could undermine the effectiveness of judicial investigations, victims' access to justice and the protection of the right to life, urging France to reconsider its adoption.
Students vow to keep protesting, accusing government of repression
Barely an hour after police officers had ended their rally on thursday, students and trade unionists started marching from Bastille towards Nation in eastern Paris, vowing to continue their mobilisation, and chanting slogans denouncing police violence.
“The government is trying to wear down the movement. It's closing high schools and universities,” Mathis Aversenq, a member of the student coordination Interfac Île-de-France, and of the far left NPA-Révolutionnaires party told Euronews, citing the deployment of gendarmes to monitor high school students in Nancy and the use of tear gas at a high school in Nantes.
“They're hoping the mobilisation will end through repression alone. But the movement is continuing, with general assemblies bringing together hundreds of high school students.”
Coppélia Moreau, also member of the Interfac mobilisation committee, and president of the UNEF student union Paris Nanterre University branch slammed what she described as an unprecedented police presence in universities, the heavy armament of police officers and police violence during demonstrations.
“Why is the government doing this? To evade its own responsibilities, which means responding to our demands,” she said.
Students' demands include increased university capacity, the recruitment of teaching staff, improved educational facilities and learning conditions, higher student grants and an end to selective university admissions.
In late October, the government announced a series of concessions, including €4 billion in low-interest loans to regional authorities to renovate school buildings and €1 billion for university infrastructure by 2029.
It has since reportedly increased the number of additional places promised in higher education from 15,000 to 20,000, pledged to replace the controversial Parcoursup university admissions platform by 2028 and announced that student grants would be adjusted in line with inflation.
But student organisations want the immediate scrapping of Parcoursup and Mon Master, the national admissions platform for master's degree programmes, and a much more substantial increase in higher education admission capacities.
“We know the money is there to create university places and renovate high schools,” said Aversenq. “But the government is throwing crumbs in our faces along with its tear gas.”
As long as we don’t get a response to our demands, namely, the immediate end of the Parcoursup system and the creation of 300,000 additional places in higher education, we will continue our mobilisation. »
Seeking to broaden the movement
With university exams approaching and turnout at demonstrations declining, the ability of student organisations to sustain their mobilisation is being put to the test.
But student activists rejects claims that the movement is running out of steam.
“Despite all the measures taken by the government to cause the movement to lose steam, including orders banning demonstrations, gatherings, general assemblies, and meetings of high school students in front of their schools, there has been no return to normal. » said Coppelia Moreau.
Inter-university assemblies are continuing to coordinate actions, while student activists are seeking to broaden their movement by linking their demands to those of workers and trade unions.
“We want funding. Not for war, but for schools, high schools and universities. And we want higher wages, because we cannot accept workers being paid €1,400 a month, which isn't even enough to live on. So, we will continue the mobilisation, and we will organise ourselves to amplify it. »
The next major test of the movement's momentum will come on Tuesday, 1 December, with another day of nationwide strikes and demonstrations.
“We're calling on the whole of society to join us because we know that together, we can force this government to back down and even give in.” said Aversenq.
Social discontent shows little sign of subsiding at a time when the government is struggling to reduce France's budget deficit. Reconciling fiscal constraints with mounting social demands is becoming an increasingly difficult political balancing act as France heads into the election year.

noticias.titulo: EU budget row: Macron accuses Le Pen of 'strange arrogance'
noticias.resumen: The RN presidential candidate accuses the European Commission of seeking to "rush" adoption of the next EU budget before the 2027 French election.
noticias.texto:
The RN presidential candidate accuses the European Commission of seeking to "rush" adoption of the next EU budget before the 2027 French election.
Talks over the EU budget have sparked a new clash between Emmanuel Macron and Marine Le Pen.
The National Rally candidate accuses the European Commission of trying to hurry through an agreement on the next multiannual EU budget before the French presidential election. She says this strategy is intended to prevent "the democratic expression of the French people".
Emmanuel Macron did not appreciate the remark, recalling that he "was elected until 13 May 2027" and therefore "remains president until 13 May 2027".
The head of state retorted during a press conference in Brussels on Monday: "It is a strange kind of arrogance to think that she is already in charge of France's destiny. Because, until proven otherwise, she has not been elected".
The 27 member states are struggling to reach agreement on the Union's next budget, after most EU countries rejected the Commission's initial proposal, set at €2,000 billion.
The President of the European Council, António Costa, has tried to ease divisions by cutting the budget by €204 billion, but the latest negotiations in Brussels have produced no decisive breakthrough.
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is insisting in particular that aid to Ukraine should be guaranteed by all 27 EU countries, even as funding for Kyiv faces growing opposition across Europe.
European Union leaders will meet again on 17 December, a last chance to reach an agreement before the end of the year.

noticias.titulo: We’d be ‘stupid’ not to: Poland defends $300M military AI deal with Palantir
noticias.resumen: Poland's defense minister said it would be “wrong” not to use the software, despite concerns over reliance on American technology.
noticias.texto: Poland signed a five-year deal worth around $300 million with U.S. tech giant Palantir on Friday to expand the use of artificial intelligence across its armed forces. Warsaw’s decision to adopt Palantir’s Maven system, already used by Ukraine and NATO, comes as European militaries grapple with how to strengthen their defenses against Russia while reducing their reliance on American technology. “It would be stupid and wrong not to use it,” Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told reporters, crediting Palantir’s technology with helping Ukraine withstand more than four years of fighting Russia. Maven uses AI to analyze military data, supporting everything from logistics to the identification of battlefield targets. Palantir celebrated the deal on X, calling Maven “the vanguard of next-generation AI warfare” and saying it was proud to stand with Poland in defending a “sovereign Europe.” The company, which has drawn criticism for its work with U.S. immigration authorities and the Israeli military, faced protests in Warsaw earlier this month over concerns about data security and technological independence. “All the keys, servers and information are — and will remain — exclusively in the possession of the Polish Armed Forces,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said. Defense authorities in Denmark, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden already use Palantir software , though not all use Maven. Some are seeking to reduce that dependence. The Dutch military said in late October it wanted a European alternative by 2028, while France and Germany agreed in July to explore developing their own defense software. Kosiniak-Kamysz said he would have chosen a Polish supplier had one offered comparable technology, suggesting Poland could develop its own alternative by the time the contract expires.

noticias.titulo: Meta’s UK rollout for Muse AI agent exposes it to more liability
noticias.resumen: The U.K. terms of service for Muse give consumers far more protection than in the U.S.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Meta will be on the hook for more of Muse’s mistakes in the U.K. than in the U.S., according to a comparison of the AI agent’s fine print in both countries by POLITICO. Following conversations with regulators, Muse’s terms of service give British consumers more scope to seek redress if the personal AI agent makes mistakes compared with users in the U.S. The findings indicate the tech giant was willing to commit to meeting higher liability standards to gain access to the U.K. market, and show that tech companies and users will face different liability and consumer law rules as personal AI agents roll out globally. Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators. The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law. Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.” The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval. The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.” They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.” In the U.K. there is no financial cap and a narrower list of exceptions to Meta’s liability applies only where the company has “acted with reasonable skill and care / professional diligence.” Under U.K. consumer law, this standard is automatically implied into contracts for services between a business and a consumer. How U.K. consumers would fare in practice when seeking redress for any problems caused by personal AI agents is yet to be tested in court. Since its debut in the U.S., Meta staffers have reportedly raised concerns internally about “undesired actions” by the agent, from accessing encrypted messages to supplying bogus information about purchases. (A Meta spokesperson said these were “isolated incidents.”) The CMA said it expects Muse to be the first of many personal AI agents to come to the U.K. and has invited users to report any issues they experience with personal AI agents. Other British regulators are also watching closely. The Financial Conduct Authority said in a statement that as AI agents become capable of making transactions, payments and investment decisions, companies developing and deploying them “must understand which activities require authorisation and where regulatory requirements may apply.” It also highlighted that a broad Consumer Duty could also apply to regulated firms’ use of AI agents, and that all companies must decide carefully whether they should accept payments initiated by an agent. As well as contract law, consumer law, negligence and sector-specific regulation, users of AI agents may soon also be able to seek redress through product liability laws. The Law Commission is reviewing the U.K.’s product liability laws and has proposed extending the definition to software, including AI. Doing so could make firms developing or deploying AI agents strictly liable for certain types of harm they cause.

noticias.resumen: Severe storms battered the US East Coast on Thursday, bringing torrential rain, strong winds and coastal flooding. Nearly one million homes were left without power, while hundreds of flights were cancelled and thousands delayed during one of the country's busiest travel periods. The weather also forced the postponement of New York's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday.

noticias.titulo: Airlines bankroll travel influencers — and normalise a high‑carbon lifestyle for Europeans
noticias.resumen: Influencers can sell a glamorised lifestyle without it looking like an ad, and consumers are fooled. Though airlines get the win, the effects of over-tourism, climate deterioration, and basic legal transparency are increasingly difficult to ignore.
noticias.texto: Travel influencers are selling a glamourised lifestyle to consumers without sufficient transparency or control – and with a dire price tag for the climate. A report by Berlin-based T3 Transportation think tank on Thursday (26 November) shows that constant posting of photogenic locations shapes consumers’ destination preferences, inciting long-distance flying, fuelling air travel demand, accelerating over-tourism, and contributing to climate change. Airlines’ PR strategies have increasingly relied on the so-called ‘disguised advertiser ‘. That means aspirational trip content posted by online creators creeps into online feeds more smoothly than traditional advertising – and seem to pull in a significant audience. In concrete numbers, content creators take an average of 16 flights per year, visiting four times as many destinations and generating a climate impact 16.7 times higher than the average European’s four leisure round trips a year – “creating and normalising a desire for frequent, long-haul flying,” said Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, aviation campaigner at advocacy group European Federation for Transport and Environment. Read more Social media influencers now roam EU corridors of power: free trips, selfies with leaders but a grey zone for ethics “However, influencer posts often fail to disclose that they are paid promotions by airlines,” Rodrigues Akhtar told EUobserver. The report estimated that about one-third of digital advertising budget in airlines is spent on social media in 2025, with low-cost flyer Easyjet leading the charts at €10m. “Consumers often do not realise that they are being targeted by marketing and rarely given a balanced picture of the environmental cost,” said the European consumer organisation’s ( BEUC ) head of consumer rights, Patrycja Gautier. noticias.titulo: Swedish Gripen jets with Meteor missiles will arrive in Ukraine in January, posing the first serious threat to Russian aviation (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,737)
noticias.resumen: A war that has already emptied towns like Avdiivka and sent villagers herding cows to safety may be on the verge of its most dramatic shift yet.
noticias.texto: Why the new weapon is a threat, especially to the Su-34. What the Su-34 means for the Russian air force. Komar is already under Ukrainian control; the attack on Velyka Novosilka continues. Russia has spent €206bn on weapons and ammunition alone since the start of the invasion. Ukraine could lose almost €9bn a year as a result of the blockade of Black Sea ports. How Russia is destroying Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Maps of the day — the distribution of attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure from August to October; Komar and the Velyka Novosilka direction. Videos of the day — Avdiivka three years after its “liberation” by the Russians; a Ukrainian soldier saw his children after four months; rural residents rescue their livestock. Why the new weapon is a threat, especially to the Su-34. “A manoeuvrable fighter. We have flown against such aircraft over the Baltic Sea. Under current conditions, most of them will be destroyed on the ground,” Russian pilot Ilya Tumanov (Fighterbomber) wrote tersely and confidently in May, when it was confirmed that Ukraine would receive 16 Gripen C/D fighter jets from Sweden. The Czech and Hungarian air forces operate the same version. Sweden is gradually switching to the E/F version, which Ukrainians are also expected to receive by the end of the decade. Tumanov’s assessment was wrong, first because Russia has not destroyed a single F-16 or Mirage 2000 on the ground to date — or at least nothing of the sort is known. If Russia had proof, it would immediately have publicised it. There is therefore no reason to assume that the situation will be dramatically different with the Gripens. The second problem with his argument is that while Gripens are indeed agile aircraft, their greatest significance for the course of the air war will probably lie in the fact that Meteor air-to-air missiles will arrive on the battlefield with them. This has now been definitively confirmed. The Ukrainian president announced first that the first Gripens would arrive in January, or February at the latest. Pilots and ground personnel have been in Sweden at least since May . The aircraft will arrive with a substantial arsenal of various air-to-air missiles. But the Meteors are the most interesting. In July, Sweden’s defence minister confirmed that Ukraine had permission to use them against targets over Russian territory. Then, on 17 November, an agreement on equipment to be provided for the Gripens was signed in Brussels, with the Meteors a key part of it. This is the most important weapon Western allies have supplied to Ukraine since the arrival of HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems and British-French Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG missiles. noticias.titulo: Why isn’t European TV drama responding to the threat of war?
noticias.resumen: The possibility of nuclear war in Europe is openly discussed. Studios and broadcasters can treat these threats as too bleak, too political, or too hard to sell. Or they can recognise that loyalty, power, fear, and responsibility to our children are the oldest dramatic subjects, and that they have never mattered more.
noticias.texto: After more than 40 years producing film and television, as I watch the evening news with warnings of an imminent threat of war, rising death tolls in Russia and Ukraine, and ongoing missile strikes in the Middle East, I find myself asking why so little of our drama addresses these existential threats that dominate our airwaves. This is at a time when warnings of the next blitzkrieg bombard us daily while our leaders seem to ‘whistle past the graveyard’ (an English saying for being complacent in the face of death.) We have some wonderful entertainment, exceptional writers and actors, and more ways to watch their work than any previous generation. There is some fine drama about social injustice and the pressures of daily life. But across our broadcasters and the global platforms, there is remarkably little sustained exploration of the crises that will shape our children’s future. Audiences are not indifferent. A 2026 Eurobarometer survey found that 72 percent of EU citizens are highly worried about active conflicts and wars near Europe’s borders, and more than two-thirds believe their own country is under threat. Read more Nuclear weapons – the elephant in the room in Ukraine peace talks These are the circumstances in which our viewers live. Journalism establishes the facts, investigates wrongdoing, and holds power to account, sometimes at the cost of journalists’ lives. Drama completes that work. It can take us inside a family, a workplace, or a negotiating room, and expose the distance between what people say they believe and what they do when those beliefs become costly. And it can imagine where they might lead, bringing consequences into view before they become tomorrow’s news. Proud history of TV dramas British television once did this superbly. Cathy Come Home brought homelessness into the living room through one young family’s disintegration. Boys from the Blackstuff explored unemployment through the dignity, humour, and despair of men whose working lives had collapsed. In 1984, Threads imagined nuclear war through its consequences for Sheffield, asking what the language of deterrence would mean for ordinary streets, hospitals, and families. Its terror came from recognising the world being destroyed. That same year, Edgar Reitz’s landmark German series Heimat proved just how powerfully this kind of storytelling can resonate across borders. Following the quiet village of Schabbach as it was gradually seduced into fascism and war through the promise of economic progress, the series became a huge critical and popular success – showing millions of viewers how ordinary neighbours slowly normalise and comply with an approaching catastrophe. That tradition was never easy: the BBC withheld The War Game , its own film about a nuclear attack, from television for 20 years. Nor has ambition disappeared. ITV’s Mr Bates vs the Post Office drew an average audience of 14 million, turning years of journalism into a national reckoning. Netflix’s Adolescence won eight Emmys; Chernobyl , HBO and Sky’s drama of institutional lies and nuclear disaster, won 10. The producers behind Adolescence have now acquired the rights to a new adaptation of Threads. Chernobyl – the HBO TV mini series of 2019 That is welcome, but one project cannot answer the wider question. Our public service broadcasters air hundreds of hours of new British drama every year. Surely there is room within it for a sustained commitment to the threats that hang over us all. The obstacles are real. Broadcasters face falling revenues and fierce competition from global platforms. A story that matters profoundly to domestic viewers can struggle to raise money across many markets. Even Mr Bates, sold to 12 overseas broadcasters, had reportedly lost ITV around £1m [€1.2m] by April 2024. Independent producers often have to surrender most of their rights to a major platform to get a series made, losing the returns that would fund the next ambitious project. There is no silver bullet solution, but there are pockets of progress throughout Europe. Five Nordic public broadcasters pooled their drama co-production through Nordic12, explicitly to sustain their cultures amid global competition. Joined by Germany’s ZDF, the Netherlands’ NPO and Belgium’s VRT, they now form New8, renewed in January for another three years. The UK should build similar partnerships with European and Canadian broadcasters, sharing development, financing, and access to programmes. Read more Europe is losing the algorithmic war for streaming – and that’s a policy failure Governments, which have named the creative industries a priority for growth, should help independent companies keep a stake in their own work. And the debate over the BBC’s next charter is an immediate chance to make distinctive drama about our shared uncertainties an explicit part of its purpose. But better financing only makes such drama possible; commissioners must still choose to back it. The devastation in Gaza, the conflict involving Iran and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, give our anxieties a terrible human reality. The possibility of nuclear war is openly discussed. Behind every report are families living with bereavement, displacement and fear. Studios and broadcasters can treat these threats as too bleak, too political, or too hard to sell. Or they can recognise that loyalty, power, fear, and responsibility to our children are the oldest dramatic subjects, and that they have never mattered more. Drama with purpose can entertain us, confront what we share and help us understand what this would mean for our families and friendships, and help us recognise what is at stake while there is still time to act. But to tell these stories, we must preserve an independent European industry with the ambition and courage to make them, and the determination to reflect our values.

noticias.titulo: Feijóo insta a "contestar en las urnas" los silencios de Sánchez" y promete "verdad, decencia y gestion"
noticias.texto:
Feijóo insta a "contestar en las urnas" los silencios de Sánchez" y promete "verdad, decencia y gestion"
- El PP denuncia a RTVE ante la JEC y Feijóo no acude a la entrevista electoral con Silvia Intxaurrondo
- Este viernes por la tarde cerrará la campaña con un gran mitin en Sevilla
El líder del PP y candidato a la Presidencia del Gobierno, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha elegido Barcelona y Sevilla para cerrar la campaña electoral del 29-N, con sendos actos celebrados por la mañana y por la tarde. En el primero de los actos de la jornada, en L´Hospitalet de Llobregat (Barcelona), Feijóo ha llamado a "contestar en las urnas" a los "silencios" de Pedro Sánchez sobre su gestión y sobre la "corrupción" cuando le preguntó sobre ello este jueves en el debate a cuatro.
Para Feijóo, la estrategia del candidato socialista durante el debate fue la del "avestruz", que consiste en "bajo tierra y esperar a que pase". Pero ha señalado que el "avestruz" tiene "un problema", porque aunque esconda la cabeza "todos los demás siguen viendo lo que pasa" y a este Gobierno se le han visto "todas las vergüenzas". Y ha avisado de que "todo se sabrá" y "habrá consecuencias".
Feijóo ha asegurado que acudió "tranquilo" al debate a cuatro porque fue con la "verdad" y no a "engañar" a nadie. "Yo no tengo nada que temer. Quien dice la verdad duerme bien la víspera y yo dormí bien. La tensión estaba en el otro atril", ha asegurado. Y lo ha contrastado con Pedro Sánchez, quien, en su opinión, fue solo a "defenderse a sí mismo" y "mantener su puesto", mientras él fue a "defender a la gente".
Promete "verdad, decencia y gestión"
Por ello, se ha mostrado confiado en que en esta ocasión sí que podrá llegar a la Moncloa. "Esta vez sí vamos a conseguirlo", ha clamado en un mitin ante unas 1.500 perosnas, en el que ha estado acompañado por el número uno al Congresos por esta provincia y alcalde de Badalona, Xavier García Albiol, y el presidente del PP de Cataluña, Alejandro Fernández. Además, ha prometido "verdad, decencia y gestión" si gana el próximo 29-N.
También ha garantizado que no va a "mentir". "Todas las decisiones que tomaré las tomaré por el interés general de España, no por el mío", ha sostenido.
Una vez más ha pedido el voto a todos, incluso a gente de izquierdas, a los que les ha dicho que no quiere que cambien de "ideología", solo que le ayuden a "cambiar el país".
"Me dirijo a todos: a los que quieren el cambio y aún dudan.[...] No pido que dejes de ser de izquierdas, sino que si no te gusta lo que ves, vota distinto. La decencia no es de derecha ni de izquierda, es una exigencia por encima de la ideología", ha insistido.
Es la tercera vez en esta campaña electoral que Feijóo visita Cataluña, después que diera el pistoletazo de salida en Badalona el pasado jueves 12 de noviembre, y regresara a Lleida para un acto con el sector del campo, unos días después.
En Cataluña, el próximo 29-N están en juego 48 escaños, que pueden ser cruciales para la investidura del próximo presidente del Gobierno. En las pasadas generales, el PP fue quinto, con 6 escaños, 13 menos que el PSC, que fue el ganador. Esta comunidad fue de las pocas regiones que no se pintó de azul en la cita del 23-J de 2023.
El PP denuncia a RTVE ante la JEC
El PP ha denunciado ante la Junta Electoral Central (JEC) la "falta de neutralidad informativa de RTVE" en plena campaña electoral, exigiendo el amparo urgente de dicho organismo ante a la omisión en sus informativos de hechos de evidente relevancia electoral, según fuentes 'populares'.
Entre los hechos que destacan que se han omitido está el "acoso y la intimidación a sus candidatos, así como las publicaciones de altos cargos de dicha Corporación dirigidas contra dirigentes del PP". En concreto, el PP denuncia que la "censura" de los Telediarios de TVE que "omitieron en sus ediciones el acoso" de los Jon Echeverría y Ester Muñoz en Andoain (Guipúzcoa).
RTVE Noticias sí que se hizo eco de este asunto en varias noticias publicadas durante la campaña.
En el primer sábado de campaña se contó que Jon Echevarría, no había podido celebrar su mitin en Hernani porque "una caterva de proetarras" les agredieron con "petardos, huevazos y pedradas", y fueron evacuados por la Ertzaintza.
Días después de la agresión en Hernani, el líder del PP viajó hasta Eibar (Guipúzcoa) para mostrar su apoyo al candidato 'popular' al Congreso por esta provincia, Jon Echeverría.
Además, el PP ha rechazado la entrevista electoral ofrecida por TVE en el programa de La Hora de La 1 a todos los candidatos de las formaciones con representación parlamentaria, alegando que la presentadora del programa, Silvia Intxaurrondo "ha desafiado a la Justicia", tras haber recibido un escrito de la JEC.
La periodista, por su parte, ha reprochado la ausencia del presidente del PP este viernes al inicio del programa mostrando dos sillas vacías en el set que tenían preparado para la entrevista de 30 minutos, que tenían "asignados" por la Junta Electoral Central en este espacio. Ha asegurado que su reproche no era por no ir, porque, ha dicho, "por supuesto que el señor Feijóo tiene derecho a no venir", sino porque "nunca" comunicó al programa ni a RTVE si iba a asistir o no. Y denuncia que días antes fuentes populares habían confirmado a otros medios que Feijóo sí aceptaba la invitación del programa para ser entrevistado.
Pero no es la única denuncia que ha presentado el PP ante la JEC. También ha presentado un escrito urgente denunciando las presuntas "irregularidades" y "graves incidencias" en el voto por correo y el reparto de la propaganda electoral.
El PP asegura haber recibido "numerosas quejas de electores que, habiendo solicitado el voto por correo, no han recibido la documentación o la han recibido con retraso", cuando el plazo de depósito concluyó este jueves a las 14:00 horas.
También afirman que la Junta Electoral Provincial de Madrid les informó de una denuncia de un ciudadano que encontró cientos de sobres de la propaganda electoral del PP y de otro partido en "un contenedor de residuos" de Madrid. "Ante la posible relevancia penal de estos hechos, hemos reclamado a la Junta que remita toda esta documentación a la Fiscalía", indican.
Asimimo exigen a Correos que informe a la JEC de las solicitudes de voto por correo admitidas, así como las documentaciones remitidas y entregadas, y los votos recibidos para su traslado a las Mesas de los electores temporalmente ausentes y los residentes en el extranjero. Tambien piden a Correos que "esclarezca los hechos denunciados y depure responsabilidades".
Último acto en Sevilla
Por la tarde, a partir de las 19:00 horas en el Pabellón de la Navegación de Sevilla, Feijóo cerrará su último acto de esta campaña junto al presidente de la Junta de Andalucía y del PP andaluz, Juanma Moreno, al candidato número uno al Congreso por Sevilla y vicesecretario del PP, Juan Bravo, y al alcalde de Sevilla, José Luis Sanz.
Es la primera y única vez en esta campaña electoral que el presidente del PP visita Andalucía, una región clave por el número de escaños que reparte. Es la autonomía con más diputados: 60 diputados.
En las pasadas elecciones generales, el PP fue la fuerza más votada en Andalucía, con 25 escaños -aunque entonces estaban en juego 61-, seguida del PSOE, con 21. Los 'populares' ganaron en todas las provincias, memos en Sevilla, donde les adelantaron los socialistas.

noticias.titulo: Sánchez confía en el voto de las mujeres para ganar el 29N: "La España de 2026 no tiene calladitas a las mujeres"
noticias.texto:
Sánchez confía en el voto de las mujeres para ganar el 29N: "La España de 2026 no tiene calladitas a las mujeres"
- Rechaza el recorte anunciado por Figaredo (Vox): "Llevan en su programa electoral comprarle las armas a Trump"
- El candidato socialista pisa Extremadura el último día de campaña y dice que España seguirá siendo "la aldea gala progresista en Europa"
El presidente del Gobierno y candidato del PSOE a la reelección, Pedro Sánchez, ha aprovechado la última mañana de esta campaña electoral para viajar hasta Extremadura y celebrar un mitin en Plasencia (Cáceres). Desde allí, Sánchez ha defendido los derechos de las mujeres y ha criticado abiertamente las palabras que dirigió el candidato del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, a la candidata del Frente Amplio, Ada Colau, en el debate de este jueves, cuando le espetó "y tu, calladita" tras la dana de Valencia.
Sánchez ha recogido esta frase para mostrar la "involución" que, según él, representan PP y Vox. "El problema es que quieren gobernar una España que no existe, porque la España de 2026 no tiene calladitas a las mujeres. Van a habar alto y fuerte con su voto el 29 de noviembre para frenar la involución de Feijóo y de Abascal", ha dicho ante centenares de personas y vestido con una camiseta en la que se podía leer 'La fuerza de las mujeres'.
"Lo vimos ayer, fue una vergüenza, fue lamentable ver al jefe de la oposición y del PP levantar el dedo y decir "tú calladita", ha insistido el candidato socialista. Al mismo tiempo, ha denunciado que también fue "una vergüenza el que el líder de Vox no fuera capaz de condenar la violencia de género en este país".
Para Sánchez, lo "grave en esa coalición reaccionaria de Feijóo y Abascal es que quien dice que si hay que condenar la violencia de género sea el señor Abascal y no Feijóo", ha lamentado.
Con este contexto, el presidente del Gobierno se ha erigido como la única papeleta que puede defender los derechos de las mujeres y se ha mostrado convencido de que el voto femenino "va a ser la fuerza vuelva a hacer que haya un Gobierno de coalición progresista al frente del país".
Sánchez ha vuelto a nombrar las dos cifras que tiene en mente: 75% de participación y 176 escaños. "Necesitamos más de un 75% de participación, nadie se puede quedar en casa", ha pedido. Si esto se logra, el presidente del Gobierno confía en que España siga siendo "la aldea gala progresista en Europa".
Sánchez habla de los recortes "moderados" anunciados por Figaredo (Vox)
Sánchez también se ha hecho eco de una entrevista que ha ofrecido el portavoz económico de Vox, José María Figaredo, en la que plantea un "recorte moderado" de 112.000 millones de euros de gasto público. Según Figaredo, su formación propone revisar 44.000 millones de euros en subvenciones del Gobierno central y 180.000 millones de euros en transferencias a las comunidades autónomas.
"¿Para qué quieren hacer eso? Pues porque, entre otras, cosas llevan en su programa electoral algo que nosotros dijimos que no, al 5% del presupuesto en defensa en relación con el PIB. Eso es lo que quieren hacer, que haya menos pensiones, menos educación publica para comprarle las armas a Trump en Estados Unidos", ha resumido Sánchez.
El candidato socialista a la reelección también ha evidenciado que, tras los recortes de Milei en Argentina, "todo ello ha derivado en una recesión económica y en una desigualdad desesperada".
Cierre de campaña en Madrid
Pedro Sánchez cerrará la campaña electoral este viernes por la tarde en Madrid, en un acto a partir de las 18.30 horas que se espera multitudinario en la Caja Mágica. Se esperan actuaciones musicales e intervenciones que el PSOE todavía no ha desvelado.
La campaña de los socialistas para las elecciones del 29N arrancó en Sevilla, en el Auditorio Fibes, con la presencia y la participación en el mitin de Begoña Gómez, la mujer del presidente del Gobierno.

noticias.titulo: Abascal asegura que "no le sorprende" que Europa rechace la prioridad nacional, pero avisa: "Nos presentamos para tumbar a la Comisión"
noticias.texto:
Abascal asegura que "no le sorprende" que Europa rechace la prioridad nacional, pero avisa: "Nos presentamos para tumbar a la Comisión"
- El líder de Vox reacciona a la decisión de la Comisión Europea sobre las polémicas leyes pactadas con el PP
- Abascal cierra campaña electoral este vierners en la Plaza de Toros de Valencia
De camino a su cierre de campaña en Valencia en la tarde de este viernes, el líder de Vox ha hecho un alto en el camino en Tarancón, Cuenca. Desviándose unos metros de la carretera que conecta Madrid con Valencia, Abascal ha parado para hacer una atención a medios y dar un pequeño discurso de adelanto a lo que será su gran acto de cierre. Desde Tarancón, el líder de Vox ha vuelto a defender la prioridad nacional y ha reaccionado a la decisión de la Comisión Europea de mostrarse en contra.
"No nos sorprende que la Comisión Europea haya tumbado la prioridad nacional", ha valorado al ser preguntado por ello. "Nos presentamos a estas elecciones para cambiar las leyes y tumbar a la Comisión Europea. Y vamos a conseguirlo", ha avisado.
A juicio de Abascal, "las cosas están cambiando en estos momentos en toda Europa" y "ya hay una mayoría en el parlamento que no es la de siempre, de PSOE y PP. Es la que hay entre Patriotas - grupo al que pertence Vox - y el PP. Está en manos del PP acabar con la discriminación de los europeos", ha enfatizado poniendo la presión en su posible socio del Gobierno en un futuro.
El comisario europeo de Interior, Magnus Brunner, ha señalado este viernes que la ley que aplica el concepto de la "prioridad nacional" en la Comunidad Valenciana, que prosperó con los votos a favor de PP y Vox, en el mismo sentido que lo aprobado en Castilla y León, vulnera la legislación europea al exigir más de cinco años de empadronamiento para acceder a la compra de vivienda protegida.
Antes de continuar en su camino hacia Valencia, Abascal ha pedido "el respaldo para Vox" porque solo su formación, dice, "ofrece un cambio de rumbo".
Durante su atención a medios, Abascal ha vuelto a valorar el desarrollo del debate a cuatro de este jueves. "Muy satisfecho", ha asegurado el líder de Vox. A su parecer, su mensaje "pudo llegar a diez millones de españoles" y es por eso por lo que se marcha muy positivo del último debate antes del 29N y que va a permitir "una movilización masiva".
Además, ha criticado las tácticas del presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y la candidata de Frente Amplio, Ada Colau, durante el debate. "La estratagema de Colau y Sánchez tengo que decirlo me dio bastante asco. La pregunta era muy ofensiva. Preguntar si condena violencia contra la mujer, es una ofensa. Yo quiero denunciar la traición de Sánchez a las españolas por el machismo importado", ha añadido.
